Both words mean rock, the name Jesus himself gave him (John 1:42).

And remained with him fifteen days. The length is the argument. Fifteen days is long enough for two men to talk themselves hoarse. It is nothing like long enough to train an apostle, and everyone in the ancient world knew what a rabbinic apprenticeship looked like: years, not a fortnight. A short visit, not a long training.

One would like to have been in that house. Peter had denied the Lord three times beside a charcoal fire and been restored beside another one (John 18:18; 21:9). Paul had hunted down the people Peter was pastoring. Neither man had a past he could be proud of, and both had been handled by the same mercy. Whatever else those fifteen days contained, they surely contained the eyewitness accounts: Peter describing what it was like in the boat, in the courtyard, on the shore, and a man who had never seen any of it listening to every word.

But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother. This is Jesus’ own brother, raised in the same house in Nazareth, and during the ministry he did not believe: for not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). Then his brother was killed, and then, we are told in a single line, he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). Whatever passed between them, that meeting turned an unbelieving brother into the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; 21:18) and the author of a letter that calls himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1). It takes something considerable to make a man worship the boy he grew up beside.

Was James Jesus’ full brother? The plain reading is that he was a son of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brother, since Jesus had no human father. The early church developed other views, that he was Joseph’s son by an earlier marriage or a cousin, to protect the belief that Mary remained a virgin, but the New Testament never suggests either. And Paul’s except James shows that he counted James among the apostles in a wider sense; the risen Christ had appeared to him, and he became the leading elder at Jerusalem.

Does Paul contradict Acts? Luke’s account of the same visit says Barnabas brought him to the apostles, plural, and that he went in and out among them at Jerusalem (Acts 9:27–28). Paul says he saw none of them except James. Is one of them wrong? No. Luke is summarising a visit in two verses and uses “the apostles” the way anyone uses a collective term, Peter and James being, between them, the most prominent figures of that circle and its recognised leadership. A man who met the Prime Minister and the Chancellor says he met the government. Paul, whose whole argument depends on the precise number, gives the precise number. The other apostles were probably elsewhere. The accounts are answering different questions, and both answers are true.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul avoided the other apostles or held them in contempt. It means he was not their student. When he later met them properly, they recognised the same gospel in him and gave him the right hand of fellowship (2:9).

Did Paul and Peter preach the same gospel? Yes, and Paul says so: whether it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed (1 Corinthians 15:11). The point of these verses is not that Paul had a different gospel from Peter but that he had the same gospel from the same source. Two men, one a fisherman and one a Pharisee, received it independently from the same risen Lord, and when they compared notes they found they were preaching the same Christ. That is not a weakness in the evidence. It is one of its strengths.

In a sentence. Then after three years, he went up to Jerusalem to get acquainted with Peter and stayed with him fifteen days. He saw none of the other apostles, only James, the Lord’s brother.

On a Tuesday. Look for the Christians whose stories are not yours: older believers, believers from other backgrounds, people who have walked with Christ through things you have not. Paul did not need Peter’s permission, but he went to get to know him. Ask someone this month to tell you how they came to Christ and what he has been to them since, and listen as Paul listened. It will not change your gospel. It will deepen your sense of how big the same gospel is.

For worship. Three men in one city, a few years after the cross, and every one of them had seen the risen Lord with his own eyes. Paul names them himself in a single list: he appeared to Cephas, then to James, and last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). Not one of the three was gathered by a committee or a shared temperament. They were gathered by an empty tomb. The living Christ went looking for each of them, and there is no one his mercy cannot turn into a witness.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. James the Lord’s brother led the church in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)

In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie! Paul stops the narrative, turns to the reader, and swears an oath. He is halfway through a plain account of dates, places and names, and he breaks off to call God as his witness that he is not making it up. Nobody does that unless something is at stake.

He was being called a liar. Paul was not merely arguing with people of different opinions. A rival account of his life was circulating in the Galatian churches: apparently that he had been taught and authorised by Jerusalem and had then departed from their teaching. It had enough detail and enough plausibility that a straightforward denial would not do. Somebody had told these congregations a different story about where their founder got his message, and the story was sticking. So Paul swears before God that his account is true.

Did Jesus not forbid oaths? Did the Lord not say do not take an oath at all, and let what you say be simply yes or no (Matthew 5:34–37)? Does James not repeat it (James 5:12)? And here is an apostle swearing in writing. Look at what Jesus was actually forbidding. The system in view was one where oaths had become a sliding scale of honesty: swear by the temple and you may wriggle out; swear by the gold of the temple and you are held to it (Matthew 23:16–22). The whole apparatus existed so that a man could indicate how much of what he was saying he intended to stand behind, which meant that his ordinary word was worth nothing. Christ abolishes the scale. A disciple’s plain yes is to carry the full weight of an oath, always.

A solemn witness, not a sliding scale. That is not what Paul is doing. He is not grading his own truthfulness; he is under formal accusation, testifying to the truth of a matter on which souls depend. Scripture is not embarrassed by that kind of solemn witness. The same Paul does it more than once (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23), and God himself, having no one greater to swear by, swore by himself to guarantee a promise (Hebrews 6:13–17).

The faithful witness. Behind Paul’s oath stands his Lord’s. When the high priest said, I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God, the Lord who had forbidden careless oaths answered under oath, and his true answer was the sentence that sent him to the cross (Matthew 26:63–66). A lie would have saved his life. He would not tell one. Scripture calls him the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), and Paul, under accusation, is walking where his Master walked: telling the truth before God when it costs him, because the truth in question is Christ himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may swear casually. Paul uses an oath for a matter of great importance. What Jesus forbids in Matthew 5:33–37 is careless, evasive or deceptive swearing, not solemn testimony before God when truth and justice require it.

May a Christian take an oath in court? Yes. The Reformed confessions, the 1689 London Baptist Confession as well as Westminster, teach that a lawful oath is part of religious worship, in which a person solemnly calls God to witness what he asserts, and that it may rightly be taken when lawful authority requires it in a weighty matter (Westminster 22.1–3). Swear only to what you know is true, and only when the matter is serious. Some Christians, from tender conscience, prefer to affirm instead of swearing, and most courts allow it. Either way, the point is the same: you are speaking before God, and you speak that way every day.

The tell is what he protects. Paul does not defend his character: no wounded paragraph about years of service, no list of what these churches owe him. He swears to one thing only: the facts of where the gospel came from. That restraint is the tell. A man defending his reputation protects his reputation. Paul lets his name take whatever damage it takes and puts the oath where the danger actually is, because he is not the thing under threat. If the Galatians conclude that Paul is unimpressive, nobody is lost. If they conclude that the gospel is a human product, everything is.

In a sentence. Paul assures you before God that what he is writing to you is no lie.

On a Tuesday. Speak the truth as before God, always, because you always are before God. Notice the small untruths that ease a day along: the exaggeration in the story, the excuse that is slightly more flattering than the reason, the I’m fine. And when you are slandered, as Paul was, take his way: care more about the truth of the gospel than about your reputation, say what is true plainly, and leave your name with God.

For worship. All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). He is not a God who must swear to be believed, as though his plain word needed propping up; when he binds himself by an oath, it is a kindness to our slowness, not a confession of his. The Father has never said a word he did not mean, and the Son has never held back a word the Father gave him (John 17:8). The gospel rests on the word of a God who has never once spoken falsely, spoken to us in a Son who is himself the truth (John 14:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.

Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. The point is still the distance. Syria included Antioch; Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus, where he was born (Acts 22:3). Which is to say Paul went home. Luke fills in why: the Hellenists in Jerusalem were seeking to kill him, so the brothers brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus (Acts 9:29–30). And then Luke leaves him there, and the book of Acts simply carries on without him, until Barnabas, some years later, goes to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (Acts 11:25–26).

The years nobody reported. Add up the years between and it may be as many as ten, years with no recorded sermon, no named convert, no letter, no church we know the name of. He was preaching (v. 23), and he may have founded the churches of Syria and Cilicia that the Jerusalem Council later wrote to (Acts 15:23, 41). But the New Testament does not consider the details worth reporting, which is a striking thing to be true of the man who wrote a quarter of it. There is something steadying in that for anyone whose Christian life has no audience. Most believers are unknown by face to almost everybody, and the years in Cilicia produced no headline, but they produced the apostle to the Gentiles.

And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. Literally, unknown by face. The churches in Judea, the very congregations he had once hunted through, would not have recognised him if he had walked past them in the street. That is the argument, and it is now airtight. These are the churches closest to Jerusalem, most saturated with apostolic teaching, most likely to have shaped a young convert’s theology. If Paul’s gospel had been absorbed from that world, its members would at least have known what he looked like. They did not. He could not have been their student or their representative. He was, to them, a name in a story.

That are in Christ. Notice how Paul describes those churches: not the churches of Jerusalem’s region, or of the apostles, but the churches of Judea that are in Christ. Being in Christ is not a vague sense of closeness. It means being joined to him by faith, so that what is true of him is counted true of everyone joined to him: his death is their death to sin, his righteousness their standing before God, his Father their Father (Romans 6:4–5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That is the only place where what happened next could have happened. The families Saul had broken and the man who broke them now stood before God on exactly the same ground, and it was not their own.

What it does not mean. It does not mean he was idle. He was preaching the faith (v. 23). Unknown is not the same as unused.

Restoration at a distance. Paul is not simply hidden here; he is hidden from the people he had wronged. He had helped put some of their members to death, and now they were praising God for a man they would not have recognised. There is a kind of restoration that God does at a distance, where the people harmed are not asked to manage the person who harmed them, and both sides are carried by the same grace without ever meeting.

Someone who hurt me has become a Christian. Must I now be close to him? You must forgive him, and you should rejoice that God has saved him; that is what the Judean churches did. But forgiveness is not the same as restored trust, and it does not require you to put yourself back in harm’s way. Notice that God did not send Saul to live among the families he had wronged. Where a wrong was serious, and especially where there has been abuse, it is right to keep wise distance, to let the church and, where needed, the authorities deal with what must be dealt with, and to let trust be rebuilt slowly, if at all. You can bless a man from a distance. God often does his healing work on both sides without asking you to stand in the same room.

In a sentence. Then he went to Syria and Cilicia. He was personally unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.

On a Tuesday. God uses hidden years of faithful service. Do not despise your quiet seasons, or measure your usefulness by how many people know your face. Do today’s unseen work, the prayer no one hears, the kindness no one reports, the faithfulness in a job no one admires, as the work of a servant whose Master sees.

For worship. The Lord of the church kept his greatest missionary in obscurity for years, and did not consider them wasted. He is the God who sees in secret, who counts the hairs of heads no one else looks at, and who was himself unknown by face to almost the whole world while he did the work that saved it. The churches of Judea in Christ and the man in Cilicia were held in the same hand, and that hand never needs an audience to do its best work.
verseByVerse.note: Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus.

verseByVerse.quote: They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.

They only were hearing it said. Paul had not seen these churches. But something had reached them, and Paul preserves it: the actual sentence they kept repeating about him. The tense is continuous, the report going round and round the villages of Judea, told again at every gathering the way a church tells the story it cannot get over. They knew Paul only by reputation, and the reputation had changed.

He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy. Notice us. The report is passed between the very people he hunted: families who had lost someone, congregations that had scattered, men and women who had been dragged out of their homes by the man now being described. “The faith” here means the gospel, the content of what Christians believe, the thing itself. The man who set out to make sure this message did not survive is now the one carrying it across the empire. It is one line long, and it is the whole gospel: a before and an after, a total change the man did not manage himself, and evidence in what he now does rather than in what he says.

And they glorified God because of me. Then the last verse of the chapter, and it lands somewhere nobody would have predicted. Not: and they were reassured about my credentials. Not: and they admired my transformation. The literal phrase is that they glorified God in me. They looked at what had become of Saul of Tarsus and they worshipped. He was, to them, a piece of evidence about God, and the evidence made them praise.

In me. They are the same two words Paul used of his conversion: God was pleased to reveal his Son in me (1:16). What the churches of Judea glorified God for was the Son revealed in that man. They did not see a reformed character; they saw Christ living in a former persecutor, and they knew that no one but God could have put him there. That is what a converted life is: not a self improved, but a life in which Christ has taken up residence and begun to show. Paul says it outright later in the letter: it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (2:20).

The question already settled. He has spent twenty-four verses arguing that his gospel did not come from men. The Judean churches settled the question years earlier, on the strength of one report, without weighing his credentials. They looked at the impossibility of what had happened and knew whose work it was. No committee produces a man like that. And notice the sharp contrast with the teachers in Galatia. The Jewish Christians of Judea did not oppose Paul’s gospel; they praised God for it. If the churches nearest Jerusalem glorified God for Paul’s ministry, how can the Galatians reject it on the say-so of men claiming to speak for Jerusalem?

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul sought their praise. They praised God, not Paul. The glory went past the man to the God who had changed him, which is exactly where Paul wanted it to go.

What if my conversion was not dramatic? Then your story still ends the same way: with God glorified. Most Christians were not knocked off a horse; many cannot remember a time when they did not trust Christ. That is not a lesser grace. A child kept from the far country by God’s mercy is as much a wonder as a prodigal brought home from it. What made the Judean churches praise was not the drama but the change: the persecutor now preaching. If you love Christ today and live for him, however quietly, the same God has done the same work in you, and it is right for others to give thanks for it.

Should I tell my story? Yes, simply and honestly, with Christ at the centre and not yourself. Paul’s story is told in this chapter so that the gospel can be seen, not so that Paul can be admired. Tell what you were, what Christ did, and what he is to you now, and resist the temptation to make the before more lurid or the after more impressive than it was. People can argue with your theology. It is much harder to argue with what God has evidently done to you.

In a sentence. They only heard the report: “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they praised God because of him.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of someone’s conversion, especially someone you had written off, give God the glory before you give anything else, including suspicion. And let your own life give others reason to glorify God. Ask what the people who knew you before Christ would say has changed, and whether it would make them think of God or only of you.

For worship. A chapter that opened with a curse pronounced on angels closes with worship rising from villages that had suffered at the hands of the man being spoken of. The persecutor is preaching. The people he hunted are glorifying God. The church he meant to leave uninhabitable is on its knees giving thanks for him. This is what the risen Christ does with his enemies when he means to have them: he does not merely stop them; he turns them into the reason his people worship. And the last word of the chapter is glory, and it is not Paul’s.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—<sup>2</sup>and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:<sup>3</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>4</sup>who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,<sup>5</sup>to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—<sup>7</sup>not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.<sup>8</sup>But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed.<sup>9</sup>As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.<sup>10</sup>For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.<sup>11</sup>For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel.<sup>12</sup>For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.<sup>13</sup>For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it.<sup>14</sup>And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.<sup>15</sup>But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace,<sup>16</sup>was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;<sup>17</sup>nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.<sup>18</sup>Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days.<sup>19</sup>But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.<sup>20</sup>(In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)<sup>21</sup>Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.<sup>22</sup>And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.<sup>23</sup>They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.”<sup>24</sup>And they glorified God because of me.

2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the biographical argument’s climax and the letter’s theological turning point. Two episodes dominate: the Jerusalem conference (vv. 1–10), where the apostles affirmed Paul’s gospel of grace without requiring Gentile circumcision; and the Antioch confrontation (vv. 11–14), where Paul opposed Peter to his face because Peter’s behavior contradicted the gospel he believed. Both episodes illustrate the same point: the gospel of justification by faith alone is the non-negotiable centre of Christianity, and it must be defended even when the offender is the most respected leader in the church.

The chapter’s second half (vv. 15–21) is the theological centrepiece of the entire letter — the most concentrated statement of justification by faith in Paul’s letters apart from Romans 3. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” The verb “justified” (dikaioō) is a forensic term: to be declared righteous by the divine judge, to have one’s legal status before God established as “not guilty.” This declaration is made not on the basis of law-keeping (which can only expose and condemn sin) but on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ.

The chapter ends with the most luminous personal testimony in Paul’s letters: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” This is the gospel arriving at its destination: not merely a changed legal status but a transformed life — union with Christ, the old self crucified, the new life animated by faith in the one who loved and gave himself for me, personally, individually, sacrificially.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 opens with a number that is itself the argument: after fourteen years of preaching and planting without Jerusalem laying a hand on his message. He goes up with Barnabas, who had once vouched for him when the Jerusalem church would not go near him, and with Titus, an uncircumcised Greek — not a companion so much as an exhibit. In v. 2 he goes because of a revelation, not by summons, and meets the leaders privately rather than staging a public showdown he could have won.

His stated purpose, to make sure he was not “running in vain,” is easily misread as doubt about his gospel; chapter 1 forbids that. The danger he is guarding against is that the church might become two churches, a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms.

Verse 3 gives the verdict in one line: even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. With the test case standing in the room, Jerusalem did not require him to become a Jew. Verses 4–5 explain the pressure that made this a fight. The language is the language of espionage — false brothers secretly brought in, men who slipped in to spy out the freedom of the Gentile churches, whose stated object was slavery. Paul did not yield even for a moment, and gives a pastoral reason rather than a principled one: so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. Doctrinal firmness is a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free.

Verse 6 reports the outcome in a phrase — they added nothing to me — and grounds it in the fact that God shows no partiality, a principle Paul turns on the apostles themselves. Verses 7–8 set out the shape of the agreement: Paul entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised just as Peter to the circumcised, one gospel and two mission fields, with God himself named as the one who worked through both men. In v. 9 the order of the clauses carries the theology: the pillars first perceived the grace that was given and only then gave the right hand of fellowship — recognition of what God had done, not a handshake that conferred it. And v. 10 adds the single request Jerusalem made, that they remember the poor, which Paul was already eager to do.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Gospel, One People, One Way In

The Titus decision of v. 3 settles a question of the first order: justification is on identical terms for Jew and Gentile, and no covenant marker supplements faith at the point of acceptance with God. This is not a statement about cultural inclusion; it is a claim about the nature of justification itself, and the Reformed understanding of the covenant of grace — one covenant, one people, one Saviour, one way of entry — finds its clearest apostolic expression here.

Two further principles sit inside the passage. The word entrusted (v. 7) is a steward’s word, and it quietly disqualifies everyone in the dispute from editing the message: Paul may not adjust it to suit Gentiles and Jerusalem may not adjust it to suit Jews, for the same reason, which is that neither owns it. And the sequence of v. 9 — grace perceived, then fellowship extended — gives the church its permanent task in recognising anyone. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church perceives what God has given and says so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Galatia was being told that Gentile believers needed circumcision added to their faith. Paul’s answer is that he took this precise question to Jerusalem with an uncircumcised Greek at his side (vv. 1–3), and the men whose authority the Judaizers were invoking added nothing (v. 6) and shook his hand (v. 9). The Judaizers are not following the Jerusalem apostles; they are contradicting them.

Now: Anything may be done for the gospel; nothing may be added to it — which is why Paul could later circumcise Timothy (Acts 16:3) and would not let anyone touch Titus. The same test still sorts real questions from false ones. Where a practice is offered as helpful, Christians may differ; where it is required for full acceptance, the gospel is at stake. And v. 10 guards the other flank: having refused to add one item to the gospel, Paul accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because that is not an addition but what grace does once it has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.

Meaning first. Galatians 2 completes Paul’s defence of his gospel and states it in its clearest form. First, on a later visit to Jerusalem, Paul laid his gospel before the leading apostles. They added nothing to it, did not require the Gentile Titus to be circumcised, and gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (vv. 1–10). Second, at Antioch, Peter himself, under pressure from Jewish believers, stopped eating with Gentile Christians, and Paul opposed him publicly, because his conduct denied the gospel: if Gentiles are accepted by faith, they cannot be required to live like Jews (vv. 11–14). Third, Paul states the gospel: a person is justified not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Paul has died to the law and been crucified with Christ; Christ now lives in him, and he lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him. If righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing (vv. 15–21). The chapter moves from a private meeting, through a quarrel over a dinner table, to the summit of the whole letter: the Son of God, who loved me.

Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas. Paul is still counting years, and the number is the argument. Fourteen years after his conversion, or after the first visit: fourteen years of preaching, planting, and being run out of towns, without the Jerusalem apostles laying a hand on his message. If his gospel had needed their sign-off, it had been operating without it for well over a decade, and it had been working. And with Barnabas: the man who had vouched for Paul when the Jerusalem church would not go near him (Acts 9:27).

Taking Titus along with me. Titus is a Greek, an uncircumcised Gentile convert, and Paul walks him into the middle of a meeting about whether Greeks must be circumcised. He is not carrying a companion. He is carrying an exhibit, a deliberate test case.

I went up because of a revelation. Not because he was summoned, not because his nerve had failed. God told him to go, not the Jerusalem apostles; perhaps it came through the prophecy of Agabus about the famine (Acts 11:28). He was sent, by the same authority that had sent him everywhere else.

Though privately before those who seemed influential. He set the gospel he proclaims among the Gentiles before the leaders first, in a closed room, rather than staging a confrontation in front of a crowd. He could have forced a public showdown and won it. He chose the room where a thing can be settled instead of the platform where a thing gets performed. The phrase “those who seemed influential” is hoi dokountes, the ones held in repute. Paul is not overawed, but he is not sneering at Peter and James either; he calls them pillars and shakes their hands. He is refusing one thing only: the idea that reputation is what makes a gospel true. The Judaizers had been trading on Jerusalem’s prestige. Paul will grant Jerusalem everything except the right to be the reason.

In order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain. This is the line most likely to be misread, because it sounds as if Paul had doubts about his message and went to have them settled. He did not, and the whole of chapter 1 forbids that reading. The danger he is guarding against is not that his gospel might turn out to be false. It is that the church might turn out to be two churches, a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms. If Jerusalem rejected his gospel, the unity of the church and his work among the Gentiles would be gravely damaged, and everything he had built could come apart in a generation. He is not checking his doctrine. He is protecting the unity that his doctrine requires.

The gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles. What Paul set on the table in that room was not a method of mission but a person: Jesus Christ, crucified for Gentiles exactly as for Jews, and received by faith without the law. The question was whether Christ alone is enough for a Greek, and Titus standing in the room was that question with a face. So the danger of running in vain was a danger to Christ’s own body. Two churches with two sets of terms would mean a Christ cut in half, and Paul’s indignant question to the Corinthians has only one answer: Is Christ divided? (1 Corinthians 1:13). There is one Lord, and so there can be only one church.

Which visit was this? Honest scholars land in different places, so it is worth stating plainly. Acts records several visits. Many take this to be the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, where exactly this question was decided, and the subject matter fits it. Others take it to be the earlier famine-relief visit of Acts 11:27–30, which would mean Galatians was written before the Council ever met. That view has one strong argument in its favour: Paul describes a private meeting, whereas Acts 15 was a public assembly; and if a formal apostolic ruling on circumcision already existed, it is hard to explain why Paul, fighting on precisely that issue, never once quotes it. The famine visit fits well with the southern Galatian churches and an early date for the letter. But nothing in the letter’s argument depends on settling it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul needed Jerusalem’s approval for his gospel to be true. He sought unity, not permission.

Should I submit my beliefs to church leaders? Submit them to Scripture first, and hold them humbly before the church. Paul would not let Jerusalem’s reputation decide his gospel; Christ and his word decide it. But Paul also did not go off alone. He laid what he preached before mature leaders and was glad to find them agreed. That is a healthy pattern: test your understanding against the Bible, and then against the wise believers and the historic confessions of the church. If you find yourself believing something no faithful Christian has ever believed, be very slow to trust it. If your leaders ask you to believe what Scripture contradicts, Scripture wins.

In a sentence. Then after fourteen years, Paul went up again to Jerusalem, this time with Barnabas. He took Titus along too. He went in response to a revelation and, meeting privately with those esteemed as leaders, presented to them the gospel that he preaches among the Gentiles. He wanted to be sure he was not running and had not been running his race in vain.

On a Tuesday. Seek unity with fellow believers on the gospel. It is worth the effort. When you disagree with another Christian, notice whether you instinctively want the platform or the room: the public post, the meeting where you can be seen to win, or the quiet conversation where the matter can actually be settled. Paul, who was right, chose the room. Choose it too.

For worship. Fourteen years of a man’s life were poured out among the Gentiles before anyone in Jerusalem formally recognised what God was doing, and God did not need them to. The gospel had been doing its work in the high country of Galatia, in Syria and Cilicia, in towns nobody in Jerusalem had visited, because the Lord who sent it was running ahead of every committee. And when the leaders finally met, he had already prepared the room. The unity of his church is his own work, and he guards it with more care than any of us.
verseByVerse.note: It is debated whether this visit is the famine visit of Acts 11 or the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery— to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery—to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.

But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised. Everything came down to one man standing in the room, and whether anybody would reach for a knife. The apostles looked at an uncircumcised Gentile believer and did not require him to become a Jew. If the Judaizers were right, Jerusalem had a duty to say so with Titus standing there. Jerusalem said nothing of the kind. This settles the Galatian question.

Though he was a Greek. That small clause matters. Titus was not half-Jewish, not a God-fearer who had kept some of the law already. He was a Greek, and he was received as a brother just as he was.

The circumcision Titus already had. Titus did not need the knife, and the reason is a person. Paul tells the Colossians that believers have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by the circumcision of Christ, and buried with him (Colossians 2:11–12). The circumcision of Christ most likely means his death: there the old self under sin was cut away, and everyone joined to him by faith shares in it. Circumcision marked a man as belonging to God’s covenant people. Everything the sign pointed to, belonging, cleansing, a place in Abraham’s family (3:29), Titus already had in Christ. To demand the sign now would be to say that Christ’s work had not quite reached him.

Why circumcise Timothy and not Titus? A reader who knows Acts will feel this immediately. Paul later took Timothy and circumcised him (Acts 16:3). How is that not the very thing he refused here? The difference is everything. Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer (Acts 16:1), so he was already reckoned a Jew by birth and had simply never been marked as one; and nobody was demanding it as a condition of his salvation. Paul did it so that Timothy could get into synagogues and preach. Titus was a Gentile, and the demand was being made as a requirement of acceptance with God. So the rule Paul is working by is not that circumcision is forbidden. It is that anything may be done for the sake of the gospel, and nothing may be added to it. The moment a thing stops being free and starts being necessary, Paul will not move, and the same man who circumcised Timothy would not let anyone touch Titus.

Because of false brothers secretly brought in. Then the sentence turns dark. “False brothers” is pseudadelphoi: they claimed to be Christians but were not. The vocabulary that follows is the vocabulary of espionage. They were secretly brought in (pareisaktos), the word used of smuggling something in under cover; they slipped in like men getting over a wall at night; they came to spy out, the word for reconnoitring an enemy position. These were not honest men with a different opinion who lost an argument. They came to gather intelligence on how free the Gentile churches actually were.

To spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery. Paul names their object without softening it. Freedom: from the law as a way of justification, and from its ceremonies. Slavery: to the law as a way of standing before God (4:9; 5:1). That is the whole letter in a single phrase. What was on offer looked like a promotion: full membership, proper standing, the marks of the covenant. What it actually was, was chains. Anything that makes acceptance with God depend on a performance puts a man back on a treadmill he cannot get off, because the performance is never finished and the verdict is never in.

To them we did not yield in submission even for a moment. Not for an hour. Compromise never looks like surrender from the inside: it presents itself as a small, reasonable, temporary allowance for the sake of peace. Paul knew what the first inch was worth. On the gospel, no compromise.

So that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. And then he says why, and it is the most pastoral sentence in the paragraph. Not so that Paul might win. Not for the principle of the thing. For you: for a congregation of Gentile converts hundreds of miles away who would never know the meeting had happened. The truth of the gospel is the gospel in its true meaning, free grace, kept from being bent into something else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was always inflexible. He circumcised Timothy for missionary reasons (Acts 16:3), because it was not required for salvation. With Titus, it was demanded as necessary, so he refused. Paul was flexible about methods and immovable about the message.

What exactly is Christian freedom? It is freedom from the law as a way of earning God’s acceptance, from its curse on our sins, and from the ceremonies that pointed forward to Christ, such as circumcision, the food laws and the sacrificial system. It is not freedom to sin: Paul will say so sharply in 5:13. It is freedom for something: to serve God as sons rather than slaves, gladly, from love. A slave works to avoid punishment; a son works because he belongs to the family. Christian freedom means you never again have to wonder whether today’s obedience was enough to keep you in. You are in, and you obey from there.

In a sentence. Yet not even Titus, who was with Paul, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek. This matter arose because some false believers had infiltrated their ranks to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus and to make us slaves. They did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.

On a Tuesday. Notice the small, reasonable allowances. A rule that began as a helpful habit and has quietly become a test of whether someone is a real Christian. A preference about worship, schooling or Bible translation that you now hold over other believers. Ask of each one: is this free, or have I made it necessary? Hold it loosely if it is free, and put it down if you have made it a condition of acceptance.

For worship. The freedom Titus carried out of that room was never Jerusalem’s to grant or withhold. It had been bought. The Son of God was born under the law to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (4:4–5). He put himself under every demand the false brothers wanted to lay on Gentile shoulders, kept it all, and bore its curse, and so the chains they brought have nothing left to fasten to. If the Son sets you free, you are free indeed (John 8:36). No spy can find that freedom and confiscate it, because it is kept where he is.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised — a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),

And from those who seemed to be influential. Added nothing to me. Two words in Greek, and they end the argument. The Judaizers’ case rested on the claim that Paul’s gospel was incomplete: that the men in Jerusalem had the full version and Paul had been handing out an abridgement. So Paul reports the outcome of the meeting in the bluntest possible terms. The pillars of the Jerusalem church heard his gospel in full, and they had nothing to add to it. No correction. No supplement. No condition attached. Whatever the Galatians were being told is missing, the men supposedly missing it did not think so. “Seemed” is dokeō, were reputed. Paul is not mocking them, but noting that the false teachers made much of their reputation.

What they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality. Whatever status they had, as companions of the earthly Jesus or as his relatives, does not matter to the question. The phrase is close to an Old Testament formula: God does not lift up faces, does not take the important man’s side because he is important (Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7; Acts 10:34). Paul turns it on the apostles themselves. Peter had walked with Jesus and Paul had not, and it makes no difference to the truth of the gospel, because God is not impressed by credentials. It is a dangerous principle to hold and a liberating one: the same God who is unimpressed by Peter’s record is unimpressed by anyone else’s, which means nobody in the room outranks the truth.

When they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised. Then the reason they added nothing, and it is not that they were persuaded by Paul’s arguments. They looked at the evidence. Something had plainly been happening in the Gentile world, and it was not Paul’s doing. And the word is entrusted: the language of a steward handed something that belongs to someone else. It quietly settles the entire dispute. A man entrusted with a message has no authority to revise it; that is what entrusting means. Paul cannot edit this gospel to please Gentiles and Jerusalem cannot edit it to please Jews, for exactly the same reason. Neither of them owns it.

Just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised. The parallel is careful. One gospel, two mission fields: Peter mainly to Jews, Paul mainly to Gentiles. Not two gospels, and not a senior apostle with a junior assistant.

One Lord behind both commissions. The parallel has a face behind it. Peter was recommissioned by the risen Christ beside the Sea of Galilee, told three times to feed his sheep (John 21:15–17). Paul was commissioned by the same risen Christ on the Damascus road and sent to open the eyes of the Gentiles (Acts 26:16–18). One had walked with Jesus for three years and the other had hunted his followers, and the commission came from the same mouth. That is why the gospel to the circumcised and the gospel to the uncircumcised are one gospel. It has one owner and one content, the crucified and risen Christ, who is the same Lord of Jew and Greek alike, rich towards all who call on him (Romans 10:12).

For he who worked through Peter worked also through me. Then verse 8, in brackets, and the brackets hide the best sentence in the paragraph. Notice the subject. It is not Peter who worked, and not Paul. There is a third party in that sentence and he is the only one doing anything. The same God energised both ministries; the verb is the one from which we get energy. Peter and Paul are the instruments through which he worked. Which is why the comparison never becomes a competition. Two men were used, and one God was working, and the results in Jerusalem and the results in Galatia have precisely the same author. The evidence of Paul’s apostleship was God’s work through him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there are two gospels, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. One gospel, different audiences. Peter would say it himself at the Council: we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will (Acts 15:11).

Does “God shows no partiality” mean church leaders deserve no respect? No. Paul honours these men; he calls them pillars and accepts their handshake gladly, and elsewhere he tells churches to esteem their leaders very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13). What he refuses is to let their status decide what is true. Respect your pastor, pray for him, follow his teaching gladly when it is faithful to Scripture. But never believe something because of who said it, and never dismiss something because of who said it. The question is always whether it is the gospel.

In a sentence. As for those who were held in high esteem, whatever they were makes no difference to Paul, for God does not show favouritism; they added nothing to his message. On the contrary, they recognised that he had been entrusted with the task of preaching the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised. For God, who was at work in Peter as an apostle to the circumcised, was also at work in Paul as an apostle to the Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. There is a quiet mercy here for anyone who has ever measured his own service against somebody else’s and come away discouraged: the teacher whose class is small beside the one whose hall is full, the parent whose children came slowly to faith beside the family where it all seemed easy. The verse does not say the two men were equally gifted. It says one God was at work in both. Do your work this week as one entrusted with something that is not yours, and stop comparing the results. They have the same author.

For worship. God is not divided among his servants, spending himself heavily on the impressive ones and thinly on the rest. The whole of him works in each. The God who worked through a Galilean fisherman among the Jews and through a converted Pharisee among the Gentiles works still, through different people in different places, all with the one gospel. He shows no partiality, and so the least of his servants has the same Lord at work in him as the greatest.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.

When James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me. Watch the order of this sentence, because the order is the point. They did not shake hands and then discover the grace. First they saw the grace; then they extended the hand. The handshake did not confer anything. It acknowledged something God had already done. They recognised God’s grace in Paul’s calling and ministry.

The church perceives; it does not manufacture. That is the pattern for how the church recognises anything. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church’s task is to perceive what God has given and then say so publicly. Where grace is evidently at work, the only faithful response is to acknowledge it, and where it is not, no ceremony will supply it.

Pillars. The picture is architectural: the men on whom the weight rests, the leaders of the Jerusalem church (Revelation 3:12). James here is not the apostle John’s brother, who had already been executed by Herod (Acts 12:2), but James the Lord’s brother, the one who had not believed during the ministry and now leads the Jerusalem church. Then Peter, and John the son of Zebedee.

They gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me. It is the oldest gesture there is, and it means the same thing in every century: an open right hand holds no weapon, and a man who gives it is saying that between us this is finished. The word behind fellowship is koinōnia, partnership: a joint stake in the same enterprise, not merely a truce. A public sign of agreement and full acceptance.

A company of forgiven enemies. Consider what actually happened in that room. The apostle who had been hunting Christians and the apostle who had denied Christ in a courtyard put their hands together over a gospel neither of them had earned, and agreed to spend their lives on it in different countries. Each owed everything to the same person: Peter had been restored by the risen Lord after his denials, Paul stopped by him on the way to Damascus, and neither had been dismissed. Paul uses this same word, koinōnia, for what every believer is called into: the fellowship of God’s Son (1 Corinthians 1:9). The handshake was a partnership in a mission because it was first a shared life in Christ. Nobody in it had a record worth defending. That is what made it possible.

That we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. A division of labour, not a division of message, and it was never watertight, since Peter opened the Gentile door in the first place (Acts 10) and Paul went to the synagogue first in almost every town he entered.

Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do. One request. After a meeting about circumcision, the law, and the terms of salvation, the single thing Jerusalem asks is that the poor believers in Jerusalem not be forgotten. Not the law, but love. And Paul says he was already eager to do it. He meant it. Years of his life went into the collection for the struggling believers in Judea, and he wrote whole chapters raising it (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

Not an addition. It is a striking place for the paragraph to land. Paul has just refused to add one item to the gospel, and immediately accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because it is not an addition. Nothing has been placed between a sinner and God. What has been named is what grace does once it has arrived. A church that has understood justification by faith alone and has no interest in the hungry has not understood it (James 2:15–17; 1 John 3:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not preach to Jews or Peter to Gentiles. Both did. It was a primary focus, not a boundary.

Who are the poor I am to remember, and how? First, needy believers, the household of faith, as Paul will say in 6:10; then everyone in need as we have opportunity. Start near: the widow in your congregation, the family where a job has been lost, the asylum seeker who has turned up on Sunday, the student who cannot afford the trip. Give regularly and deliberately, not only when moved. Give through your church so that help is wise and sustained. Give time and friendship as well as money, because the poor are usually lonely as well as short. And remember the persecuted and impoverished church abroad. Do it gladly; Paul was eager, not pressured.

In a sentence. James, Peter and John, those esteemed as pillars, gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship when they recognised the grace given to him. They agreed that Paul and Barnabas should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised. All they asked was that they should continue to remember the poor, the very thing Paul had been eager to do all along.

On a Tuesday. Remember the poor. It is one of the marks of gospel faithfulness. Name one person or family in need you know of, and do something concrete for them before the week is out. And when you see grace at work in another Christian, especially one from a different background, church or tradition, perceive it and say so: give him the right hand, in words if not in a handshake.

For worship. The gospel that refuses to add anything to Christ is the gospel that sends its people to the poor, because it is the gospel of the one who, though he was rich, for our sake became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He did not wait for us to be worth helping. He came to us with an open hand that held no weapon, and in it were the scars. Every gift to the poor in his name is an echo of that one.
verseByVerse.note: Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church. The poor were the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recounts how he confronted Peter at Antioch. Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he drew back and separated himself, afraid of the circumcision party, and other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed his lead in this pretence. Paul saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, so he challenged Peter publicly: if you, a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you force Gentiles to live like Jews?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Governs the Feet, Not Only the Confession

Peter’s failure was not doctrinal. He had proclaimed the equality of Jew and Gentile before God and won the argument for it. What v. 14 exposes is a gap between a confession genuinely held and a life not walking in line with it — which is what hypocrisy means in Paul’s usage, not the cynical pretence of faith one does not have. The Reformers’ principle that the church is always to be reformed by the gospel bites here: the gospel must govern table habits, social pressure and power dynamics, not merely statements of faith.

There is a further point of some weight. Peter is treated in this passage as a fallible man who can be publicly withstood and corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel — and Scripture records it without embarrassment. Whatever authority the Jerusalem leadership had, it was never authority over the message, which is precisely the argument of vv. 6–9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch was socially motivated, not theologically: v. 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the same snare Paul named at 1:10 — am I trying to please man? — and it swept up the whole Jewish contingent and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now:Two things in this section reach a reader directly: the room in which he is a slightly different Christian, and the question of when a leader should be confronted in public. Paul’s case meets every condition at once — public conduct, the gospel itself at stake, others being carried away, and the rebuke spoken to Peter’s face rather than about him — and the friendship survived it (2 Pet. 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.

But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face. The scene changes to Antioch in Syria, the first great Gentile church (Acts 11:19–26), and the man who has just been called a pillar is about to be called wrong. Not a letter. Not a word with him afterwards. Not a delegation. Face to face, and in front of everybody (v. 14): openly, not behind his back.

Because he stood condemned. The word is a courtroom word, and the tense matters: not that Paul condemned him, but that he stood already condemned, by his own behaviour, by the contradiction between what he believed and what he was doing, and by the gospel. Paul did not pass the sentence. He read it out.

For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles. Eating together was not a casual matter in that world. A shared table meant shared life, mutual acceptance, family, and in the church it may well have included the Lord’s Supper. For a Jew to sit down to a Gentile meal was to declare that the wall had come down, and Peter had been doing it, meal after meal, which means the church at Antioch had watched their most famous visitor live out the gospel in the most visible way available. He had learned that God accepts Gentiles (Acts 10:28; 11:3).

But when they came he drew back and separated himself. Two verbs, and both are gradual; the tense pictures him withdrawing bit by bit. He drew back, a word used of a ship easing away from a quay, of a soldier giving ground. He separated himself, aphorizō, the very word from which the name Pharisee may come, the separated ones. Nobody announced a policy. He simply began sitting elsewhere, and everyone knew what it meant.

Fearing the circumcision party. There it is, and Paul does not let anyone pretend otherwise. It was not conviction. Peter had not changed his mind about anything; he changed his seat because of who was watching. It is the fear of man (Proverbs 29:25), the same weakness that once led Peter to deny Jesus.

How was this possible? This is the man who had the vision on the rooftop and heard the voice saying, what God has made clean, do not call common; who walked into Cornelius’s house and watched the Spirit fall on Gentiles; who defended the whole thing to the Jerusalem church and won the argument (Acts 10–11). He was not under-informed. He was the leading expert in the room on precisely this point. Which is the lesson, and it is a hard one. Knowing a truth and having settled it publicly does not immunise a man against abandoning it when the wrong people walk in. The mechanism had not changed in twenty years: not doubt, not argument, but the sudden weight of a watching face. Fear of man is not a beginner’s sin that maturity leaves behind.

A table the Lord had opened. And Peter was not only stepping back from his own vision. He was stepping back from his Lord. Mark, whose Gospel the early church connected with Peter’s preaching, records Jesus teaching that what goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, and adds: thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). The voice on the rooftop in Joppa said the same again. So when Peter moved his plate away from Gentile believers, he was putting back a wall that Christ himself had taken down. The question at that table was never really about menus. It was whether Christ’s word and Christ’s cleansing were enough to make a Gentile fit company.

Certain men from James. The phrase has been used to blame James, and probably should not be. Luke records the Jerusalem church later writing to Antioch about men who had gone out from them and troubled them, although we gave them no instructions (Acts 15:24). They may have claimed James’s authority without his approval. Men who arrive claiming a great name are not always carrying it. What is certain is the effect: their arrival was enough, and Peter did not even wait to be asked.

Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that Peter was the head of the apostles and the first pope, with a primacy passed to his successors, including infallibility in defining doctrine. Roman Catholic teaching limits that infallibility to formal definitions, not conduct; but the point here is wider. Verdict: Peter was a great apostle and leader. But here Paul publicly rebukes him for a serious error affecting the gospel. Peter was neither infallible in practice nor above correction by another apostle. The gospel judges Peter, not Peter the gospel, and that is true of every church leader since. The authority of the church rests on the apostolic teaching recorded in Scripture, not on the succession of one office (Ephesians 2:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Peter’s theology was wrong. His practice contradicted his theology. Paul rebukes his hypocrisy.

Is it wrong to adapt to the people I am with? Not in itself. Paul said he became as a Jew to Jews and as one outside the law to those outside the law, so that he might win them (1 Corinthians 9:20–22). Adapting your customs, your food, your manner, for the sake of love and the gospel is Christlike. What Peter did was different in two ways. His motive was fear, not love. And his action told fellow believers that they were not fully acceptable unless they changed. The question to ask is: am I adapting to serve these people, or to protect myself? And does my adapting tell any brother or sister in Christ that they are second-class?

In a sentence. When Peter came to Antioch, Paul opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself from the Gentiles because he was afraid of those who belonged to the circumcision group.

On a Tuesday. You may test yourself here more easily than you would like. Everyone has a room in which he is a slightly different Christian: the workplace where faith goes quiet, the family table where a conviction is not mentioned, the group of old friends where the language changes. Peter did not deny the gospel at Antioch. He simply moved to a different table when certain people were looking, and Paul calls that standing condemned. Name your room. Then go into it this week as the same person you are on Sunday.

For worship. There is one man in all of Scripture who never once changed his table because of who was watching. He ate with tax collectors in front of the Pharisees and with Pharisees in front of the tax collectors, and he was called a glutton and a drunkard for it. He was not afraid of any face, because he lived before the face of his Father. And when Peter failed again, as he had failed before, that same Lord did not cast him off; he sent him a brother to tell him the truth. The Lord who restored Peter by a charcoal fire restored him again at Antioch, and he is patient still with every one of us who has changed seats.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church. Eating together was the test: strict Jews would not share a table with Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”

And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him. The damage spreads in a single verse, and the name at the end of it is the one that hurts. The word is synypokrinomai, to play the actor together, from the theatre, the word for playing a part, speaking lines that are not your own. Paul is not accusing these men of secret unbelief. He is saying they were acting: behaving in a way their convictions did not support because the audience had changed. Leaders’ example spreads.

So that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. Even Barnabas. The man whose name means son of encouragement (Acts 4:36). The man who had stood up for Paul when the Jerusalem church was afraid of him, who had gone to Tarsus to fetch him out of obscurity, who had travelled the first missionary journey at his side through all its dangers and defended Gentile believers (Acts 11:22–26; 13–14). If one man in Antioch could be counted on, it was Barnabas, and he was carried away too. That detail is not there to shame Barnabas. It is there to show how strong the current was. It did not take an argument; nobody has recorded a single word of persuasion in this passage. It took a few significant people sitting at a different table, and the whole church moved.

But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel. The verb is orthopodeō, to walk straight, from which we get orthopaedics: they were not walking straight, not keeping to the line. And this is the sentence that gives the whole episode its weight. Paul does not say their doctrine was wrong. Their doctrine was fine; every man at those tables would have signed the same confession. Their feet were wrong. The gospel is not merely something to be believed accurately; it is something to be walked in, and it can be denied by a seating plan as effectively as by a sermon. And the truth their feet contradicted has a name. In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, because all who belong to him are one in him (3:28). His death had made the Gentile believer clean, and his Spirit had made him a son. To leave that man eating alone was to say, without a word, that Christ had not been quite enough to bring him in.

I said to Cephas before them all. Public sin with public effect required public correction (1 Timothy 5:20). Then the rebuke itself: if you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews? Peter had been living freely, eating what Gentiles ate, not keeping the Jewish food laws, so he plainly did not believe they still bound him. Yet by withdrawing he was telling Gentile believers that if they wanted his company at the table, they would have to take on the very rules he himself had stopped keeping: to have full fellowship with us, you must become Jews. That denied the gospel. And nobody had said it out loud: pressure does not have to be spoken to be applied, and Gentile Christians in Antioch had just been shown, with no words at all, what it would cost them to be treated as brothers.

Should a Christian confront leaders publicly? Usually not, and Scripture is careful about it. The Lord’s instruction for sin between brothers is to go privately first, and only widen the circle if there is no repentance (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul himself tells Timothy not to admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. But the same passage adds the other half: as for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Four things line up here, and they rarely all line up. The conduct was public, so a private word could not undo it. The matter was the gospel itself, not a preference or a personality. Others were already being swept away, Barnabas among them. And Paul said it to his face, in the room, at cost to himself, not about him, afterwards, to somebody else. That last one is the test most often failed. A great deal of what calls itself courage in the church is a message sent to a third party, or a post written about a man who will never be in the room. Paul’s way is harder and kinder: he said it where Peter could answer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul relished confronting Peter. He did it because the gospel was at stake. And it did not end the friendship. Years later, an old man writing his last letter mentioned our beloved brother Paul, and the wisdom given him, and the things in his letters that are hard to understand (2 Peter 3:15–16). Peter took it. There is no bitterness anywhere in the record. Two men who both knew what it was to be forgiven could survive being told the truth.

What are the separate tables today? Rarely food laws. More often it is the church where the professionals sit together and the cleaners sit together, the congregation that welcomes newcomers who look like the existing members, the fellowship that is warm to the respectable and cool to the man who has come out of prison or the woman with a messy history. Wherever believers make others feel that full acceptance requires them to become like us, culturally, socially, in class or race, the Antioch problem is back. The gospel says that whoever is in Christ belongs at the table, and the table is the Lord’s, not ours.

What if I am the one who has been rebuked? Do what Peter evidently did: listen, and do not defend yourself first. Ask whether the rebuke is true, even if it was delivered badly. If it is, own it plainly before God and before those affected, without excuses, and change course. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6). A believer who can receive correction is a believer who is resting on Christ’s righteousness rather than his own, because he has nothing to protect.

In a sentence. The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray. When Paul saw that they were not acting in line with the truth of the gospel, he said to Peter in front of them all, “You are a Jew, yet you live like a Gentile and not like a Jew. How is it, then, that you force Gentiles to follow Jewish customs?”

On a Tuesday. Does your conduct walk in step with the gospel? Do you treat all believers as equally accepted in Christ? Look at your own table this week, literally: who eats with you, who is invited to your home, who you sit beside after the service. Then invite someone who would not naturally be there.

For worship. The table at Antioch was always meant to be a picture of something bigger: the marriage supper of the Lamb, where people from every tribe and language and nation will sit down together, and no one will ask anyone else to become something first. The one who spreads that table is the Lord who broke down the dividing wall of hostility in his own flesh (Ephesians 2:14). He paid for every seat, and he does not move anyone to a lower one. His gospel walks straight, and in the end he will make all our feet walk straight with it.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul spells out the principle. Even Jewish believers know that no one is justified by doing what the law requires but only through faith in Jesus Christ, so they too have trusted Christ in order to be justified by faith. If seeking justification in Christ shows that we are still sinners, that does not make Christ a servant of sin; rebuilding the law as a way of standing with God is what makes a person a transgressor. Through the law Paul died to the law so that he might live for God. He has been crucified with Christ; his life now is Christ living in him, and he lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him. He will not set aside God’s grace, for if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith: The Article by Which the Church Stands or Falls

Protestant theology came to call justification by faith articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae, the article by which the church stands or falls — a summary of Luther’s own conviction — and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is forensic — a declaration of status, not an infusion of goodness, though transformation certainly follows. It is by faith alone, its object is Christ alone, and it is by grace alone; and the Reformed tradition has always insisted the three stand or fall together. If faith is not the exclusive instrument, it is not by grace; if Christ is not the exclusive object of faith, it is not grace either.

One point of translation deserves noting since a reader may meet it. The phrase rendered faith in Jesus Christ in v. 16 can also be read as “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ” — his own obedience to the cross as the ground of acceptance. The majority Reformed rendering takes it as faith directed toward him; either way, faith is not a work that earns the verdict but the empty hand that takes it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). The argument from the insider to the outsider is conclusive: if the law cannot justify those to whom it was given, it will not justify anyone else. And v. 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into a wall that had been pulled down.

Now:The person who comes to faith from a life of moral respectability and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on identical ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability is as irrelevant to the verdict as the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.

The sentence the Reformation was built on. Here is the letter’s own centre of gravity: a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Paul says it, then says it again, then says it a third time inside one verse, because everything else stands on it. Paul is probably still addressing Peter, or expanding on what he said to him, and the words become a statement of the gospel for every reader.
