We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners. Paul is reasoning. Gentiles were regarded as sinners because they were outside the law, and Paul may be quoting the Jewish attitude. Take the most advantaged religious people on earth: the covenant, the Scriptures, the temple, the sacrifices, a lifetime of training. And what did they do? We also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith. The insiders had to come the same way as the outsiders. If the law could have justified anybody, it would have justified them, and instead they abandoned the attempt and trusted a crucified man.

Yet we know that a person is not justified. The word to get clear is justified (dikaioō), and it is not a word most people use on a Tuesday. It is a courtroom word. To justify is not to make someone good; it is to declare someone to be in the right: acquitted, accepted. A judge who justifies a defendant does not improve him or treat him or educate him. He pronounces a verdict, and the man walks out of the court with a status he did not have when he walked in.

A verdict, not a treatment. That distinction is worth holding on to, because almost everyone instinctively thinks of salvation in medical terms: God as a physician gradually curing us, with heaven at the end if the treatment works. Justification is not the doctor’s slow progress; it is the judge’s verdict, given whole, in a moment, and given at the beginning rather than the end. God does also heal the sinner he acquits, and that work goes on for a lifetime. But he does not acquit him because the healing is going well.

What “justified” means, and what it does not. To be justified is to be declared righteous by God as judge: the verdict of not guilty, and more, of accepted as righteous. It is the opposite of being condemned (Romans 8:33–34; Deuteronomy 25:1). It does not mean being made inwardly good, though God does that too, in the separate work of sanctification. It does not mean God pretends we are good when we are not. He declares us righteous because the righteousness of Christ is counted to us, credited to our account (Romans 4:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Our sins were counted to him at the cross; his obedience is counted to us. The verdict rests on what he has done, not on what we are or do.

By works of the law. The ground of that verdict is the whole quarrel. Works of the law means, first, deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses, and particularly the visible markers that separated Jew from Gentile: circumcision, the food rules, the holy days. Those were the exact issues on the table in Antioch. But Paul’s conclusion is wider than the markers, and the last clause shows it.

Because by works of the law no one will be justified. From Psalm 143:2: enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you. No one. Not the Gentile without the law, and not the Pharisee who kept it better than his peers. No human being will be declared righteous by keeping the law, because no one keeps it perfectly (3:10; Romans 3:20). The reason is not that the law is a bad thing. Paul will insist that it is holy and was given by God for good purposes. The reason is that the law is a mirror, and a mirror has never washed a face. It was given to show what righteousness looks like and, in showing it, to show a man what he is not.

But through faith in Jesus Christ. Faith receives Christ and his righteousness, and it justifies not because it is strong but because he is. A weak faith in a strong Saviour is as fully justified as a strong faith, because the righteousness it receives is his, not its own.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? Some scholars of the New Perspective on Paul, such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, argue that works of the law mean mainly the boundary markers that separated Jews from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath. So justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people, not how a sinner is made right with God. Verdict: works of the law certainly include those boundary markers, as the Antioch incident shows; the New Perspective is right about the occasion. But Paul’s argument goes deeper: no one is justified by the law because no one keeps the whole law (3:10–12; 5:3). Justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, received by faith alone (Romans 4:4–8). It certainly has consequences for who belongs together at the table. But it is first about how a guilty person can stand before a holy God (Westminster 11.1).

Where Christians differ: declared righteous or made righteous? The Roman Catholic Church teaches (Council of Trent, 1547) that justification is a process in which God pours grace into the soul and makes the person inwardly righteous; it grows through the sacraments and good works, can be lost by mortal sin, and is restored by penance. On that view a person is accepted by God as far as he has been made righteous. The Reformers taught that justification is God’s once-for-all legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness alone, and that sanctification, the lifelong work of making us holy, always follows it but is distinct from it. Verdict: the Reformation view is right. Paul’s word is a law-court word: God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), which cannot mean he finds them already godly. Justification is complete the moment a person believes (Romans 5:1; 8:1), and so it cannot grow or be lost. Works matter greatly, but as the fruit of justification, not its ground (Ephesians 2:8–10; Westminster 11.1–2). If our acceptance depended on how far we had been made righteous, no one could ever be sure of it, and the cross would be only a beginning; but Christ died for no purpose if righteousness comes by anything we do (v. 21).

Where Christians differ: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? The Greek phrase pistis Christou, used twice in this verse, can be read as faith in Christ (our trust in him) or as the faith or faithfulness of Christ (his own faithful obedience to the Father, even to the cross). Some recent scholars prefer the second, and say Paul means we are justified by Christ’s faithfulness. Verdict: faith in Christ is the better reading. In this very verse Paul adds, “we also have believed in Christ Jesus,” which leaves no doubt that he is talking about our believing. Both truths are biblical: we are saved by Christ’s faithful obedience (Romans 5:19), and we receive it by trusting him. But here Paul’s point is that the way to receive righteousness is believing, not doing. Either way the doing is his; the receiving is ours.

Do Paul and James contradict each other? James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:24). No, they do not contradict. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is declared righteous before God, and answers: by faith, apart from works. James asks how a claim to faith is shown to be real, and answers that faith without works is dead (James 2:17). Paul opposes works as the ground of acceptance; James opposes a faith that is only words. Paul agrees that true faith works: faith working through love (5:6). We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is a work that earns justification. Faith is the empty hand that receives Christ. It is not what we are justified for, but how we receive the one for whose sake we are justified. Even the receiving is not a contribution.

If I am justified, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings lag behind facts, and because you still sin, and a tender conscience notices. Real conviction of a specific sin is the Spirit’s kindness, calling you to confess it and be cleansed (1 John 1:9). But a general cloud of condemnation that hangs over you after you have confessed is not from God, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). When that cloud comes, do not argue with it from your record. Argue from his. Say to your conscience: the verdict was given at the cross, on the ground of what Christ did, and it does not move with my moods.

In a sentence. We who are Jews by birth and not sinful Gentiles know that a person is not justified by the works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ. So we, too, have put our faith in Christ Jesus that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, because by the works of the law no one will be justified.

On a Tuesday. There is a test in this that can be run on any ordinary week. Ask what would have to be true for God to be pleased with you by Friday. If the honest answer involves a better performance than this week’s, then something is being trusted that is not Christ, and the good news is that the verdict was never waiting on Friday. It was handed down at the cross and received by faith, and it does not move (Romans 3:20–24; Philippians 3:8–9). Begin each day by remembering it, and then obey from it, not towards it.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth has a verdict to give on every human life, and he has given it in advance for everyone who trusts his Son: righteous. Not because he was deceived about us, nor because he lowered his standard, but because his own Son met the standard in our place and bore the sentence we had earned. God is just, and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). There is no higher court and no appeal against it, and the one who sits on the bench is our Father.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!

But if, in our endeavour to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners. Paul stops to answer an objection, and it is the objection this doctrine has always attracted. The argument runs like this. If a man is accepted by God on the basis of faith rather than obedience, then his obedience does not finally matter, and look at what actually follows. Jewish believers who came to Christ stopped keeping the food laws and started eating with Gentiles. By the law’s reckoning they became sinners in the process, sinners like the Gentiles.

Is Christ then a servant of sin? So Christ has taken observant men and made them law-breakers. Is he then a servant of sin: not merely tolerating it but actively promoting it, running errands for it? Does Christ encourage sin by freeing people from the law? It was the common objection to justification by faith (Romans 6:1).

Certainly not! Paul’s reply is the most violent negative in his vocabulary. The Greek is mē genoito, the phrase he reaches for when a suggestion is not to be weighed but thrown out of the room: may it never be, God forbid, perish the thought. Christ does not promote sin. Justification by faith leads to holiness, not licence (5:13–25).

Where the fault lies. The shape of Paul’s answer is already in the way he frames the question. He does not say that grace makes sin unimportant, and he does not deny that a justified person is still a sinner. He says something more careful: the fault cannot possibly lie where the objection puts it. Whatever is wrong when a believer sins, it is not that Christ put him up to it.

An insult to a friend. And there is a reason that is more than logic. To call Christ a servant of sin is to say something about the character of the one who died to destroy it: the man who took the whole weight of it into his own body and went into the dark under it. The objection is not merely mistaken; it is an insult to a person, and Paul reacts the way anyone reacts when someone slanders a friend who is not there to answer.

A strange compliment. Paul faced the same objection in Romans, put more sharply: are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? (Romans 6:1). It is a compliment of a strange sort. If a preacher has never once been accused of making grace too free, it is worth asking whether he has actually preached it, because Paul, who was preaching it exactly right, was accused constantly.

Grace changes the person, not only the paperwork. Paul’s answer is not a retreat into rule-keeping. It is a statement about what happened to the person. Grace does not leave a sinner where it found him and merely change his paperwork. It puts him to death and raises him, and a man who has died to something does not go back to it as though nothing occurred. That is why Paul’s answer ends at a cross, I have been crucified with Christ (2:20), rather than at a code of conduct.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers do not sin. It means Christ is not to blame for their sin, and the gospel does not encourage it.

Then why do Christians still sin, and does that make grace a failure? Christians still sin because sanctification is lifelong; the old desires are defeated but not yet removed, and the war goes on until we see Christ (5:17; 1 John 3:2). That is not grace failing. It is grace still at work. The difference between a Christian and an unbeliever is not that one sins and the other does not, but that the Christian has a new master, hates his sin, fights it, confesses it, and is slowly changed. If you are using grace as an excuse to keep a sin you love, do not comfort yourself with this verse; it says certainly not. If you are grieving your sin and running to Christ with it, grace has not failed you. It has hold of you.

In a sentence. But if, in seeking to be justified in Christ, we Jews find ourselves also among the sinners, does that mean Christ promotes sin? Absolutely not!

On a Tuesday. Free grace never means freedom to sin. Live holy because you are free. When you notice yourself thinking, it does not matter, I am forgiven anyway, stop and look at who forgave you and what it cost him. Then ask him for strength to obey in the very thing you were about to excuse.

For worship. Christ is not the servant of sin. He is its executioner. He came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and he did it by letting sin do its worst to him, and rising out from under it. Everyone he justifies he also begins to make holy, and he never leaves the work half done. The Saviour who is accused of indulging sinners is the only one who has ever truly set them free from it.

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.

For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. Paul answers the objection about himself, with a picture. Imagine a man who has spent years constructing a building, stone by stone, and has finally looked at it, judged it unsound, and pulled it down. Now imagine him going back and putting every stone up again. He has not merely wasted his time. He has publicly declared that the demolition was the crime.

What Paul tore down. It was the whole structure of acceptance by performance: the life he describes in chapter 1, advancing beyond his peers, zealous for the traditions, building a righteousness of his own. He took it apart when he met Christ. And this is the answer to the man who says grace makes sinners: the transgression would not be in leaving the law behind as a way of righteousness, it would be in going back to it. If he rebuilds that system, he condemns himself either way. Either he was wrong to pull it down, or he is wrong to put it up. What he cannot claim is that reconstruction is obedience. And there is a direct application to Antioch, which is surely why he uses the first person so pointedly. Peter had been living in the freedom of the gospel and had begun laying stones back in place, one meal at a time.

For through the law I died to the law. One of the strangest and best sentences in the letter. Through the law: not in spite of it, not by escaping it; the law itself was the instrument of his death to the law. In Christ, who bore the law’s curse, Paul died to the law’s claims (Romans 7:4).

How can the law make me die to the law? This is one of Paul’s most compressed sentences, so it helps to take it in steps. First, the law demands perfect obedience and pronounces death on every transgressor (3:10). Second, Paul was a transgressor, so the law’s sentence on him was death. Third, Christ took that sentence for him: he was born under the law (4:4) and died under its curse in his people’s place (3:13). Fourth, Paul was united to Christ by faith, so when Christ died, Paul died with him (v. 20). So the law did carry out its sentence on Paul: in Christ, he died. And a dead man is free from the law’s claim; the law has nothing more to say to someone whose sentence has been fully carried out (Romans 7:1–4, where Paul uses the picture of a marriage ended by death). That is why it was through the law: the law itself demanded the death by which he was set free from it. There is a second strand too: the law, by exposing his sin, drove him to stop trusting it and to flee to Christ (3:24; Romans 7:9–10).

How the law kills. That second strand is worth watching at work. The law came to a man doing rather well and kept raising the standard until it had him. It said: not just murder, but anger; not just adultery, but the look; not just the deed, but the desire. And it kept saying it until the promising young Pharisee understood that he was not ahead of his peers at all, that the system he had trusted could only convict him, and that on those terms he was a dead man. So the law did precisely what God gave it to do. It killed him, and it killed him so that he could stop trying to live by it.

The last kindness of a schoolmaster. There is no gentler road to grace than this one, and it is worth saying honestly, because it is where many people actually are. Nobody comes to Christ while his own account still looks solvent. The ache underneath religious striving, the sense that it is never enough, that the standard keeps moving, that a good week is only ever a reprieve, is not a malfunction. It is the law doing its work, and its work is not cruelty. It is the last kindness of a guardian who intends to hand the pupil over to someone else (3:24).

What it does not mean. Dying to the law does not mean becoming lawless. Paul died to the law as a way of being right with God, and as a master that condemns him; he did not die to God’s will. He is now under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21), and the Spirit leads him to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement in love (5:14; Romans 8:4). Nor does it mean the law is bad or that its moral teaching no longer matters. It means the law is no longer the way to righteousness or the master over believers.

So that I might live to God. The purpose of dying to the law is not lawlessness but life for God. That is what the whole demolition was for: not to leave a man in the rubble, but to get him out from under a life spent proving himself, and into a life lived toward God. The law could not make him live for God; Christ does.

Do Christians still need to keep the Ten Commandments? Not as a way of being accepted by God, and not under the law’s curse. But the moral will of God that the commandments express has not changed, because it flows from God’s own character. Jesus deepened the commandments rather than abolishing them (Matthew 5:17–48), and the apostles repeat their substance to Christians (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:1–3). So the believer reads the moral law as the shape of a life of love, the path his Father has marked out for children who are already his. Christians differ on how the fourth commandment applies today, and on how much of the old covenant law carries over; but no Christian is free to steal, lie, covet or commit adultery. The ceremonial laws that pointed to Christ, such as circumcision and the food laws, are fulfilled in him and no longer bind.

In a sentence. If Paul rebuilds what he destroyed, then he really would be a lawbreaker. For through the law he died to the law so that he might live for God.

On a Tuesday. Notice the stones you keep laying back in place: the private rules by which you measure whether God is pleased with you this week, the spiritual achievements you quietly count. Each one is a piece of the old building. Put it down. Then ask the question Paul’s life now asks: what would it look like today to live to God? Not to prove yourself to him, but to live towards him, gladly, as a man let out of prison lives towards the friend who paid his fine.

For worship. The law’s sentence on us was death, and God did not cancel the sentence. He carried it out, on his Son, and counted us as having died in him. That is the strange mercy of the gospel: our freedom from the law was purchased by the law being fully satisfied. Christ honoured every demand of it, in his life and in his death, so that sinners could be set free from it without the law being dishonoured at all. We died in him, so that we might live to God, and the life we now live, we owe entirely to him.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

I have been crucified with Christ. This is the summit of the letter, and one of the best-loved verses in the New Testament, and it begins with a funeral. The tense is one English does not carry well: the perfect, a thing done in the past whose results stand permanently in the present. Crucified, and remain so. Not I am dying daily, and not I try to crucify myself. It happened. It is finished. When Christ died, Paul died, because Christ died as a representative, the way Adam acted for a race, so that what happened to him happened to everyone joined to him. United to Christ, Paul shared in his death. His old self, under the law’s condemnation, died (Romans 6:6).

Crucified. It is a deliberate word to choose. Crucifixion was not a dignified death or a private one. Paul could have said he died with Christ; he says he was crucified, which is what you do to a criminal in public with nothing left of his standing. The old self, the impressive one, the one with the record and the achievements and the rising reputation in Judaism, did not retire honourably. It was executed.

It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. Taken alone, the sentence sounds as if Paul has been erased, as if becoming a Christian means being emptied out and replaced, personality and all. Two things forbid that reading. The first is the very next clause, where Paul says the life I now live: there is plainly still an I doing the living. The second is the letter itself. The man who wrote it is unmistakably himself on every page, angry, tender, sarcastic and affectionate by turns. Grace did not flatten Saul of Tarsus into a generic believer. It killed what he was living for and left him more himself than before. What died was the old Paul, the self-righteous Pharisee, the self that had to be somebody. What lives is a man indwelt. Christ now lives in Paul by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Colossians 1:27), the source and centre of his new life.

And the life I now live in the flesh. In the body, in this world, in ordinary circumstances, with a stomach and a temper and a tentmaking business. Here “the flesh” means ordinary bodily, earthly life, not the sinful nature, which is how Paul uses the word in 5:16–24 and in Romans 8. Paul is saying that his new life in Christ is lived out in a real human body, in the everyday world, by faith. This is Monday he is describing.

I live by faith in the Son of God. Faith is not just the door into the Christian life; it is the way of living it, every day. And that is worth saying plainly, because people who love this verse sometimes expect it to feel like something and are troubled when it does not. Paul does not say he lives by a sensation of Christ’s presence, or by a continual awareness, or by spiritual experiences. He says he lives by faith: by trusting a person he cannot see, on days when nothing is felt at all. The indwelling is a fact about where Christ is, not a report on how the believer is doing.

Who loved me and gave himself for me. And then the last clause, and Paul’s grammar goes suddenly singular. He has spent the whole chapter on councils, delegations, apostles, mission fields, the terms of justification for the nations. And it ends here, with one man saying me twice. Personal and particular. Paul does not say only that Christ loved the world, but that he loved me. Christ’s death was a personal act of love for each of his people. The cross is wide enough for the world and narrow enough to have a single name written on it. This is the same Paul who had been dragging women out of houses to prison (Acts 8:3). Luther urged his readers to read the words me and for me with great vehemence, and to take them as spoken of themselves.

What “crucified with Christ” does not mean. It is not a special experience that some advanced Christians reach, nor a feeling to be worked up, nor a command (crucify yourself!). It is a fact that is true of every believer by union with Christ: when he died, we died with him, and that death can never be undone (the perfect tense; Romans 6:3–6). What died was the old self: the person Paul was under the law, condemned and ruled by sin. It does not mean Paul no longer struggles with sin (5:17), or that he no longer has a will of his own. It means Christ has replaced self as the centre, the source of his life, and the object of his trust. The practical result is in the next words: Paul lives by faith, looking to the Son of God who loved him.

How do I live by faith on an ordinary day? By turning, again and again, from yourself to Christ. In the morning, before the list, remind yourself who you are in him: crucified with him, raised with him, loved by him. When temptation comes, say no on the strength of the fact that the old self who loved that sin was put to death. When you fail, go straight back to the one who loved you and gave himself for you, without waiting to feel better first. When you have to do something hard, ask him for the strength, and expect him to give it, because he lives in you. None of this needs a feeling. It needs only the habit of looking at him.

Can I say “for me” if I am not sure I am chosen? Yes. You do not need to look into God’s secret decree before you come to Christ; no one can. The gospel invites every sinner who hears it to trust Christ, and promises that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37). Christ did die for his people in particular, and his death secured their salvation; but you discover that you are one of them not by peering into heaven but by coming to him. If you trust Christ, you may say, without presumption, the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. Paul’s me is the word of every believer.

In a sentence. Paul has been crucified with Christ and no longer lives, but Christ lives in him. The life he now lives in the body, he lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him.

On a Tuesday. Say it for yourself, slowly, in the first person: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. Then pick the hardest moment you can foresee today, the meeting, the conversation, the empty evening, and decide now that you will live that moment by faith in him: not by your mood, not by your record, but by trusting the one who loved you. And when you look at the people around you, remember that if they are in Christ, the same sentence is true of them.

For worship. The Son of God loved: not the abstraction of humanity, but this particular man, with this particular record, while that record was still being written. And he did not send help; he gave himself, which is the only gift that costs the giver everything and leaves nothing in reserve. He had the Father’s glory and set it down. He had legions and did not call them. He went to a public execution for people who were his enemies at the time, and he did it gladly, and he would not be talked out of it (Ephesians 5:2; 1 John 3:16). There is nothing in heaven or earth to set beside a love like that, and eternity will not be long enough to get to the end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

I do not nullify the grace of God. The chapter ends with its sharpest sentence. “Nullify” is atheteō, to set aside, reject, cancel: the term for treating a legal instrument as void. And it is almost certainly a charge being thrown back where it came from. Paul is the one being accused of treating God’s law as though it counted for nothing; he answers that it is the other side who are annulling something, and it is not the law. Going back to the law as a way of righteousness cancels grace.

For if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose. The argument is a single move, and there is no way round it. Suppose there is any route to being right with God that runs through human obedience: any at all, even a small one, even as a supplement to grace. Then on that road God had a way of saving people that did not require the death of his Son. And in that case Calvary was not a rescue; it was the most appalling waste in the history of the universe. A Father watched his Son die in the dark for something that could have been managed another way.

For no purpose. The phrase is dōrean: without cause, for nothing, in vain. It is the same word Paul uses elsewhere for freely, as a gift (Romans 3:24), and the play is bitter. Either righteousness is given freely, or Christ died freely, for nothing. Every religion of human achievement, however sincerely held, ends up saying the second about the crucifixion, whether it means to or not. If we could save ourselves by keeping the law, the cross was unnecessary.

Why Paul’s temper is not disproportionate. The Judaizers thought they were adding a little rigour to a message that had gone soft. Paul shows them what their addition actually implies about the cross, and the implication is blasphemous. You cannot say Christ plus my performance without saying, underneath it, that his performance was insufficient, and the cross does not survive being called a supplement. Every addition to grace is an insult to the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean obedience is unimportant. It means obedience is not the ground of our acceptance with God.

Does this mean sincere, good people of other religions are lost? Paul’s logic answers it. If righteousness could come through the law of Moses, given by God himself, then Christ died for nothing; how much more if it could come through any other path. The cross was necessary because there is no other way to God, and so salvation is through conscious faith in Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). That is not arrogance on the Christian’s part; we are saved the same way, as beggars. It is a reason for urgency and compassion. The people you love who trust in their own goodness need to hear about the one who died because their goodness could never be enough.

What if I keep feeling I must earn God’s favour? Most Christians do; the instinct to pay our way runs deep. Treat the feeling as a temptation, not a revelation. When it comes, answer it with this verse: if I could earn it, Christ died for nothing, and he did not die for nothing. Thank God out loud for what Christ has already done. Then go and obey, not to earn, but because you are loved; and when the obedience goes badly, do not let that reopen the question. The question was closed at the cross.

In a sentence. Paul does not set aside the grace of God, for if righteousness could be gained through the law, Christ died for nothing!

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to earn God’s favour, remember: if you could, Christ died for nothing. Trust his finished work. Look for the places where you are quietly adding something: the sense that God will hear you better if you have read your Bible today, that you must feel sorry enough before you may come back, that your service has bought you some credit. Each time, say it plainly: Christ did not die for no purpose. He died for me, and it is finished.

For worship. Had there been another way, the Son of God would have taken it; he asked in the garden whether there was, three times, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground (Matthew 26:39–44; Luke 22:44). There was not. He went to the cross because nothing less would do, and he went knowing exactly what it cost, and he did not die for no purpose. He died for sinners, and it worked, and it is finished, and there is nothing to add to it (Hebrews 10:11–14).

It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.<sup>21</sup>I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological heart of Galatians: a sustained argument from Scripture that the gospel of grace by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the foundation on which all of God’s dealings with Abraham and his descendants have always rested. The law came 430 years after the Abrahamic covenant. It cannot therefore revoke the promise made to Abraham; it operates within a different register, serving a different purpose, pointing toward its own fulfillment and supersession in Christ.

Paul opens with an emotional appeal: the Galatians had experienced the Spirit. They knew it. Signs and wonders had accompanied their conversion. Did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The answer is obvious — and the answer settles the question about the ground of their acceptance with God. The same Spirit-receiving faith that initiated their Christian life is also the ongoing basis of their standing. Maturity in Christ is not a movement from faith toward law; it is a deepening of faith in the one in whom all the law finds its fulfillment.

The chapter’s christological climax is the most audacious claim in the letter: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (v. 13). The cross was not merely a sacrifice; it was a specific legal exchange. Christ took the law’s curse — the curse pronounced on all who fail to keep it perfectly — onto himself, becoming the accused on behalf of the accused, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has finished defending his apostleship and turns on the Galatians themselves, and the first line has no courtesy in it. In v. 1 he calls them un-minded and asks who has bewitched them, when what had been placarded before their eyes was Jesus Christ crucified. Then, instead of an argument, he asks about their own biography. Verse 2 puts the one question he says is sufficient: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? They knew the answer. They were, for the most part, uncircumcised pagans who heard and believed, and God moved in.

Verse 3 exposes the folly precisely: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Not sin — religion; the whole realm of what a man can do, mark and show. Verse 4 asks whether their suffering was wasted, and then Paul cannot finish the sentence. Verse 5 makes the question present tense: God is still supplying the Spirit and working miracles among them, and the evidence stands in the room while the argument goes on.

The sentence of v. 5 runs on a dash straight into v. 6, so Abraham is not a new topic but the last clause of the question. Genesis 15:6 is quoted: Abraham believed God and it was posted to his account as righteousness. Verse 7 draws the conclusion that overturns the whole Judaizing offer — it is those of faith who are Abraham’s sons. Verse 8 goes further: Scripture pre-gospelled Abraham, so the Gentiles were in view in God’s first sentence to him. And v. 9 sets every believer alongside the patriarch himself: blessed along with Abraham, on the same footing, in one queue.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Is Received by Faith, and the Reception Settles Everything

The appeal of vv. 2 and 5 is not to religious feeling but to a fact of record: the mechanism by which God gives his Spirit. Reformed theology has always held that the Spirit is the agent of union with Christ and that union with Christ is received by faith alone; here Paul argues it backwards from experience. If the Spirit came through the hearing of the gospel and not through law-works, then the law-works were never the channel, and no later addition can make them one.

The force of v. 3 is that the Christian life is not two-stage. There is no beginning by grace followed by an advance by performance. What justifies also sanctifies, and it is the same Spirit received in the same way from first to last. And vv. 6–9 place this outside the new covenant altogether: Abraham was justified by faith in Genesis 15, two chapters and many years before the sign of circumcision was given in Genesis 17. Justification by faith is not a Christian innovation. It is how God has always dealt with sinners.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were not asking the Galatians to abandon Christ. They were offering completion — take the mark, keep the calendar, and become full sons of Abraham like us. From inside, it looked generous and it looked mature. Paul’s answer in vv. 1–5 is to make them look at their own conversion: nothing in their hands, no circumcision, no Sabbath kept, and God gave them his Spirit. Then vv. 6–9 take Abraham, the Judaizers’ own trump card, and turn it over.

Now: Almost no believer decides to be justified by works; the drift of v. 3 is quieter than that. Over a few years the empty hands fill with real and often good things — a devotional habit, a serving rota, a reputation — and the ground of confidence migrates without anyone noticing the day it moved. The test is the one v. 2 implies. Think of your worst week, and ask whether God was as pleased with you that Sunday as on your best. If something flinches, the flinch is the answer, and vv. 6–9 are the cure: one queue, one way in, and Abraham himself is standing in it.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.

Meaning first. Galatians 3 is Paul’s great argument that God has always justified people by faith, not by the law. He argues from their experience: they received the Spirit by believing the gospel, not by keeping the law, so why go back to the flesh now (vv. 1–5)? He argues from Abraham: Abraham believed God and was counted righteous, and God promised that in him all nations would be blessed; so those of faith are Abraham’s true children (vv. 6–9). He argues from the law itself: the law curses everyone who fails to keep it completely, and Scripture says the righteous live by faith; Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us on the cross (vv. 10–14). He argues from history: God’s covenant promise to Abraham and his offspring, Christ, came 430 years before the law and cannot be cancelled by it (vv. 15–18). Then he explains why the law was given: it was added because of transgressions, to imprison all under sin and act as a guardian until Christ came (vv. 19–25). Now, through faith, all believers are God’s children, clothed with Christ, one in him whatever their race, status or sex, and heirs of the promise to Abraham (vv. 26–29). The chapter climbs from a placard in a Galatian marketplace to a tree outside Jerusalem, and from there to an oath God swore alone under the night sky and kept alone on Calvary.

O foolish Galatians! The letter has already withheld the thanksgiving every other Pauline letter to a church opens with. Now it drops the courtesy altogether. The word is anoētoi: not stupid, not uneducated, but literally un-minded, without understanding, people with a perfectly good brain who have stopped using it on the one subject where everything is at stake. A man can hold a degree and read the market correctly every morning and still be anoētos about the gospel. Paul is not insulting their intelligence. He is telling them they have failed to think clearly about what they already know.

Who has bewitched you? The verb is baskainō, from the world of the evil eye: the malign look that was thought to wither a crop or sicken a child. Galatia was a region full of magic and superstition, and Paul’s readers knew the idea well. Paul does not believe in the evil eye, and he is not saying a spell was cast. He is reaching for the only category that fits what he is looking at: something has come over these people that ordinary argument does not explain. They have not been out-reasoned. They have been charmed. The false teaching worked like a spell, fascinating them away from the truth.

Two sights competing. See where he puts the eye. Something has looked at them and done them harm, and yet, he says, what was set before your eyes was Jesus Christ crucified. Two sights competing for the same congregation. Whichever one you keep looking at is the one that will shape you.

Publicly portrayed as crucified. The word is prographō: posted up, placarded, written large in a public place. In a Galatian town, if the governor issued a ruling or a runaway slave was being sought, a notice went up in the marketplace where everyone passing had to walk by it. That is Paul’s picture of his own preaching. He had not offered them a religious option or a spiritual perspective. He had put up a public notice in their town, and the notice said: the Son of God was executed, and it was for you. How could they look away from the cross to the law?

Before your eyes. Which raises the obvious question. None of the Galatians had been at Golgotha. Neither had Paul. So in what sense was it before their eyes? In this sense: preaching that does its work does not merely inform people about the cross, it sets the cross in front of them until they can see it. Not theatre, not sentiment, but the plain announcement of what happened, made so clear that a farmer in Lystra could shut his eyes and see a man on a Roman beam dying in his place. That is what they had been given. That is what they are drifting away from.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul literally showed them a picture. It means his preaching set the crucified Christ clearly before them. The power was in the word, not in an image.

The diagnosis of the whole chapter. The Galatian problem is not that they were never told. They were told with total clarity. The problem is that a clearly seen cross can be talked out of a person’s field of vision, and it can happen without the person noticing that anything has moved. Nobody in Galatia had announced that they were abandoning Christ. They were adding a little, adjusting a little, tidying up the edges of a gospel that had felt untidily free.

How do I keep Christ crucified before my eyes? By putting yourself, deliberately and often, where the cross is set before you. Sit under preaching that is full of Christ and his cross, not only of advice. Come to the Lord’s Supper as the moment the Lord himself places his death in front of you (1 Corinthians 11:26). Read the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion slowly, more than once a year. Sing hymns that dwell on it. And when your conscience accuses you, train yourself to answer it by looking there first, not at your week. The cross does not fade because it changes. It fades because we stop looking.

In a sentence. You foolish Galatians! Who has cast a spell on you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified.

On a Tuesday. Here is a way to find out where you stand. Not: do you believe the cross happened? Almost everyone reading this does. Rather: when you last examined whether God is pleased with you, what did you actually look at? If the honest answer is your week, your prayer, your temper, your record since Sunday, then something has moved into the field of vision that was not there when you first believed, and the notice on the wall has been papered over. Keep Christ crucified before your eyes. When you are tempted to trust your own performance, look at the cross.

For worship. God did not leave the Galatians to guess what he is like. He put it on a placard in their town, and the placard was his own Son, dying for enemies. There is nothing more to see of the heart of God than this, and nothing less will do. Every spell that dazzles us away from it is a cheap light beside the glory of a crucified Lord, and the God who painted that picture before our eyes is still the one who opens them to see it.
verseByVerse.note: “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye. “Publicly portrayed” uses the word for a public notice posted for all to read.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?

Let me ask you only this. Paul has a whole letter of arguments ready, covenants, chronology, Abraham, Moses, an allegory about two women, and before he uses any of them he says he will ask one question, and one only. One question settles the matter. If they answer it honestly, the entire Judaizing programme collapses without another word being spoken.

Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The question is not about theology. It is about their own biography. He does not ask them what they believe now, because that is exactly what is in dispute and is being renegotiated weekly by men with impressive credentials. He asks them what happened to them then. That is not up for negotiation. It is a matter of record, and every one of them was there. And the Spirit is the decisive mark of belonging to God: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). So if they have the Spirit, they already belong.

What had happened. They knew perfectly well. Paul had walked into their towns, a stranger with a travel-worn face, and announced a crucified and risen Jew as the Lord of the world. Some of them believed it. And when they did, God gave them himself. The Spirit came, not as a doctrine they later worked out, but as an event they lived through: sins forgiven, a new hunger for God, a love for people they had previously despised, and in some cases manifest power. Most of them had not been circumcised when it happened. Most had never kept a Sabbath, refused a piece of pork, or observed a Jewish festival. They were, for the most part, uncircumcised pagans who heard and believed, and God moved in.

The question answers itself. That is the point. The Judaizers were teaching that the law completes what faith begins. Paul says: run the tape back. At the moment God gave you the greatest gift he has ever given anyone, his own Spirit, indwelling, what was in your hands? Nothing. What had you done? Heard, and believed. Since they began with the Spirit by faith, they do not need the law to be complete.

Hearing with faith. The phrase is akoē pisteōs, and it is deliberately loose in Greek. It can mean the hearing that consists of faith, or the message that is heard and produces faith (Romans 10:17). Paul may well intend both, because in his mind they are one motion: a message announced, and a heart that stops arguing and takes it. That is the whole of the human contribution, and even the taking is worked in us by the Spirit we are receiving.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit is received in a second experience after faith. They received him when they believed. There is no Christian without the Spirit, and no later stage at which a believer is given him for the first time.

How do I know I have received the Spirit? Not mainly by an unusual experience, though God may give one, but by what the Spirit does. He makes you trust Christ and call God Father (4:6; Romans 8:15–16). He makes Christ precious to you and the Bible alive to you. He gives you a new hatred of your sin and a new desire to please God. He grows love, joy, peace and the rest of his fruit, slowly and often unnoticed (5:22–23). He draws you to other believers. If you believe in Jesus and want to follow him, however weakly, the Spirit is already at work in you, because no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).

In a sentence. Paul would like to learn just one thing from you: did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by believing what you heard?

On a Tuesday. The question survives the twenty centuries intact, and it is worth answering out loud. When God first became real to you, not when you were christened, not when you joined the church, but the day the thing became true rather than inherited, what were you holding? If you are honest, nothing at all. You heard, and something in you gave way. Anyone who now tells you that your standing depends on what you bring is describing a different transaction from the one you actually made. Live today the way you began: hearing God’s word and believing it.

For worship. The entire Christian life is the working out of a transaction in which you brought no capital. God did not wait for the Galatians to become respectable, Jewish or devout. He gave them himself, the Spirit of the living God, the greatest gift there is, to people who could only listen and believe. That is what God is like. He gives the best first, and he gives it to the empty-handed.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?

Are you so foolish? He asks it a second time, repeated in amazement, and this time he supplies the content of the folly. It is the sentence in this letter that ordinary Christians most need to hear: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?

Begun and perfected. Two words carry it. Begun is enarxamenoi and perfected is epiteleō, to complete, to bring to maturity: a matched pair that could be used in the ancient world of a sacrifice, where you begin the rite and you bring it to completion. So the Galatians are not proposing to abandon the Spirit. Nobody in Galatia was. The false teachers said: faith is the start, but circumcision and law-keeping complete you. Paul says the proposal is not maturity but madness: you began at the level of God and you are now finishing at the level of meat. You cannot complete by the flesh, by human effort and outward rituals, what the Spirit began.

What “flesh” means here. Flesh here is not what most readers assume. It is not first lust or greed or temper. Circumcision is a cut in literal flesh; the whole Judaizing programme lands on the body. So the flesh Paul means is the entire realm of what a human being can do, mark, keep and show: religious achievement, visible, measurable, and yours. He is not warning them off sin here. He is warning them off religion as self-effort.

How it happens to us. That is why this verse finds the reader who is doing nothing obviously wrong. Almost no Christian consciously decides to be justified by works; hardly anyone would say it out loud. What actually happens is quieter. You come to Christ with empty hands and you are received with joy. Then, over about five years, the empty hands slowly fill: a devotional habit, a serving rota, a standard of speech, a reputation for reliability. None of it is bad. All of it may be the Spirit’s own fruit. But somewhere in there the ground of your confidence migrates from the finished work of Christ to the visible evidence of your progress, and you never notice the day it moved.

Did you suffer so many things in vain? Then verse 4, and the tone changes. The verb paschō can mean suffer or simply experience. These people had paid for their faith. Paul had been stoned in Lystra and dragged out of the city for dead, and the young churches watching had taken their own share of it; Paul and Barnabas told them that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:2, 5, 19–22). Or Paul may mean the many blessings they had experienced. Either way, would they throw it away? He is asking whether all of that was for nothing.

If indeed it was in vain. And then he cannot finish the sentence. The great polemicist, mid-thunder, breaks off and refuses to say it. He will not pronounce them lost. He has raised the possibility because they need to feel the danger, and then, with the sentence still hanging, he will not close his hand on it. That half-line is worth more than a paragraph of reassurance: this is a man who is furious with them and cannot bear the thought of losing them, and the two things are not in tension (2 Corinthians 2:4; Galatians 4:19). Paul hopes it is not in vain.

Where Christians differ: sanctification by effort? Some think justification is by faith, but sanctification is by our own effort and rule-keeping. Verdict: sanctification, like justification, is a work of the Spirit received by faith. It involves real effort and obedience (Philippians 2:12–13), but effort that depends on the Spirit, not on the flesh. Christians grow not by adding laws but by walking in the Spirit (5:16, 25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians make no effort. It means the effort is Spirit-empowered faith, not self-reliant striving. Paul worked harder than anyone, and said in the same breath that it was not he, but the grace of God that was with him (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Then what do I actually do to grow? Use the means God has given, and use them as a needy child, not as a contractor. Read and hear his word, because the Spirit grows faith through it. Pray, because prayer is the confession that you cannot do it alone. Come to the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. Obey in the specific thing in front of you, asking for strength as you do it. Put sin to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13): name it, flee it, cut off what feeds it. The difference between Spirit and flesh is not whether you make an effort, but what you lean on while you make it, and who gets the credit when it works.

In a sentence. Are you so foolish? After beginning by means of the Spirit, are you now trying to finish by means of the flesh? Have you experienced so much in vain, if it really was in vain?

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is exact. Take your worst week: the one where you prayed nothing, snapped at everyone, and went to church because it was easier than explaining why you had not. Now ask: on that Sunday, was God as pleased with you in Christ as he was on your best Sunday of the year? If something in you flinches at that question, the flinch is the answer. It is not your morals that have gone wrong. It is that you have started finishing by the flesh what was begun by the Spirit. Are you trying to grow as a Christian by your own willpower? Ask the Spirit to work in you, and walk by faith.

For worship. The God who began a good work in us is the one who will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). He does not hand over the finishing to us. The Spirit who first opened our eyes is the same Spirit who will one day present us faultless, and every step between is his. We did not begin ourselves, and we will not finish ourselves, and that is not our humiliation. It is our rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith— just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?

Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you. The last of Paul’s questions, and it moves the argument from their past into their present. Not did God supply the Spirit, but does he: epichorēgōn, a present participle, going on supplying. And works miracles among you is present too (Acts 14:3, 8–10). Whatever the Judaizers were saying about the Galatians’ deficient standing, God had evidently not stopped moving among them. The evidence was in the room while the argument was going on.

Supplies. The word Paul chooses is worth a moment. Chorēgeō comes from the world of the theatre: the chorēgos was the wealthy citizen who paid for a chorus for the civic festival, costumes, training, musicians, the lot, at his own expense and as an honour. The word came to mean lavish provision by someone under no obligation to provide anything. That is the verb for what God does with the Holy Spirit. He is not paying wages. He is underwriting the whole thing, generously, because he chose to.

Do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? The same question as verse 2, and the answer is just as obvious: by faith. And the question does not end there. It runs straight on into verse 6: or by hearing with faith, just as Abraham believed God? Abraham is not a new topic. He is the last clause of the question, and the question is still a question when his name arrives.

Just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”. The quotation is Genesis 15:6, and Paul chose his ground with care. The false teachers appealed to Abraham, who was circumcised (Genesis 17). Paul appeals to Abraham too: before he was circumcised, he was counted righteous by faith (Romans 4:9–11). So what happened in Galatia last year and what happened to Abraham two thousand years earlier are the same transaction. God spoke; a man believed him; God credited it to him as righteousness. Uncircumcised Gentiles in Asia Minor were justified by exactly the way that justified the father of the Jewish nation, and the Judaizers had somehow managed to hold up Abraham as the argument against them.

Counted. The verb is a bookkeeping term: logizomai, to credit, to reckon, to post an entry to an account. Abraham had done nothing to earn the entry; he was a childless old man standing under a sky full of stars being told his descendants would be that many, and he took God at his word. God then wrote righteous in the ledger against his name. Not improving. Not on probation. Righteous, in full, that night, before circumcision, before Moriah, before any work that could be set against the account. This is imputation: God credited righteousness to his account.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith itself is the righteousness. Faith is the means by which righteousness, God’s gift in Christ, is received. It does not say Abraham’s faith was so admirable that God accepted it in place of the righteousness he lacked; that would make faith a rather cheap work, and would put the ground of acceptance back inside the man. It says that faith is the empty hand that receives a righteousness belonging to another. The credit posted to Abraham’s account was real, and it was not generated by Abraham (Romans 4:3–5; Philippians 3:9).

Where Christians differ: do miracles continue? They were the signs that accompanied the first preaching of the gospel in Galatia; Luke says that at Iconium the Lord bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands (Acts 14:3). Paul’s point is not that miracles are normal, but that God gave the Spirit and his powers to people who believed, not to people who kept the law. Continuationists take the present tense here as evidence that such works go on in every church. Verdict: the more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic founding of the churches, the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and have ceased in that form; the Spirit himself, received by faith, remains, and God still answers prayer, heals and acts in his providence as he pleases. Brothers who see it differently are to be loved as brothers.

Do Paul and James disagree about Abraham? James quotes the same verse about Abraham and says he was justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac (James 2:21–23). Genesis 15 gives the verdict; Genesis 22, many years later, shows the faith was real. James speaks of faith vindicated, Paul of faith counted (see on 2:16). There is one Abraham, with one faith: the faith that received God’s verdict under the stars was the same faith that climbed Moriah.

Is my faith strong enough to be counted? It is not the strength of your faith that saves you, but the strength of the one you trust. Abraham’s faith was real but not flawless; between Genesis 15 and 22 he lied about his wife and tried to force the promise through Hagar. A drowning man who grabs a rope with a trembling hand is pulled out just as surely as one with a firm grip, because the rope does the saving. If you are trusting Christ, even with doubts and fears, God counts his righteousness to you in full. Ask him to strengthen your faith, as the father did who said, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24).

In a sentence. So again: does God give you his Spirit and work miracles among you because you keep the law, or because you believe what you heard? So also Abraham “believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”

On a Tuesday. If that is how the account was settled for Abraham, then no one who comes after him has a better arrangement available. There is no advanced tier. The man who stands at the head of the whole story got in the way the newest and least impressive believer in Galatia got in: God spoke, and he believed him. Like Abraham, believe God. Take one promise of God this week, read it slowly, and say to him plainly: I believe you.

For worship. The God who stood with Abraham under the stars is the God who still keeps the books, and he keeps them in our favour. He supplies his Spirit lavishly, like a patron who will not count the cost, and he writes righteous against the names of people who have nothing to offer but trust. He has never needed our merit to keep his word, and he has never once posted a false entry.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.

Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. Paul is drawing a conclusion, and it is a bombshell in a first-century synagogue. To be a son of Abraham was not a compliment; it was a legal identity. It meant you were inside the covenant, inside the promises, inside the people God had bound himself to. It was traced by blood and marked in the body, and a Gentile could enter it only by becoming, in effect, a Jew. That was precisely the offer the Judaizers were making to the Galatians, and from the inside it looked generous: come the whole way, take the mark, and be a full son of Abraham like us.

Faith, not blood. Paul cuts the ground out from under it in a single sentence. Abraham’s true children are not his physical descendants or those circumcised, but those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12, 16). Jesus said the same to men who boasted of their descent: if you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did (John 8:39). Descent from Abraham was never the thing that made a man Abraham’s son in the sense that counted, or Ishmael and Esau would have been in.

And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith. Here Paul says something startling about the Old Testament. Observe who is doing the speaking. Scripture foresaw and Scripture preached, which is a striking way to talk about a book. Scripture is personified: what Scripture says, God says; the text is so entirely God’s speech that its voice and his are one. God planned from the start to justify Gentiles by faith. Any believer should feel the weight of that when he opens his Bible. He is not reading about a God who once spoke. He is being spoken to.

Preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham. The verb is proeuangelizomai: to announce the gospel in advance. That is not a Christian reading imposed on Genesis at a distance of two thousand years. Paul is claiming that when God said to a childless man from Mesopotamia, in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 18:18), the gospel was already being announced: the actual gospel, the one Paul preaches, in its seed form. The gospel is not new; it is the fulfilment of God’s oldest promise. God had the Gentiles in view from the first sentence he ever spoke to Abraham.

Inside out. So the Judaizers had the whole story inside out. They were treating Gentile inclusion as a late concession, an awkward extension of a Jewish covenant, to be granted only on Jewish terms. Paul says it was the point from the beginning. God’s plan was always worldwide. The blessing was never meant to stop at Abraham’s family; the family existed so the blessing could reach everyone else. To demand that a Galatian become a Jew before he could be blessed was to obstruct the very purpose for which the Jewish nation had been called into existence.

So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith. Not blessed after him, at a lower grade, in a side chamber. Along with him. “Man of faith” translates pistos, believing or faithful. An Anatolian farmer who believed a travelling preacher stands in the same blessing as the patriarch, and stands in it on the same footing: justification, the Spirit, and the inheritance.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists distinguish sharply between Israel and the church as two peoples with separate promises. Verdict: Paul teaches that all who have faith, Jew or Gentile, are Abraham’s children and heirs of the promise (v. 29). There is one people of God across history, united by faith in the promised offspring, Christ. This is covenant theology’s insight: the one covenant of grace, administered in different ways, runs from Abraham to the church (Westminster 7.5–6). God’s purposes for ethnic Israel continue (Romans 11), but within the one people, not alongside it.

Has the church then replaced Israel? Not in the sense the question usually means. Paul is not saying that the Jewish people have no future, but that Abraham’s true family has always been defined by faith, not blood. Gentiles who believe are added to that family; Jews who believe are its natural members; and unbelieving Jews can be grafted back in (Romans 11:23). The family was never replaced. It was enlarged to its intended size.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham knew all the details of the gospel. He trusted God’s promise, which pointed to Christ, and Jesus said that Abraham rejoiced that he would see his day; he saw it and was glad (John 8:56).

Do Jewish people today need to believe in Jesus? Yes, and to say so is not hostility but love. Paul, a Jew, wept over his own people and prayed that they would be saved (Romans 9:1–3; 10:1). Since Abraham’s true children are those of faith, and the promise was always to his offspring, Christ, there is no way to Abraham’s blessing that bypasses Abraham’s Seed. Christians should therefore love Jewish people, reject every form of antisemitism as a sin against the people from whom Christ came, and share the gospel with them gladly, humbly, and first (Romans 1:16).

In a sentence. Understand, then, that those who have faith are children of Abraham. Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and announced the gospel in advance to Abraham: “All nations will be blessed through you.” So those who rely on faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.

On a Tuesday. Carry this into a Sunday morning. Most congregations have people in them who quietly assume they are the auxiliary members: the late convert, the one with the disgraceful decade, the one whose family has no Christian memory at all, the one who cannot follow the sermon’s longer arguments. There is a persistent instinct that the real Christians are somewhere further in. Verse 9 has no room for it. If you believe, you are Abraham’s child, whatever your background. Live as an heir of his blessing, and treat the person beside you as one too.

For worship. Abraham has been a believer for four thousand years and is blessed by faith. You believed last March and are blessed by faith. There is one queue, and everybody in it got in the same way. And at the head of it stands not Abraham but the God who called him: who looked at a childless man under the stars and saw, already, the farmers of Galatia and the city-dwellers of every continent, and promised to bless them all through one Seed. He has been keeping that promise ever since, one believer at a time, and he will not stop until every nation has come in.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having proved his case from Abraham, Paul now proves it from the law, and he does it by letting the law speak. Verse 10 says something nobody expects: it is not those who break the law who are under a curse but those who rely on it — the serious, observant, early-rising ones. The proof is Deuteronomy 27:26, the last of the twelve curses Israel answered with its own Amen. Four words carry it: everyone, all things, abide by, and do them. The law is not a pass mark; it is a seamless garment, and it cannot be scored out of a hundred.

Verse 11 states the conclusion as something already plain — no one is justified before God by the law — and grounds it in Habakkuk 2:4, the verse that broke the medieval church open. Verse 12 sets the opposing principle beside it from Leviticus 18:5: the one who does them shall live by them. A thoughtful reader feels the difficulty, since Leviticus is God’s word too. The answer is that the law’s offer was never a bluff; the fault lies not in the law but in the material it works with.

Then v. 13, the summit of the chapter. Christ redeemed us — bought us out of the slave market — from the law’s curse by becoming a curse himself, and the text quoted is Deuteronomy 21:23, the very verse that made a crucified Messiah unthinkable to Saul the Pharisee. Verse 14 gives the purpose twice: so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith — which closes the circle opened by the question in v. 2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

That Christ bore the penalty due to sinners in their place, exhausting the law’s sentence, is not a later development of doctrine but the explicit content of v. 13. The exchange is legally precise. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could fall on those who have no claim to it. This is not sympathetic solidarity — he suffered with us — but substitution: he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

Two guards belong here. First, becoming a curse does not mean the Father ceased to love the Son or turned on him in temper; Jesus said the opposite (John 10:17). The sentence was real and the Father’s delight in the obedient Son was real at the same hour. Second, the Deuteronomy text is about the public display of an already-condemned man, so the tree did not make him cursed — it published the verdict. Saul had read that publication correctly and been wrong about only one thing: whose curse it was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement, a way of securing what faith had begun. Verses 10–12 show that the law has no supplementary setting. It accepts one condition only, and no son of Adam has ever met it, so those who take their stand there have entered a system whose only two verdicts are flawless obedience and curse. Verse 13 names the single exit, and vv. 13–14 together explain how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up holding the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 with their stomach already tight, half expecting confirmation that God is disappointed with them. Read it exactly. The curse is aimed not at their failure but at the thing they were using to cover it. And v. 13 says what became of it: the sentence was carried out, and not on you. Verse 14 adds that the Spirit you already have is the receipt.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”

For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse. Paul has proved his case from Abraham. Now he turns and proves it from the law itself, and the argument is devastating, because he lets the law do the talking. Read the sentence slowly, because it is not what anyone expects. He does not say that those who break the law are under a curse. He says that those who rely on it are: the serious ones, the observant ones, the men who get up early to keep it. “Rely on” is literally are of the works of the law: those whose standing with God depends on law-keeping. The very people who thought the law was their shelter are told they are standing under the one thing it actually guarantees for sinners.

For it is written. And then the proof, quoted from the law’s own closing ceremony. In Deuteronomy 27, Israel is drawn up in two halves on two mountains, Ebal and Gerizim, with the covenant read aloud between them, and the last of twelve curses is the one Paul takes: cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them (Deuteronomy 27:26). At the end of every curse the whole nation answered Amen. They said it. Out loud. They ratified the terms themselves. The law offers blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience.

Four words. Now weigh the words Paul leans on. Everyone: no exemptions, no distinguished-service discount. All things: the whole code, not a representative selection. Abide by: continuously, not in a good season. And do them: performance, not agreement; you can admire a command all your life without once obeying it. The law demands perfect, complete obedience. And the unstated premise of the whole argument is the one every reader knows: no one does all things.

A seamless garment. Put those together and the law turns out not to be a pass mark but a seamless garment. It cannot be scored out of a hundred. James says the same thing from the other end: whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it (James 2:10). That sounds harsh until you see why it is true. The law is not a list of separate regulations; it is the expression of one Person’s will. To break any of it is to have said no to him, and you do not need to say no on every subject to have said no.

A road and a cliff. So the choice Paul lays out is not between an easier and a harder road to God. It is between a road and a cliff. Anyone who takes his stand on law-keeping has entered a system in which the only two possible verdicts are flawless obedience and curse, and he has already failed, and he knows it, which is why the religion of the law-keeper is so often anxious under its composure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean obeying the law is bad. It means no sinner can obey it perfectly, so it cannot be the way to blessing.

Is God disappointed with me? This is where a certain kind of reader needs to be met honestly, because he is reading with his stomach tight. He is not a Judaizer. He has simply never been able to shake the sense that God is disappointed with him, and this verse looks like proof. If you are that reader, notice exactly what Paul says and what he does not. He does not say that people who sin are cursed with no way out; if he did, there would be no hope for anyone in this letter or out of it. He says that people who rely on law-keeping are cursed, because they have chosen a standard that will certainly convict them. The curse is not aimed at your failure so much as at the thing you were trying to use to cover your failure. And in three verses he will tell you what happened to the curse.

Were the Israelites of the Old Testament all under this curse? Not those who trusted God. Old Testament believers were saved the same way Abraham was: by faith in God’s promise, looking forward to the Redeemer. The law itself provided sacrifices for sin, pointing to Christ, and the psalms are full of people who knew they could not stand on their own record and cast themselves on God’s mercy (Psalm 32:1–2; 130:3–4). What Paul condemns is relying on the law as the ground of acceptance, which the faithful in Israel never did. David, Isaiah and Daniel were not law-climbers; they were forgiven sinners who loved God’s law because they had first received his mercy.

In a sentence. For all who rely on the works of the law are under a curse, as it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.”

On a Tuesday. Notice when you are quietly standing on your record: when you feel you deserve an answer to prayer because you have been faithful, or that God owes you a smoother life because of your service. Those are small reliances on works, and they lead to anxiety or resentment. Step off the cliff edge. Thank God that you do not have to stand on your own record, because Christ has taken the curse.
