For worship. The law is holy, and its curse was just. God did not pretend the terms were softer than they were, and he did not let the Amen of Ebal fall to the ground. Instead he sent his Son to stand where the cursed stand. The God who is too holy to cancel his own law is the God who loves sinners too much to leave them under it, and at the cross both are seen at once: his justice satisfied to the last letter, and his mercy flowing out through the very place it was satisfied.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”

Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law. Two verses, two quotations from the Old Testament, and between them Paul settles the question of how anyone has ever been right with God. Evident is dēlon, plain, obvious, in view. He is not about to prove something contested; he is pointing at something already established. Before God: in his sight, by his standard.

For “The righteous shall live by faith.” The proof is Habakkuk 2:4 (also Romans 1:17; Hebrews 10:38). Habakkuk had been watching the Babylonians come, and he could not square the horizon with the character of God. The answer he was given was not an explanation but a way to survive: the righteous man will live, keep breathing, keep standing, keep his footing when everything visible is against him, by faith. Paul takes that sentence as the shape of the whole Christian life. Luther took it from Paul, and it was the verse that opened the gospel to him and broke the medieval church open. The way to life is by faith.

But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them”. That quotation is Leviticus 18:5. As a way to righteousness, the law works on a different principle from faith. The law’s principle is: do and live. Faith’s principle is: believe and live. They are opposite ways. Since no one does them perfectly, life by the law is impossible.

How can Paul set Moses against Habakkuk? It can look as if Paul is pitting one Old Testament verse against another. He is not. In Leviticus 18:5, God speaks to a people he has already redeemed from Egypt: keep my laws and you will enjoy life with me in the land. For them, obedience was the grateful way of life of the redeemed, and the sacrifices were provided for their failures. But the false teachers were using the law as a ladder to climb up to God: do these things and you will be accepted. Paul takes them at their word. If you make the law the ground of your acceptance, then Leviticus 18:5 states the terms: you must do them, all of them (v. 10), to live by them. No sinner can meet those terms. Habakkuk 2:4 states the other way, the only way open to sinners: the righteous live by trusting God. Christ is the one person who met the terms of Leviticus 18:5, and he did it for us (4:4–5; Romans 10:4–5).

A sound contract offered to a bankrupt. Leviticus 18:5 states the law’s principle truthfully. The law really does promise life to whoever keeps it. That offer was never a bluff, and there is nothing defective about the law: it is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). The defect is in the material it has to work with. As Paul puts it elsewhere, the law was weakened by the flesh (Romans 8:3), like a perfectly sound contract offered to a bankrupt. The terms are excellent. He cannot meet them.

Two kinds of sentence. So the two verses are not two rival ways to God, one strict and one generous. They are two different kinds of sentence. Do these things and live puts the weight on the doer. The righteous shall live by faith puts the weight on the one believed. And that is why they cannot be blended, however reasonable a blend sounds. Faith and works are not two ingredients that improve each other; they are two answers to the question: who is responsible for my standing before God? The second answer cancels the first.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law was never connected with faith. Old Testament believers lived by faith too. It means the law as a system of earning life is opposed to faith.

What does living by faith look like when life is hard? It looks like Habakkuk. He did not get an explanation of why the Babylonians were coming; he got a promise, and a God to trust. By the end of his book the fig tree has not blossomed, the fields have failed and the stalls are empty, and he says he will still rejoice in the LORD and take joy in the God of his salvation (Habakkuk 3:17–18). Living by faith does not mean pretending things are fine. It means telling God honestly that they are not, and then deciding to trust what he has said about himself over what your circumstances are saying. The righteous do not live by understanding. They live by faith.

In a sentence. Clearly no one who relies on the law is justified before God, because “the righteous will live by faith.” The law is not based on faith; on the contrary, it says, “The person who does these things will live by them.”

On a Tuesday. Live by faith today, not by trying to prove yourself. When the day goes against you, the diagnosis, the redundancy, the child who will not speak to you, say Habakkuk’s sentence back to God and ask him to make it true of you: I will trust you, though I cannot see.

For worship. Leviticus 18:5 was never revoked. Someone had to do the things and live by them, and someone did. There has been exactly one man on this earth who could stand under the law’s own terms and claim its promise honestly. He kept all things written in the Book of the Law and did them. He earned the life. And then, having earned it, he went to a place where the law had nothing but a curse to give, and he took the curse instead, and left the life to us.

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith
by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. If you had to choose one sentence in the New Testament to carry the whole doctrine of the atonement, this would be a strong candidate. Everything in the chapter has been climbing to it, and every word in it is load-bearing. Redeemed is exagorazō, a word from the slave market: to buy out, to purchase and remove, as a slave is bought out of the market. It assumes a real transaction with a real price paid to secure a real release. Nobody in a first-century town heard that word as a metaphor. They had watched it happen in the square.

From the curse of the law. And what were we bought out from? Not from the law as God’s good will, but from the curse of the law, which is verse 10 come home. The curse is the penalty the law pronounces on lawbreakers: death and God’s wrath. The sentence that stood over every human being who had ever taken his stand on his own obedience has been executed, and not on him.

By becoming a curse for us. Then the mechanism, and it is deliberately shocking. Not by pitying us, not by identifying with us, not by showing us how much God cares. He became the thing itself. “For us” is hyper hēmōn, on our behalf, in our place. Christ took the curse we deserved. This is penal substitution: he bore the penalty, so that we are free (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24).

For it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”. The proof text is one that no Jew could hear without flinching (Deuteronomy 21:23). That law is worth understanding precisely. In Deuteronomy 21 hanging is not the method of execution. A man convicted of a capital crime is put to death, and then his body is hung on a tree as a public sign of what he was, and it must be taken down by nightfall, because a hanged man is cursed by God and the land must not be defiled. The tree did not make him cursed. The tree announced it, so that everyone walking past the field could read the verdict of heaven on that man without being told.

Saul before a cross. Now put Saul of Tarsus in front of a crucified man. For a Pharisee, this text was not a difficulty about Jesus of Nazareth; it was the closing argument. Whatever that man had said, whatever the fishermen were now claiming, God had published his verdict on a beam outside the city wall for the whole province to read. A crucified Messiah was not merely improbable. It was blasphemy with a scriptural footnote, a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). Which is what makes this verse, written by that man, one of the great turnings in Scripture. On the Damascus road the argument did not go away; it went inside out. Saul had been right that the tree published a curse. He had been wrong about only one thing: whose. For us. The two smallest words in the sentence, and they are the whole gospel. He was cursed, and not for anything he had done.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was personally guilty or that God stopped loving his Son. He bore our curse as our substitute, in perfect obedience and love. To say Christ became a curse is not to say the Father was privately disgusted with him, or turned on him in temper. Jesus himself said the opposite: for this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life (John 10:17). The Son was never more precious to the Father than in the hour he was bearing our sentence, and the sentence was real, and both of those are true at once.

Why did it have to be a cross? Because God meant the manner of Christ’s death to say what it was. Any death would have shown that he died; only a death on a tree could show, in the law’s own language, that he died under the curse. The Jewish authorities wanted him crucified to prove God had rejected him, and the Romans wanted it to shame him; God used both to publish the truth they did not intend: that the curse of God was falling on this man for sinners. The shame was not an accident around the edges of the atonement. It was part of the price, and Jesus despised it for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2).

Is this fair, that an innocent man should be punished for the guilty? It would be unjust if a judge seized an unwilling bystander. But that is not what happened. The Son came willingly, as one with the Father in purpose. He is himself the Judge who was wronged, choosing to bear the penalty of those who wronged him. And he is our representative, united to us as our head, as Adam was, so that what he did counts for those who are his. God is not punishing a third party. He is, in his Son, taking the cost of our sin on himself. That is not injustice. It is the highest justice joined to the deepest love (Romans 3:25–26).

In a sentence. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written: “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a pole.”

On a Tuesday. When your past sins come back to accuse you, do not answer by listing your recent improvements. Answer with this verse. Name the sin, and then say: that curse fell on him, outside the city wall, and it will not fall on me. Then live today as someone bought out of the market: not as your own, but glad to belong to the one who paid.

For worship. Stand back and look at the exchange. The law had one thing to say to every human being who came to it for a verdict, and it said it without pity, and it was right to say it. And the Son of God walked into the courtroom, took the sentence before it reached us, and carried it out of the city on his own back. The tree that was designed to publish the curse of God has become the place where the curse of God ran out. There is nothing in the universe like this. Every other religion tells a man what he must do; here is a God who went to the gallows in his place and did it himself.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was under God’s curse.

parallels.desc: a hanged man is cursed by God

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.

So that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. Now the purpose clause, and Paul gives it twice: so that, so that. The cross was not simply a rescue from something; it was a rescue for something, and he names two results, both of which the Judaizers had been quietly denying. First, the blessing promised to Abraham, justification and life, now flows to the nations (v. 8). Trace that line back and it goes to Genesis 12, and it has been travelling for two thousand years, through Isaac and Jacob and a nation and a monarchy and an exile, and here it arrives, in a Galatian town, in the hands of people whose grandparents worshipped Zeus. That is what the cross did. It opened a promise made in Mesopotamia to the whole world.

In Christ Jesus. And observe how it arrives. Not around him, not because God relaxed the terms, not by God deciding after all these years that circumcision did not matter much. The blessing reaches the nations by way of one man’s cross. The Judaizers wanted Gentiles brought in through the door marked become a Jew; God brought them in through a door marked be in Christ, and it is the only door there has ever been.

So that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. Second, the Spirit. And with that Paul has closed the circle he opened in verse 2. He began the chapter by asking how they got the Spirit. He now says the cross is why they got him. Between the question and the answer he has laid out Abraham, the curse, and the exchange, and the whole argument lands back on the Spirit they already have. He is received through faith, not law-keeping (v. 2). The blessing of Abraham and the gift of the Spirit go together.

The promised Spirit. The phrase tells the reader what he is holding. The Spirit is not a bonus for advanced believers or a second stage for the especially earnest. He is the promise: God himself coming to live in Gentile bodies. When Ezekiel said God would put his Spirit within his people and cause them to walk in his statutes (Ezekiel 36:27), and Joel said he would pour him out on all flesh (Joel 2:28), this was what they were describing. The Galatians had it. They were being told they lacked something.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews are excluded. “We” includes Jewish and Gentile believers. The cross brings the blessing to the Gentiles and the Spirit to all who believe, so that Jew and Gentile receive one gift together.

Am I missing a deeper blessing? The most common form of Christian discouragement is not doubt about doctrine; it is the settled suspicion that you have somehow received a lesser version of the Christian faith than other people have: that there is a fuller thing, a deeper blessing, a level of God’s favour that others reached and you did not. Verse 14 forecloses it. The blessing of Abraham and the promised Spirit are not two prizes handed out at different levels of attainment. They are one gift, purchased at one cross, received by one faith, and if you are in Christ you have them. You may grow in enjoying what you have; you will never be given more of a standing than you already possess.

How do I depend on the Spirit day by day? Begin each day by acknowledging him: you live in me, and I need you today. Before you read Scripture, ask him to open it. Before a hard conversation, ask him for the right words and a gentle heart. When temptation comes, ask him for strength in the moment, and then act, trusting that he is giving it. When you fail, do not grieve him further by hiding; confess and return. Depending on the Spirit is not a feeling you wait for. It is a posture of asking, trusting and obeying, all day long.

In a sentence. He redeemed us in order that the blessing given to Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. You have the Spirit by faith. Depend on him today. And when you meet a believer from a background utterly unlike yours, a different nation, a different class, a different religious past, remember that the promise made to Abraham travelled two thousand years to reach both of you, and arrived by the same cross.

For worship. Look at what it cost to get that gift to a Gentile. The curse had to be exhausted, and it was exhausted on the Son of God outside a city wall, in the dark, at the hands of the very people the promise was aimed at. Nothing was cheapened to let the nations in. The full weight of the law’s sentence fell, and it fell on him, so that a man in Iconium with no covenant, no ancestry and no merit could be given the Spirit of the living God. He did not lower the terms. He met them, and then paid for everyone who never could.

parallels.desc: I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temperature drops and Paul takes the Galatians from Golgotha to a lawyer’s office, calling them brothers again, a warm word breaking through the anger. Verse 15 gives the principle from everyday life: once a covenant or will has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a clause. If that holds for a document drawn up by men who forget things and change their minds, how much more for one God has sworn. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise; they were proposing an amendment, and an amendment is not a modest adjustment but a legal impossibility.

Verse 16 makes the exegetical observation that troubles modern readers: the promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ. Since the word is collective in both Hebrew and Greek, this looks like a trick — until you notice that Paul himself uses it collectively in v. 29. The argument is not about grammar in isolation but about the shape of the history. The promise narrowed at every fork: Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau, Judah, David. It was always funnelling toward one person.

Verse 17 dates it. The law came 430 years after the promise, and the later document cannot cancel the earlier one; the figure follows the Greek Old Testament Paul’s churches used, which counts from Abraham to the exodus. Verse 18 states the either-or underneath: if the inheritance comes by law it no longer comes by promise. These are not two ingredients that improve each other but two answers to the question of who is responsible for my standing, and the second cancels the first.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priority and Indestructibility of the Promise

The covenant of grace — God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s seed — is prior to the Mosaic law and independent of it. This is a foundation of Reformed covenant theology, and vv. 15 and 17 are where Paul argues it. The Mosaic administration does not replace the Abrahamic covenant or amend its terms; it operates within it and serves it for a season, leaving its character as promise untouched.

Verse 16 supplies the reason the promise cannot fail, and it is more than a point of grammar. Had God covenanted with Abraham’s descendants as a body, the covenant would have rested in the hands of a nation that broke every arrangement it was given. He covenanted with one heir who would not break it, and everyone else inherits by being in him. Verse 18 draws the practical edge: God “has given” it, in the perfect tense, and it stands given. A promise whose security is the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything conditioned on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were arguing, in effect, that the later Mosaic legislation modified the conditions of the earlier Abrahamic promise. Verses 15 and 17 show why that is not a theological preference but a legal impossibility, and v. 18 shows what it would cost if it were allowed: not an improved promise but no promise at all. Verse 16 removes their last foothold by identifying the heir they were claiming to represent.

Now: The difference v. 18 describes is invisible from the outside. Two Christians can keep the same hours, give the same money and serve on the same rota, one obeying a Father who has already given him the house, the other trying to secure a house he is not sure of. You can tell them apart only when something goes wrong: one fails and runs to his Father, the other fails and hides, because for him the failure has moved the inheritance. Verses 15–18 exist to put every reader in the first category and keep him there.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.

To give a human example, brothers. The temperature drops. He has just been at Golgotha; now he takes them to a lawyer’s office for an illustration from everyday life. And he calls them brothers, the anger letting a warm word through, as it did at 1:11.

Even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. The word is diathēkē, which covers both a covenant and a last will and testament, and Paul is using the overlap. His point holds either way. Once a will is signed and legally confirmed, the seals on and the witnesses signed, an interested party cannot come along later and insert a clause. If that is true of a document drawn up by men, who forget things and change their minds, how much more of an agreement God has sworn to?

An amendment is a different document. The relevance is exact. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise to Abraham. They were proposing an amendment: the promise, plus a condition. Paul says that is not a modest adjustment. It is a legal impossibility, and anyone attempting it is not adding to God’s covenant but writing a different one.

Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. God’s promises to Abraham are repeated again and again (Genesis 12:7; 13:15; 17:8; 22:18). Then verse 16, and this is where readers stop and frown, so it must be dealt with properly.

It does not say, “And to offsprings,” but “And to your offspring,” who is Christ. Paul observes that God said to your offspring, singular, not offsprings, plural, and concludes that the promise was made to one person, who is Christ. To a modern reader that looks like a trick. Offspring (literally seed) is a collective noun, singular in form, often plural in meaning, and the Hebrew zera’ and the Greek sperma behind it work the same way. Genesis 15:5 promised Abraham descendants as numerous as the stars, and it plainly does not mean one star. Is Paul playing games with grammar? He is not, and the proof is thirteen verses later. In verse 29 Paul himself uses the same word collectively: you are Abraham’s offspring, of a whole church full of people. A man does not build an argument on a word’s singularity and then use it of a crowd unless he knows exactly what the word does.

The promise always narrowed. So what is the argument? This: the promise to Abraham always narrowed. It was never simply handed to his descendants as a body. Ishmael was a son of Abraham and was not the line of promise: through Isaac shall your offspring be named (Genesis 21:12). Esau was a son of Isaac and was passed over. The line runs to Judah, then to David, then to David’s house, and at every fork it gets narrower, never wider. Read the story forwards and it is obviously funnelling toward somebody. The singular form is what permits Paul to say what the shape of the history was always saying: this promise had one destination, and it was a person. All the promises find their fulfilment in Christ, and those united to him share in them. And Genesis itself hints at it: after the binding of Isaac God says that in Abraham’s offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, and the offspring will possess the gate of his enemies (Genesis 22:17–18). Paul is not importing Christ into the Old Testament. He is reading it the way the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is playing with grammar. He sees that Scripture narrows the promise from Abraham’s many descendants to the line of Isaac, of Judah, of David, and finally to Christ.

Do all the promises of the Old Testament apply to me? All the covenant promises of God find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and if you are in Christ you share in them: forgiveness, God as your God, his presence, his Spirit, his faithfulness, an everlasting inheritance. But read each promise in its setting. Some were given to particular people for particular situations, such as a specific word to a king or to the exiles in Babylon, and they show God’s character rather than guaranteeing you the same outcome. The safe way is to ask: what does this promise show about God, and how is it fulfilled in Christ? Then you can claim it through him without twisting it.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, let Paul take an example from everyday life. Just as no one can set aside or add to a human covenant that has been duly established, so it is in this case. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Scripture does not say “and to seeds,” meaning many people, but “and to your seed,” meaning one person, who is Christ.

On a Tuesday. The pastoral force of this is easy to miss. If the promise was made to Christ, then the promise cannot fail, because its heir cannot fail. When you doubt whether God will keep his word to you, stop looking at your own reliability and look at his Son’s. The promise does not rest on your grip. It rests on the one to whom it was made, and you are in him.

For worship. Had God made his covenant with Abraham’s descendants as a body and left it there, it would have been in the hands of a nation that broke every covenant it was ever given, and in ours. He made it with one man who would not break it, and everyone else gets in by being in him. Every promise of God to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ, and through him, to you. The God who narrowed two thousand years of history down to a single Seed did it so that the promise could never be lost, and he has kept it to the letter.
verseByVerse.note: “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one descendant or many.

parallels.desc: in your offspring shall all the nations be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.

The law, which came 430 years afterward. This is what Paul means, and now he puts a date on it. The law does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God. The promise is the older document by four centuries, and in any court the later paper cannot cancel the earlier one. A later law cannot cancel an earlier promise. God’s covenant with Abraham stands.

The 430 years. A reader with a study Bible will stop at the number, and he is right to. Exodus 12:40 says the people of Israel lived in Egypt 430 years. But the Greek Old Testament that Paul and his readers used, and the Samaritan text, read in Egypt and in Canaan, that is, 430 years from the patriarchs to the exodus in total. Paul uses this figure for the gap between the promise and the law at Sinai, counting from the promises to the patriarchs, using the text his churches had in their hands. And nothing in his argument depends on the exact figure. Four hundred and thirty years, or four hundred, or two hundred: the promise came first, and that is the whole point.

For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise. Then verse 18 states the principle underneath, and it is the cleanest either-or in the letter. Inheritance and law are opposite principles. An inheritance is given; a wage is earned. Paul is not saying that law and promise are enemies. He is saying they are different kinds of thing, and that a single inheritance cannot be received on both terms at once. A promise is something one party swears and the other receives. A law is something one party demands and the other performs. Try to hold both and you have not enriched the promise, you have dissolved it, because the moment my performance is a condition, the swearing was never the ground.

The father and the tidy room. Illustrate it and it becomes obvious. A father tells his son that the house will be his when the father dies; it is written, signed, witnessed. Later the father says: and keep your room tidy. If tidiness is housekeeping in the ordinary sense, how a son who has been given a house behaves in it, nothing has changed. But if tidiness is now the condition of inheriting, then the son does not have a promise any more. He has a contract, and he will spend the rest of his life measuring the floor, and he will never once be sure.

Obeying God, or securing God. That is precisely the difference between a Christian who obeys God and a Christian who is trying to secure God. The behaviour can look identical from the outside. Both are up early. Both give. Both serve. The difference is invisible until something goes wrong, and then it is unmistakable: one of them fails and runs to his Father, and the other fails and hides, because the failure has just moved his inheritance.

But God gave it to Abraham by a promise. The verb is charizomai, to give freely, as a gift of grace, from the same root as grace itself. And it is a perfect tense: God has given, and it stands given, once and permanently. That is the tense the whole Christian life rests on. The deed was signed before Sinai, before Moses, before there was a law to keep or break, and it was signed by someone who does not revise (Romans 4:13–16; Hebrews 6:17–18). Salvation is a promise received, not a reward earned.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law was pointless. Paul explains its purpose next.

Can I lose my inheritance? Not if it rests on God’s promise, and that is exactly Paul’s point. An inheritance that depended on your performance could be forfeited any day. One given by promise depends on the faithfulness of the one who promised, and God does not break his word. That is why Scripture can speak of an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you, by God’s power guarding you through faith (1 Peter 1:4–5). True believers persevere, not because they hold on so tightly, but because they are held. If you are worried that you have lost it, the worry itself shows you care; bring it to Christ, and rest on what he has promised.

In a sentence. What Paul means is this: the law, introduced 430 years later, does not set aside the covenant previously established by God and thus do away with the promise. For if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on the promise; but God in his grace gave it to Abraham through a promise.

On a Tuesday. Your inheritance in Christ rests on God’s promise, not your performance. Rest in it. Then notice what you do the next time you fail: do you run to your Father or hide from him? If you hide, preach this verse to yourself: God gave it by a promise, and it stands given. Then go and confess, and get up, and keep the room tidy because the house is already yours.

For worship. God signed the deed four centuries before Sinai and never once considered revising it. Through Egypt and the wilderness, through judges and kings and exile, through every generation that failed to keep the law, the promise stood untouched, because it had never rested on them. He is the God who gives freely and does not take back, and every inheritance he has ever granted by grace is as secure today as the day he swore it.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt; Paul uses the figure for the long gap between the promise and the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify, cannot give life and cannot amend the promise, the obvious objection has to be faced, and v. 19 faces it: why then the law? Paul answers with three phrases, each of which puts the law in its place without insulting it. It was added because of transgressions — drawing the line that turns vague wrongness into named counts. It was until the offspring should come, with an expiry written into it, not a failure but a term. And it was put in place through angels by an intermediary, which is the sharpest demotion of all.

Verse 20 is the most compressed sentence in the letter, and honest commentators admit that its details are disputed. But the direction is clear from the chain Paul has just counted. A mediator implies two parties; the presence of Moses on the mountain tells you Sinai was a two-sided arrangement that could fail, and it failed at the foot of the mountain. God is one: when he came to Abraham there was no second party, and in Genesis 15 he passed alone between the pieces while Abraham slept through his own covenant.

Verse 21 asks whether the law is therefore contrary to God’s promises and answers with Paul’s strongest negative. They are not rivals but a diagnosis and a cure. He grants freely that if any law could give life, righteousness would have come that way. Verse 22 gives the true verdict: Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, shut in like fish in a net, so that the promise might be given by faith. Verses 23–25 name the jailer’s office — the law was our paidagōgos, the household slave who walked the boy to school until he came of age. Verse 24 says he was doing it so we might be justified by faith, and v. 25 says the arrangement has ended.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Genuine, Severe, Temporary, Fulfilled

Reformed theology has always held to the unity of the covenant of grace across both Testaments while recognising the distinct function of the Mosaic administration within it. Verses 19 and 24 are the classic ground for that. The law was genuinely from God, genuinely binding in its time, and genuinely serving the covenant of grace — but it was designed for a phase and not for the end. Its close as a system of justification is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

Two guards belong with vv. 23–25. It does not follow that God’s moral will has been repealed: Paul will say in 5:14 that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour. What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors. Nor does it follow that Old Testament believers were second-class. They were children in the same family under the care their age required. And v. 22 shows the severity was mercy: the exits were closed so that the one open door would finally be taken.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian reinstated after the child had come of age. Verse 19 answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has expired, v. 20 that the promise never depended on two signatures anyway, and v. 25 that the arrangement is over.

Now: Verses 21–25 meet three readers: the one who assumes his problem is information or willpower, the one who finds that the harder he tries the worse the accounting gets, and the largest group of all — believers who are adults in Christ and still live as if under supervision.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.

Why then the law? Paul has been so severe about the law that the obvious objection now has to be faced, and he faces it head on. If it cannot justify, cannot give life, and cannot amend the promise, why did God give it at all? Was Sinai a mistake? The answer is three phrases, and each one puts the law in its place without insulting it.

It was added because of transgressions. Added is the first demotion: an addition is not the foundation. And because of transgressions means this: sin was in the world long before Sinai, but it was not yet transgression in the full sense. A transgression is a stepping over, the deliberate breaking of God’s known law, and you cannot step over a line that has not been drawn. The law drew the line. It took the vague human sense that something is wrong with us and turned it into ten specific counts with names on them. As Paul puts it elsewhere, he would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, you shall not covet (Romans 7:7; see also 3:20; 4:15; 5:20). The law makes sin visible, restrains it, and shows our need of a Saviour.

The diagnosis, not the medicine. That sounds like a strange gift, and it is one of the kindest things God could have done. A man who feels vaguely unwell will put off the appointment for years; a man handed a diagnosis with a name on it goes that afternoon. The law is the diagnosis. It does not cause the disease and it cannot cure it, and anyone who mistakes the chart for the medicine will die holding it. But without it we would have gone on managing our symptoms and calling ourselves basically decent people, which is exactly what most of the human race is doing.

Until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made. The second demotion, and it is the one that ends the argument with the Judaizers. The law, as the governing covenant, came with an end written into it. Not a failure but a term. It was doing a job for a period, and the period ran until the Offspring of verse 16 arrived. He has arrived. A man who insists on the old arrangement after the date is not being more faithful than everyone else; he is standing on a platform arguing about timetables while the train he was waiting for is pulling out.

And it was put in place through angels by an intermediary. The third demotion, and the sharpest. Scripture describes Sinai as attended by angelic hosts: the Lord came from ten thousands of holy ones (Deuteronomy 33:2), and the chariots of God were among them (Psalm 68:17). Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law, and both Stephen and the writer to the Hebrews take it for granted that the law was delivered by angels (Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2). Then Moses stood between the LORD and the people, because the people were afraid and begged not to hear the voice themselves (Deuteronomy 5:5; Exodus 20:19). Count the links in that chain: God, angels, Moses, Israel. Now count the links in the promise: God, Abraham. The law came down a staircase. The promise was handed over directly. If you want to know which of the two is the greater, do not ask which is louder or which has more smoke on the mountain. Ask how many people God needed between himself and the man he was speaking to.

Where Christians differ: the uses of the law. Some say the law has no role for Christians at all; others make it the centre of the Christian life. Verdict: the Reformers identified three uses of the law. First, it shows sin and drives sinners to Christ (the use Paul focuses on here). Second, it restrains evil in society. Third, it guides believers in how to please God, as the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments (Romans 13:8–10). The ceremonial and civil laws of Israel were fulfilled and ended in Christ, but the moral law remains the rule of life, not as a covenant of works, but as the will of our Father (Westminster 19.5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law is evil or that God changed his mind. It was always meant to point to Christ.

Why would God give a law he knew no one could keep? Because its main purpose was never to be the ladder by which we climb to him. It was given to a people he had already redeemed, as the shape of a holy life, with sacrifices built in for their failures. And it was given to show all of us, with total clarity, what we are and what we need. A law that sinners could keep perfectly would have flattered us and left us without Christ. A law we cannot keep strips away every excuse and sends us to the one who kept it for us. God was not setting a trap. He was drawing a map, and every road on it ends at the cross.

In a sentence. Why, then, was the law given at all? It was added because of transgressions until the Seed to whom the promise referred had come. The law was given through angels and entrusted to a mediator.

On a Tuesday. Read one of the Ten Commandments slowly this week, the way Jesus read them in the Sermon on the Mount: not only the deed but the desire, not only murder but anger, not only theft but covetousness. Let it show you where you stand. Then do what the law is meant to make you do: go to Christ with what it has shown you, and thank him that he kept it all.

For worship. Thank God for his law, which showed you your sin and sent you to Christ. The same God who thundered on Sinai through angels and a trembling mediator has now spoken to us by his Son, face to face. The law came down a staircase of messengers; the promise came straight from his mouth; and when the Offspring arrived, God himself had come down the whole staircase to stand among us. The diagnosis was given so that the cure would be wanted, and the cure is the Lord himself.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law; Moses was the intermediary.

parallels.desc: I stood between the LORD and you

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.

Now an intermediary implies more than one. This is famously one of the most compressed sentences in the letter, and commentators have counted hundreds of proposed readings of it. It is worth admitting that plainly rather than pretending to a certainty nobody has. But the direction of the thought is not really in doubt, because Paul has just spent verse 19 counting links in a chain. A mediator, by definition, stands between parties, each with obligations. You do not need one where there is only one party involved. So the very presence of Moses on the mountain tells you what kind of arrangement Sinai was: a two-sided covenant with conditions, God on one side, Israel on the other, with a man in the middle holding the terms. All that the LORD has spoken we will do, the people said (Exodus 19:8). Everything then depended on both parties keeping their word, and everyone knows how that went; the people had barely received the covenant before there was a golden calf at the foot of the mountain.

But God is one. When God came to Abraham there was no second party and no man in the middle. The promise was God’s alone, unconditional, depending only on him. Abraham did not negotiate; he was asleep. In the strangest scene in Genesis, God put him into a deep sleep and then passed alone between the pieces of the sacrifice: a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch walking the aisle of blood by themselves (Genesis 15:12, 17). In such a ceremony the two parties would walk the path together and invoke the fate of the animals on whoever broke faith. God walked it alone. He took the oath on himself, binding only himself, and Abraham slept through his own covenant.

Two signatures or one. So the contrast is not between a harsh arrangement and a kind one. It is between an agreement that can fail because it has two signatures on it, and a promise that cannot fail because it has one, and the one who signed it is God, who does not have a bad year. The main point is clear: the promise is greater than the law because it rests on God alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is not a mediator. Christ is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), and he is himself God. That is exactly why his mediation is not like Moses’. Moses stood between two parties as a third man. Christ stands between God and us as one who is both, fully God and fully man, so that in him the promise rests on God alone and is brought to us by one of us.

What is a mediator, and why do I need one? A mediator is someone who stands between two parties to bring them together. We need one because there is a real distance between a holy God and sinners: not of miles but of guilt. Moses could carry God’s words to the people, but he could not take away their sin; he once offered to be blotted out for them, and God would not accept it (Exodus 32:32–33). Christ is the mediator Moses could not be. He does not only carry messages; he offers himself, and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). You need no other go-between, no priest, saint or ritual. You come to the Father through the Son.

In a sentence. A mediator, however, implies more than one party; but God is one.

On a Tuesday. Do the sum on your own life, because it is the difference between two entirely different experiences of being a Christian. If your standing with God is a two-party arrangement, then it is only ever as secure as your last fortnight, and every failure is a breach, and you will spend your life in the anxious accounting that looks so much like devotion from the outside. If it is a one-party promise, then your failures are real, and grievous, and to be repented of, and they are not renegotiations. There is nothing for them to renegotiate. Only one name is on the document. Your salvation rests on God alone, not on your side of a bargain. Trust him.

For worship. God put a man to sleep and swore the whole covenant by himself, knowing every century of unfaithfulness that was coming, and knowing exactly what it would cost him to keep his own oath when the other side had broken theirs. He walked between the pieces alone under the night sky, and two thousand years later he walked out to a hill alone, and kept it. If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13; Hebrews 6:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.

Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! Paul has demoted the law three times in two verses, and he knows how it sounds, so he asks the question his opponents would shout. And the answer is mē genoito, the strongest negative he owns, the one he reserves for conclusions that would be blasphemous if true. The law and the promise both came from the same God and both serve the same purpose in his one plan. They are not rivals. They are a diagnosis and a cure, and only a fool sets those against each other.

For if a law had been given that could give life. Then the reason, and it is a careful sentence: then righteousness would indeed be by the law. Notice that Paul is entirely willing to say it. If any legal code could make a dead man live, God would have used it. The law is not being blamed for failing at a job it was given. It was never given that job, because no law can do it. It can command but not empower; it can show the way but not carry us along it (Romans 8:3). A speed limit has never once made a reckless man careful. It tells him what careful looks like and records the fact that he is not.

The true measure of our condition. What law cannot do is generate life, and that shows how serious our condition is. If we were merely misinformed, instruction would be enough; if we were merely weak, encouragement would be enough. Scripture says we were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), and nothing you say to a corpse improves it. We needed not better advice but resurrection.

But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin. Then verse 22, and the image is a prison. The verb is synkleiō: shut up together, locked in with no other door; it is the word Luke uses for a great shoal of fish enclosed in a net (Luke 5:6). And the object is not only everyone but everything, the whole realm, the entire order of things. Scripture declares all people guilty, locked in a prison with no escape (Romans 3:9–20; 11:32). Nobody is standing outside the net commenting on the people inside it. And note the jailer. It is Scripture that did the locking. God’s own word turned the key, which means our confinement is not an accident of history or a verdict we can appeal to a higher authority. It is published, and it is his.

So that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. That is savage, until you read the purpose clause. The imprisonment is a mercy. As long as a man believes there is another way out, he will keep trying doors. He will try being respectable, and being useful, and being sincere, and being spiritual, and each door will hold just enough to keep him busy. God locked every one of them so that we would finally turn round and see the one door that stands open, and it has a person’s name on it. The purpose of the prison is to make us look for the only way out, the promise received by faith in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is cruel. He shuts us up in order to set us free. Paul says the same in Romans: God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all (Romans 11:32).

Does “everything under sin” include the good people I know? Yes, and that includes you and me. Some people are kinder, more honest and more generous than others, and God is pleased with real kindness wherever it is found. But no one has loved God with all his heart, and no one has kept the law, and a good life lived for oneself is still a life lived apart from God. The verse is not saying everyone is as bad as he could be. It is saying everyone is shut in the same prison, the respectable and the disreputable alike, and needs the same way out. That is humbling, and it is also the great leveller: the nicest person you know and the worst person you know are invited to Christ on exactly the same terms.

In a sentence. Is the law, therefore, opposed to the promises of God? Absolutely not! For if a law had been given that could impart life, then righteousness would certainly have come by the law. But Scripture has locked up everything under the control of sin, so that what was promised, being given through faith in Jesus Christ, might be given to those who believe.

On a Tuesday. If you have come to a point where nothing you can do about yourself seems to work, and the harder you try the worse the accounting gets, do not read that as God’s absence. It may well be his kindness. He is not punishing you with failure. He is closing the exits so that you will stop trying to be your own way out and take the one he has provided. Stop rattling the locked doors. Turn round to Christ today.

For worship. Thank God that he locked you in by the law, so that he could set you free in Christ. The jailer and the deliverer are the same God, and he never meant the prison to be the end of the story. He closed every door but one, and then he himself became the door (John 10:9), and he holds it open still to everyone who believes.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,

Now before faith came. Paul is using the word in a bigger sense than the act of trusting. Abraham had faith, and so did Habakkuk. He means the era of faith: the age that opened when Christ came and the gospel went out to the nations, so that faith in Christ is now the open, public, announced way in. Not that no one had faith before, but that the age of faith in its fullness began with Christ. The Old Testament believer was looking down a corridor at a door he could not yet see. We are standing in the room.

We were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. “Held captive” is phroureō, to guard, to keep under watch, as a garrison guards a city; then the same verb as verse 22, shut in. Israel was guarded by the law. A temporary custody.

So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came. Now comes the image that governs the whole passage, and it is worth getting right, because most readers have been given a sentimental version of it. The law, Paul says, was our paidagōgos. Older English versions said schoolmaster, which is misleading. A paidagōgos was not the teacher. He was a household slave, usually an older one, often stern, sometimes harsh, and in the comic plays of the period a byword for being no fun at all. He was given charge of the boy from about six until he came of age. He walked him to school and walked him home, kept him off the wrong streets, checked his manners, and had a stick and authority to use it. He was not there to educate the boy. He was there to get him to the one who would, and to keep him out of trouble on the way. The law guarded and disciplined Israel until Christ.

Three things about the guardian. So three things follow, and they are the whole answer to the Judaizers. The paidagōgos was genuinely appointed: the father chose him, and the boy who resented him was resenting his father’s arrangement. He was genuinely strict, and strictness was the job. And he was genuinely temporary: nobody was under a paidagōgos at thirty. His whole office was defined by an end.

In order that we might be justified by faith. The law’s purpose was to lead to justification by faith in Christ. Even its strictness was aimed at the moment it would hand the boy over.

But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. Christ has come. The son has come of age. The guardian’s job is done. And the Judaizers were going to the grown man in the courtyard and telling him that if he really wanted to please his father, he should send for the old slave again and ask to be walked to school.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers may live as they please. Grown sons still honour their father’s will, but from love, not as children under supervision. God’s moral will has not been repealed; Paul will spend the last two chapters of this letter telling these people how to live, and will say the whole law is fulfilled in one word: you shall love your neighbour as yourself (5:14). What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the system of guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors, together with its ceremonies. Christians are not under the law to be saved, but they are not without law; they are under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21). Nor does it mean the Old Testament era was a mistake or that those believers were second-class. They were children in the same family, in the care their age required, waiting for the day this letter says has now arrived.

How do I stop living like a child under supervision? Many believers are technically adults in Christ and emotionally still under the guardian: still measuring the day’s performance, still expecting the stick, still surprised by kindness. Start by believing what your Father has said, that you are his son or daughter, not his employee or his ward on probation. Talk to him as a child talks to a loving father, plainly and often. When you obey, do it because you want to please him, not to keep him from punishing you. When you fail, go to him, not away. And let the Spirit’s cry of Abba, Father (4:6) become your own. It takes time to unlearn the guardian, but the guardian has been dismissed.

In a sentence. Before the coming of this faith, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until the faith that was to come would be revealed. So the law was our guardian until Christ came that we might be justified by faith. Now that this faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.

On a Tuesday. You are no longer a child under a guardian. Live as a grown son or daughter of God, from love and freedom. Notice this week where you are still waiting for the stick: the prayer you do not pray because you have not been good enough, the confession you put off because you fear the response. Your Father did not merely relax the rules. He ended the arrangement and brought you into the house as an heir.

For worship. The Father who appointed the guardian also set the date of its dismissal, and on that date he sent his own Son. Everything strict and narrow in the old arrangement was the Father’s care for children too young for the house; everything open and free in the new is the same Father’s joy in sons come of age. He has never been anything but a father, and now at last he has brought his children in.
verseByVerse.note: The “guardian” (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a child, took him to school and kept him in line until he came of age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Through faith, all of them are sons of God in Christ Jesus, for all who were baptised into Christ have put him on like a garment. In him the divisions that ruled the ancient world, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, no longer determine anyone’s standing; all are one in Christ. And if they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring and heirs of the promise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a location. He is in Christ, clothed in Christ, and therefore holds the status of the Son. This is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well; the clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer.

Verse 28 is the theological ground of the New Testament’s social revolution. The gospel does not merely change individuals, it creates a community in which the stratifications of the old age no longer determine worth or access. Sincere believers who honour this book read the verse differently when it comes to office and order, some hearing the end of every distinction of role, others holding that Paul speaks of standing here and of roles elsewhere, which is the more natural reading of the whole Pauline corpus. What neither side qualifies is what the verse indisputably says, and it is the larger thing: at the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance of v. 29 there is no smaller share.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jew and Greek was a divide so absolute that a Jew would not enter a Gentile house; slave and free described perhaps a third of a city’s population as property; male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. A saying recorded in later rabbinic sources thanked God for not having been made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Verse 28 takes those three walls and says they do not run through the room. Verses 26–27 explain why: everyone in it is wearing the same garment. Verse 29 tells Gentile believers they are not associate members of a Jewish covenant but full heirs.

Now:Every congregation holds people who have quietly concluded they are second rank. Verse 28 does not offer them a role; it says something better and harder to believe, that Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. The guardian has been dismissed in the verse before; now we are told what the boy has become. Not a graduate. A son. Take the words one at a time, because every one of them is aimed at something the Judaizers were saying. You: the Galatians, the uncircumcised, the ones being told they were not yet full members. All: no tiers. Sons: not children under a guardian, not wards, not apprentices, but adult sons with full rights of inheritance (4:5–7). Through faith: not through the knife. And in front of it all, governing everything, in Christ Jesus: by union with him. The sonship is not something we possess in ourselves; it is ours because we are in the Son.

Sons, not only children. A word about sons, since a modern reader may hear it as a door closing. Paul writes huioi, sons, and he does it deliberately, because in that world sons inherited and daughters generally did not. “Sons” includes daughters; the word is not about gender but about legal status, the standing of the heir. So when a woman reads verse 26 she is not listening in on something addressed to the men. She is being told that she holds the inheritance rights of a son in the household of God. Two verses later Paul will say so explicitly. Far from excluding her, this is the most generous word in the sentence.

For as many of you as were baptized into Christ. Paul’s readers had been baptised in water when they believed, and he speaks of their baptism as the moment they were joined to Christ, because in the New Testament faith and baptism belonged together: people believed and were baptised at once (Acts 8:12; 16:31–33). Baptism is the visible sign of that union (Romans 6:3–4). What actually unites a person to Christ is the Spirit, received through faith (v. 14; 1 Corinthians 12:13); water baptism is the outward picture and public confession of it. So Paul can speak of the sign and mean the reality it signifies, as we might say “she gave her hand in marriage” and mean the whole covenant of marriage.

Have put on Christ. The clothing image. “Put on” is endyō, the ordinary word for dressing, and in the Roman world it carried a particular resonance that fits this passage exactly. When a boy came of age, the family held a ceremony in which he laid aside the child’s toga with its purple border and put on the plain white toga virilis, the garment of a man, and from that day he was treated as one. Paul has just dismissed the guardian. Now he hands out the adult garment, and the garment is Christ himself. Believers have put on Christ: covered with his righteousness, identified with him (Romans 13:14; Isaiah 61:10).

What the Father sees. So what the Father sees when he looks at a believer is not first a person making progress. It is his Son’s own righteousness worn as clothing, covering everything the man is ashamed of and everything he has not yet dealt with. That is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well. The clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some take this verse to mean that water baptism itself unites a person to Christ and regenerates them; Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it this way. Verdict: Paul has just said we are sons through faith (v. 26), and the whole chapter has insisted that everything comes through faith (vv. 2, 14, 26) and nothing by an outward rite performed on the body. Baptism is the sign and seal of union with Christ, which is received by faith. It is not the cause of union. Those who are baptised with faith truly put on Christ; baptism without faith does not save (1 Peter 3:21; Westminster 28.5; London Baptist Confession 29.1). This app holds believer’s baptism: the sign follows the faith it signifies, which is exactly the order in this verse: sons through faith (v. 26), then baptised into Christ (v. 27). Christians who baptise infants see baptism as the sign of the covenant given, like circumcision, to believers’ children (Colossians 2:11–12); they are our brothers, and both sides confess what this verse indisputably says: what clothes a sinner before God is Christ, received by faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism is unimportant. It is commanded and precious. But it is not magic.

I was baptised as an infant. Should I be baptised now? On the view this app holds, baptism is for those who have believed, so a believer who was baptised only as an infant has not yet received believer’s baptism and should ask for it, gladly, as an act of obedience and public confession. It is not a rejection of your parents’ love or prayers, which were real gifts. Talk it through with your pastor and read the New Testament passages on baptism for yourself. And hold your view with charity: many faithful Christians and churches, including the Westminster tradition, sincerely believe infant baptism is right. Do not make the disagreement a wall between you and them. You are clothed with the same Christ.

In a sentence. So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith, for all of you who were baptised into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.

On a Tuesday. Look at what that means for an ordinary Sunday. There is no better-dressed Christian in your congregation than you. The most disciplined believer you know is wearing exactly what you are wearing, and neither of you made it, and neither of you paid for it. When you feel exposed before God this week, by a memory or a failure, remember what you are wearing, and come to him clothed in his Son.

For worship. You are clothed with Christ. The Father has taken off the rags of every child he has adopted and dressed them in the robe of his own beloved Son, and he did not weigh their merits first. I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation (Isaiah 61:10). The wedding garment is his gift, and no one at the feast is wearing anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female. Paul now says the thing that has echoed for two thousand years. Feel the size of it in its own century. Those three pairs were not opinions about society; they were the load-bearing walls of the ancient world. Jew and Greek was the great religious and ethnic divide, so deep that a strict Jew would not enter a Gentile house. Slave and free was the great social and economic divide, and a large part of the population of a city like Corinth was property. Male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. A Jewish morning prayer recorded in later rabbinic sources, probably reflecting older sentiment, thanked God for not making the man praying a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Paul reverses all three. He takes those three walls and says that in Christ they do not run through the room.

No male and female. One detail in the Greek is easy to pass over. The first two pairs are neither, nor. The third changes: no male and female, which is not clumsiness but an echo. It is the wording of Genesis 1:27 in the Greek Old Testament: male and female he created them. Paul has reached past the social order all the way back to the creation account, as if to say: even the deepest distinction God made in humanity does not determine your standing in Christ.

For you are all one in Christ Jesus. One is heis, one person: not one in the sense of identical, but one body, one new man in Christ. So what exactly is being levelled? The context answers it, because Paul has not changed the subject: he is talking about who is a son of Abraham, who is justified, who is clothed in Christ, who inherits. On that ground, the ground where a person stands before God, the three walls are gone entirely. There is not a Jewish justification and a Gentile one, a free man’s adoption and a slave’s, a fuller portion for a husband and a lesser one for his wife. One Christ, one righteousness, one inheritance, and every believer holds all of it: equally justified, equally sons, equally heirs.

Difference remains; difference as worth has gone. Is it then the abolition of the differences themselves? Plainly not in every sense, and Paul’s own letters prove it. Paul goes on being a Jew; Onesimus goes on being a slave in the eyes of Roman law while Paul works on Philemon to receive him as a brother; and men and women go on being men and women. Difference remains. What has gone is difference as a measure of worth and as a condition of access to God.

Where Christians differ: does this verse abolish gender roles? Egalitarians use this verse to argue that all distinctions of role between men and women in the church and home are abolished in Christ; they see the verse as the principle and the restrictions elsewhere as temporary concessions to Paul’s culture. Verdict: the context is about who is justified and who is an heir of Abraham: all believers equally, regardless of race, class or sex. It is about status before God, not roles in the church. The distinctions themselves are not abolished: Jews remain Jews, men remain men. Paul elsewhere teaches distinct roles for men and women in the home and church (1 Corinthians 11:3; Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Timothy 2:12), grounded in creation, not culture. Slavery is no parallel: Paul gave instructions to slaves while sowing the seeds of their freedom (Philemon), but he never grounded slavery in creation. Equal in worth, distinct in calling: the complementarian view. And headship in Scripture is the self-giving love of Christ for his church, never domination; any abuse of a wife or of any person is a grave sin that the church must never tolerate or cover.

What it does not mean. It does not mean differences of ethnicity, status or sex are unimportant in life. It means they do not affect our standing with God.

Does this verse condemn racism and snobbery in the church? Yes, plainly. If Christ has given the same standing to every believer, then any church that treats some believers as lesser because of their race, nationality, class, education or sex is denying in practice what this verse says. That was Peter’s sin at Antioch (2:11–14). It can look like separate congregations divided by colour where there is no language reason, leaders always drawn from one social group, a cool welcome for the poor or the foreigner, jokes at someone’s background. Repent of it where you see it in yourself, and gently challenge it where you see it in your church. The one table of the Lord is meant to look like the one family he has made.

In a sentence. There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Here it stops being a debating point and starts being pastoral. Every congregation contains people who have quietly concluded that they are the second rank: the woman who has been talked past in every church she has attended, the man whose accent or job or prison record marks him out, the family that will never be asked to host anything, the convert whose parents are not believers and who feels the room close slightly when testimonies are given. Look at the people in your church who are different from you. In Christ, you are one. Treat them so: seek one of them out this Sunday, and listen.

For worship. Verse 28 does not offer the overlooked a role. It says something better and harder to believe: you are not on the edge of this. Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building than the one he has already given you. The one who made us male and female, who scattered the nations at Babel and called Abraham out of them, has now gathered a people out of every tribe and class into one body in his Son. At the foot of the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance there is no smaller share.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring. The whole chapter comes to rest here, and the logic is one clean line. The promise was made to the Offspring, and the Offspring is Christ (v. 16). Therefore everything depends on one question only: are you his? If you belong to Christ, you are inside the one to whom everything was promised, and it is all yours. Now Paul uses offspring in its collective sense: in Christ, all believers are Abraham’s seed.

Not by lowering the requirements. Notice the route the argument does not take. Paul does not say you have become a good enough Jew, or you have qualified, or God has decided to be generous with the entry requirements. The requirements were never lowered. Every one of them was met by one man, and you are in him. The argument of the chapter comes to its conclusion: the Gentile Galatians do not need circumcision to become Abraham’s children. They already are, in Christ.

Heirs according to promise. Weigh the word heirs. An heir is not someone who has been given a gift; he is someone who has been given a standing, and the estate follows from the standing. He does not earn it, cannot be dismissed from it, and does not receive it because he has been useful. He receives it because of who he is in the family. This is why nobody in the New Testament is told to work at becoming an heir. You cannot work your way into a family tree (Romans 8:16–17; Ephesians 1:11). And it is not by law, but by promise.

What is actually inherited? Scripture does not leave it vague, and the vagueness of much Christian talk about the future is a loss, not a piety. Heirs of everything God promised Abraham: righteousness, the Spirit, the world to come (Romans 4:13). God himself as your portion, which is the substance of every promise (Genesis 15:1). A body that does not fail, raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). A world put right and handed over, the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5; Romans 8:17–21). A face to see, the thing Moses asked for and was not given (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4). And real service in a real kingdom (Luke 19:17). That is what stands to the account of the Galatian farmer who believed a travelling preacher, and it is what stands to yours.

Where Christians differ: the land and Israel’s future. Does this mean that the promises of land and nation to Israel are now void? Paul says that all who are Christ’s are Abraham’s heirs, so the promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared by everyone in him, Jew and Gentile alike. That is not a rejection of the Jewish people; Paul himself was one, and he insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). Dispensational Christians hold that the land and nation promises remain for ethnic Israel; covenantal premillennialists also expect a future earthly fulfilment. Many Reformed Christians hold that the promise to Abraham was always larger than a strip of land: he would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the inheritance is the renewed creation, which belongs to all who are Christ’s. All agree that God’s purposes for ethnic Israel continue (Romans 11), and that no one inherits anything apart from Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ethnic Israel has no further place in God’s plan. It means every believer, Jew or Gentile, is a full heir.

If I am an heir, why does my life feel so poor? Because you are an heir before the reading of the will. Paul will say in the next chapter that an heir, while he is a child, may look no different from a slave (4:1). The estate is real but mostly unseen, and you are living in a world that contradicts it: illness, loss, loneliness, a body that is wearing out. That is the normal Christian condition, not a sign that you have missed out. The inheritance is kept for you, not yet handed over (1 Peter 1:4). Meanwhile you have the down payment: the Spirit himself, the guarantee of what is to come (Ephesians 1:14). Live on the deposit, and look forward to the estate.

In a sentence. If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.

On a Tuesday. Hold the tense the way Paul holds it. He does not say you may one day become an heir if things go well. He says you are, now, while the estate is entirely unseen and you are still in a life that mostly contradicts it. Everything else a person owns can be taken away by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply by time. An inheritance held in Christ has none of those exposures, because its security is not your grip on it but his. When you are tempted to envy someone else’s possessions this week, remind yourself what is already in your name.

For worship. Stand back and look at what God has done. He made a promise to one man under a night sky and swore it by himself. He kept it through four hundred and thirty years of silence and fifteen hundred more of a people who broke every term they were given. He narrowed it through Isaac and Jacob and Judah and David until it came down to one, and that one carried the curse of the broken law out of the city on his own back so that the promise could be paid to everyone who had no claim on it. Nothing was cheapened, nothing was waived, and nothing failed. The oath he swore alone in Genesis 15 he kept alone on Calvary, and it is finished, and the nations are coming in.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.<sup>2</sup>Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?<sup>3</sup>Are you so foolish?
