Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?<sup>4</sup>Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?<sup>5</sup>Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—<sup>6</sup>just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?<sup>7</sup>Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham.<sup>8</sup>And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”<sup>9</sup>So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.<sup>10</sup>For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”<sup>11</sup>Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”<sup>12</sup>But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”<sup>13</sup>Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—<sup>14</sup>so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.<sup>15</sup>To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified.<sup>16</sup>Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.<sup>17</sup>This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void.<sup>18</sup>For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.<sup>19</sup>Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.<sup>20</sup>Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.<sup>21</sup>Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law.<sup>22</sup>But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.<sup>23</sup>Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed.<sup>24</sup>So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.<sup>25</sup>But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,<sup>26</sup>for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith.<sup>27</sup>For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.<sup>28</sup>There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.<sup>29</sup>And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the emotional and theological apex of the letter’s central argument. Paul has shown that the law functions as a guardian for children; now he shows what the alternative is: full sonship, the Spirit of the Son, and the cry of “Abba! Father!” from the depths of the adopted heart. The contrast is not merely between two systems but between two existences — the existence of the slave who must perform, and the existence of the son who simply belongs.

The chapter’s opening argument (vv. 1–7) draws on the legal reality of an heir who is underage: he possesses everything but controls nothing, lives under guardians and managers until the time set by the father. Israel under the law was in this condition — heirs of the promise but living under the law’s custody until “the fullness of time.” Then God acted: he sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And confirmation: he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” — the most intimate address to God in all of Scripture, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), now placed on the lips of every adopted child of God.

The chapter then turns to a personal appeal (vv. 12–20) of remarkable emotional intensity — Paul reminding the Galatians of how they received him when he first came to them, sick and in need, and how they would have plucked out their eyes for him. His anguish over their drift is the anguish of a parent whose children are being led away: “for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!” Finally, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31) makes the theological point in narrative form: the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and only the children of the free woman — the children of promise, of grace, of the Spirit — are the true heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul illustrates with an heir who is still a child: though he owns the estate, he is no better off than a slave, living under guardians until the time his father has set. In the same way, we were enslaved to the basic principles of this world. But when the appointed time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman and born under the law, to redeem those under the law so that we might be adopted as sons. And because they are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying out “Abba! Father!” So they are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs through God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Double Sending of Son and Spirit

Verses 4–6 are among the most trinitarian sentences Paul ever wrote. The Father sends the Son; the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two missions are distinct and inseparable: the Son accomplishes redemption and adoption as objective legal realities outside us, and the Spirit applies them within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls him by name.

Adoption (huiothesia) is the doctrine this chapter states most clearly, and it goes beyond forgiveness. In Roman practice the adopted son took the father’s name, inherited on the same footing as any natural son, and, in some forms of Roman adoption, found his former obligations extinguished; the act was witnessed and irreversible, because what had changed was not his conduct but his family. Verse 7 draws the conclusion in three words — no longer, son, heir — and adds through God, so that nobody imagines an inheritance of this size arriving any other way. J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe. They had the Spirit, they had cried Abba, they were heirs. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and Paul’s answer in vv. 1–3 is to show them what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians, the managers, and a calendar. A son does not earn his way into a family he is already in.

Now:The test v. 3 suggests catches good practices rather than bad ones, and v. 6 answers the reader who does not feel like a son: the Spirit is sent because you are one, so the feeling is the consequence of the status and never the cause of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.

Meaning first. Galatians 4 continues the argument that believers are God’s free sons, not slaves under the law. First, Paul uses the picture of an heir who, while a child, is no better off than a slave, until the day his father has set. So humanity was enslaved under the elementary principles of the world until the fullness of time, when God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law and give them adoption. And because they are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying Abba, Father (vv. 1–7). Second, Paul asks how the Galatians, now known by God, can turn back to slavery by observing special days and seasons (vv. 8–11). Third, he makes a tender personal appeal: remember how you welcomed me when I was ill, as if I were Christ himself; I am in the pains of childbirth again until Christ is formed in you (vv. 12–20). Finally, he reads the story of Abraham’s two sons as a picture of two covenants: Hagar and Ishmael, slavery under Sinai; Sarah and Isaac, freedom by promise. Believers are children of the free woman, the Jerusalem above (vv. 21–31). The whole chapter is a Father bringing his children home, and a Son who paid for the house.

I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child. Chapter 3 ended with the guardian dismissed and the son given the adult garment. Now Paul takes the same picture and runs it from the other end, from inside the household. The child here is nēpios: an infant, a minor, a son not yet of legal age. And the first thing Paul says about him is shocking.

Is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything. Not different in law: in law he is the owner. Paul says it in the same breath. The deeds are in his name. The land, the house, the animals, the servants, all of it is legally his. And it makes no practical difference whatever, because he is seven. He cannot sell a field or sign a contract or give an order that anyone has to obey. He eats what he is given and goes where he is taken. Watch him through the day and you could not tell him from the boy who carries the water.

Ownership and enjoyment. That picture explains something that puzzles readers of the Old Testament. Were the believers before Christ saved? Yes: genuinely, by faith, on the same ground we are, looking forward to the Christ we look back on. Then why does the New Testament speak of their condition as bondage? Because ownership and enjoyment are two different things. They held the title deeds to promises they could not yet handle. Abraham was promised that he would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and he died having buried his wife in the only field he ever bought (Genesis 23). He owned everything and held almost nothing, and he was content to wait, because he was looking for the city whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10).

But he is under guardians and managers. Verse 2 names the arrangement. The epitropoi were guardians, the men with authority over the boy’s person: his schooling, his conduct, his whereabouts. The oikonomoi were managers or stewards, who ran the property. Both were servants. Both had more practical power over the estate than its owner did. And both held it only for a time.

Until the date set by his father. That last phrase is the one to hold on to. In the ancient world the arrangements varied: Roman law fixed some ages, provincial custom left more to the father, and a man could set the term in his will. Paul is not writing a legal treatise; he is fastening on the one feature every version had in common. The boy did not choose the day. The guardians did not choose the day. The father named it, and when it came, it came. God set the time for his people’s coming of age, and the date he wrote in the will was the coming of Christ (v. 4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Old Testament believers were unsaved, or that God loved them less. They were heirs, as truly as we are, but they lived in a time of restriction and preparation. David knew the blessedness of the man whose sin is forgiven (Romans 4:6–8). What he did not have was the full daylight: the Son come, the sacrifice finished, the Spirit poured out on all God’s people.

Is God unkind to keep anyone in that position? No more than a father is unkind to his seven-year-old. The guardians were not a punishment; they were a protection, the way a loving father secures an estate for a son too young to manage it. The law kept Israel, fenced her, taught her, and kept the line of promise intact until the Christ was born. And notice that in this picture the heir is never in danger of losing the estate. His position is restricted; his inheritance is secure. Every rule that hemmed him in was a sign that something very large had been reserved for him.

In a sentence. What Paul is saying is that as long as an heir is under age, he is no different from a slave, although he owns the whole estate. He is subject to guardians and trustees until the time set by his father.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, you are no longer a minor under supervision. You have come of age, and you are meant to live like it: not anxiously checking whether you have been good enough to stay in the house, but walking about it as a son. And take the verse personally in a second way, because a great deal of Christian frustration is about timing. Not doubt; timing. The prayer that has gone unanswered for eleven years. The change in yourself you keep asking for and keep not receiving. The season that has gone on so long you have stopped expecting it to lift. Verse 2 does not promise that the date is soon. It says there is one, that it is not arbitrary, and that it was fixed by a Father, not by the guardians who currently seem to be running your life.

What does living as a son who has come of age actually look like? It looks like freedom of access rather than a ladder of rules. A minor needs a rule for everything because he does not yet know his father’s mind; a grown son has his father’s Spirit and his father’s word, and he obeys from the inside. So you pray boldly, without first proving you deserve a hearing. You confess sin quickly, because a son does not hide from his father. You read God’s commands as the family’s way of life, not as an entrance exam. And you stop treating other believers’ consciences as your guardians: you are answerable to the Father himself.

For worship. The child in this story has no say in the calendar and no reason to be afraid of it, because the hand that wrote the date is his father’s. The God of Galatians 4 is not a landlord letting rooms to tenants on good behaviour. He is a Father who drew up the will before the child was born, set the day, kept the estate through centuries of guardians, and never once forgot the name on the deeds. Everything was always ours, because it was always his, and he had always meant to give it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.

In the same way we also, when we were children. Paul takes the picture and puts the whole human race inside it. That we is broad: he is speaking to a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, and he includes himself, the Pharisee, in the same sentence as men who grew up sacrificing to Cybele. Before Christ, Jew and Gentile alike were minors.

Were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world. The phrase is ta stoicheia tou kosmou, and it is one of the genuinely disputed phrases in Paul. It is worth being honest about that rather than pretending to a certainty that does not exist. Stoicheia means things in a row: the letters of the alphabet, and by extension the ABCs, the basic building blocks of anything, and also the basic components of the world. Some take it that way here: the elementary stage of religion, the primer, the rudiments of rules and rituals the world worked through before the Son came, and to go back to them now is to be an adult sounding out letters. Others hear something darker, since Paul says enslaved, and the word was also used of the spiritual powers thought to stand behind the elements, the heavenly bodies, the nations and their calendars (Colossians 2:8, 20). On that reading, going back to law-keeping is not merely childish; it is a return to territory that has an occupant. An older view took the word for the physical elements, earth, air, fire and water, and few now hold it.

Whichever reading. Most readers today combine the first two, and the good news is that Paul’s argument does not depend on which you choose. Whatever the stoicheia are precisely, two things about them are certain in this letter: the Gentiles were under them before they knew God (vv. 8–9), and the Judaizing programme would put the Galatians back under them. Before Christ, all humanity was in bondage to a religion of rules and powers, unable to set itself free. That is what makes verse 3 so devastating. Paul has just filed the Mosaic law and the pagan festival calendar in the same drawer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law of Moses and paganism are the same. Nothing in Paul’s writing would allow that; he will say in Romans that the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). But as ways of approaching God apart from Christ, both enslave. Paul is saying something about function, not about origin. Take any good and God-given thing, the Sabbath, the law, the sacraments, a doctrinal system, a discipline of prayer, and make it the thing that secures your standing with God, and it will do to you exactly what an idol does. It will demand, it will never say enough, and you will serve it.

Disappointment or dread. Here is a test, and it is uncomfortable because it catches good practices rather than bad ones. Take the most valued religious habit in your life: the daily reading, the giving, the fasting, the service. Now imagine dropping it for a fortnight, not through rebellion but through illness. Is what rises in you disappointment, or is it dread? Disappointment is a son who has missed his father’s company. Dread is a slave who has missed a quota. The habit is identical. The relationship is not.

So should I drop my routines if they have become a burden? No. The answer to a habit that has become a quota is not to abandon the habit but to change its ground. Keep reading your Bible, keep praying, keep gathering with the church: these are the ordinary means by which God feeds his children. What has to go is the idea that they hold up your acceptance. Before you open your Bible tomorrow, say to God plainly that you are already accepted in Christ and you have come to hear your Father, not to earn his attention. Then, on the day you miss it, do not punish yourself with extra. Come back the next morning as a son comes back to the table. The routine stays; the slavery goes.

In a sentence. So also, when we were under age, we were in slavery under the elemental spiritual forces of the world.

On a Tuesday. Notice the voice in your head on the day you fall short of your own religious standard. If it says, you have let him down, and now you must make up for it, that is the voice of the stoicheia, and it is very old. Answer it with the gospel: there is nothing to make up for, because Christ has made it up. Then do the good thing anyway, gladly, because it is good and because your Father is pleased with his children’s company.

For worship. Every master the human race has served has been weak and has wanted more: the gods of wood and stone, the stars and the seasons, the long lists of the rule-keepers. None of them ever once set a single slave free. Only one Master has ever come into the market to buy his slaves out of it, and he did not come to add a rule to the primer. He came as the Word himself, the whole alphabet of God spelled out in a human life. He is not one more element of the world. He is the one by whom the world was made, and the one in whom all its elements hold together.
verseByVerse.note: The “elementary principles” may mean the basic rules of religion, or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

But when the fullness of time had come. Two words turn the letter. Everything before has been minority, guardians, waiting, bondage; and then God moves. The phrase is to plērōma tou chronou: the moment when the vessel was full to the brim, not a minute early and not a minute late. It is the moment God had set (v. 2). It answers a question honest readers ask: why then? Why leave the world in the dark for so long, and then act in an obscure province in the reign of Augustus (Mark 1:15; Ephesians 1:10)?

Why then? Some of the answer is visible even from here. There were Roman roads, for the first time, running the length of the world, and a Roman peace that made it possible to walk them. There was one language a Galatian, a Roman and an Alexandrian could all read. There were Jewish synagogues scattered through every major city, the Scriptures in Greek, and Gentile God-fearers already attached to them, so that Paul had a hearing prepared in each town he entered. And there was a civilisation whose confidence in its own gods had quietly drained away, and a deep spiritual hunger in its place. Take one of those away and the gospel travels differently. But the deeper answer is in the sentence itself: it was the date set by his father. History was not waiting for conditions to be right. It was waiting for a Father to say now, and the conditions were the Father’s preparations.

God sent forth his Son. Every clause from here is precise. The verb is exapostellō, to send out from: from heaven, from the Father’s side. God sent forth one who was already his Son, already there to be sent. This is Christ’s pre-existence and deity in four words. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem; he came from somewhere.

Born of woman. The nearest Paul ever comes to speaking of the nativity, and the phrase is a Hebrew way of saying human, mortal, of our stock: man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble (Job 14:1). He did not appear in the world; he was carried in it, and delivered into it, and fed at a human breast. Truly human, born like any human, with every weakness of our flesh except its sin.

Did Paul know of the virgin birth? A question is often raised about this phrase, and it should be answered rather than left hanging. Paul says born of woman, not born of a virgin, and it is sometimes argued from this that he knew nothing of it. But that is more weight than the sentence will carry. Paul is not writing about how Jesus was conceived; he is writing about which side of the counter he stood on, and every clause in the verse is chosen to press him further into our situation, not out of it. If anything, his wording fits the virgin birth: born of a woman, with no human father named. And Luke, who travelled with Paul, records the annunciation in detail (Luke 1:26–38).

Born under the law. He took his place inside the very jurisdiction that had every one of us condemned. He was a Jew, circumcised on the eighth day, presented in the temple with the poor family’s offering of two birds, taken up to Jerusalem at twelve (Luke 2:21–24, 41–42), and he kept every clause of the code that was killing us. He lived under the law and kept it perfectly, for us.

Why did Jesus need to keep the law, if he was going to die for us anyway? Because we needed two things, not one. We needed our guilt taken away, and we needed a righteousness we did not have. His death bore the curse we had earned (3:13); his life of perfect obedience supplied the record we had failed to produce. Theologians call these his passive and active obedience, but the point is simple: God does not merely wipe your slate clean and leave it blank. He writes his Son’s life on it. When the Father looks at a believer, he sees thirty-three years of perfect love for God and neighbour, and credits them to you (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That is why every year of the hidden life at Nazareth was for you as much as the cross.

To redeem those who were under the law. Now the purpose, in two halves. The first is exagorasē, the slave-market word again from 3:13: to buy out and take away. He bore the curse of the law to set its prisoners free, and the price was himself.

So that we might receive adoption as sons. And then something more than release. Huiothesia means placing as a son, and it is a Roman legal term; the Roman practice is the picture. A man without a suitable heir would take a young man, often an adult, out of one family and into his own by a formal legal act before witnesses. From that day the adopted son bore the new father’s name, inherited his estate on the same footing as any natural son, and in some forms of Roman adoption his old debts and obligations were extinguished. Legally he was a new person. The transaction could not be reversed, and no later misbehaviour could undo it, because what had been altered was not his conduct but his family.

Adoption and the new birth. It is worth distinguishing two things the New Testament says about believers and their Father, because holding them together is a great strengthener of assurance. The new birth makes a person a child of God by an inward act: a nature given, a heart made alive, so that he begins to want what he never wanted (John 1:12–13). Adoption is an outward, legal act: a standing conferred, a name given, an inheritance settled, done before witnesses and entered in the record. Adoption is also a distinct blessing from justification: we are not only declared righteous in the court, we are welcomed into the family, given the Father’s name, his care, his discipline and his inheritance (Westminster 12.1). One is a change in you; the other is a change in your position, and it is done by somebody else entirely. That is why assurance is not finally a matter of examining your feelings. On a day when the inward evidence is hard to find, the outward act stands exactly where it stood, because it was never yours to perform.

More than a rescue. So notice how much more the gospel gives than most Christians expect from it. Redemption alone would have been extraordinary: the slave bought out of the market and set at liberty at the gate. But a freed slave owes his liberator everything and has nowhere to go. God did not stop at the gate. He bought the slave, cancelled the debt, gave him his own name, and walked him into the house as a son with the same inheritance as the firstborn. That is not a rescue. That is a family.

Does sons leave out daughters? No. Paul uses sons because in the ancient world it was sons who inherited, and he wants every believer to know they have the heir’s full standing. He has just said there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (3:28). So a Christian woman is a son in exactly this sense: not lesser, not a dependant on someone else’s portion, but an heir in her own right. Elsewhere the Lord says it outright: you shall be sons and daughters to me (2 Corinthians 6:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ became God’s Son at his birth. He was eternally the Son; he was sent as the Son. The Son of God became the son of Mary so that the sons of Adam could become the sons of God.

In a sentence. But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship.

On a Tuesday. If you were adopted, or have adopted, you know that the paperwork matters. There is a day when the court signs, and from that day the child’s name is changed and no one can take it back. When you are tempted to think that your standing with God rises and falls with your week, remember the day the court signed. Your adoption was settled by the Son’s blood, not by your behaviour, and the family does not revoke it. Then live in the house as the child you are: talk to your Father, ask him for things, receive his correction without fearing that it means rejection (Hebrews 12:5–11).

For worship. The eternal Son, who had the Father’s glory before the world existed, waited for the hour his Father set and then came down into a womb, into a manger, into a poor family’s offering, into the jurisdiction of a law that condemned us, and kept it, and bore its curse. He was born under the law so that we might be born into the family. He became what we were so that we might become what he is by right: sons, with the Father’s name and the Father’s house. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in love predestined us for adoption through him (Ephesians 1:3–5).

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.

And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts. Read the first four words slowly, because the order of them settles more anxious questions than almost any sentence in Paul. Not: cry Abba hard enough and you will become a son. Not: work up the feeling and God will respond to it. The sonship comes first, established by the Son’s redemption in verse 5; the Spirit is sent because of it. The felt experience is the consequence of the status, never the cause. Which means that when the feeling is absent, and for many believers it is absent for long stretches, in illness, in depression, in grief, in plain tiredness, nothing has happened to the sonship. A son asleep in his bed is as much his father’s son as a son laughing at his table.

Two sendings. Notice the shape of it. God sent his Son (v. 4); God has sent the Spirit of his Son (v. 6). The same verb, twice. Here is the Trinity at work in a single paragraph: the Father sends, the Son redeems, the Spirit indwells. The Son was sent into the world to do something for us; the Spirit is sent into our hearts to do something in us. Salvation is not a transaction between God and a stranger. It is the whole Godhead, Father, Son and Spirit, bringing a family home.

The Spirit of his Son. Paul does not say the Spirit of God, though he is; here he is named as the Son’s own Spirit, because what he brings into the believer’s heart is the Son’s relationship to the Father. He makes us share it. You are not given a new arrangement of your own. You are brought inside his.

Crying, “Abba! Father!” A word about Abba, because most readers have been told something about it that is not quite true. It is often said that Abba is baby-talk, a toddler’s Daddy. It is not, and grown men in Jesus’ day used it of their fathers all their lives. But the truth is not less moving for being accurate. Abba is the Aramaic word for father used within the family: the ordinary, warm, intimate, domestic word, not the formal word for the deity, not the reverent circumlocution of the synagogue, but the word a son would use turning round in the doorway. It is the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and it is the word the Spirit puts in your mouth. And the verb, krazō, is not a whisper. It is a loud, heartfelt cry, the cry of a child who knows he will be heard.

Who is doing the crying? Paul says here that the Spirit cries, and in Romans he says we cry, the Spirit himself bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16). Both are true, and together they are enormous comfort: the prayer of a Christian is the Spirit of God praying in him. So the man who says he cannot pray, who gets three words in and dries up, who feels nothing, who is ashamed of how thin it sounds, is describing the outside of something. The cry that reaches the Father is the Son’s Spirit, and he is not thin.

So should I call God Daddy? You may speak to him with the warmth and directness of a child, and you should. But Abba is not a licence for casualness. Jesus said Abba in the garden, his sweat falling like great drops of blood, and in the same breath he said, not what I will, but what you will. The word holds intimacy and reverence together, as a good son’s love for a good father does. So come close, come often, come without rehearsing; and remember who it is you are calling Father. The nearness is astonishing precisely because he is so great.

So you are no longer a slave, but a son. Then verse 7, and watch the pronoun change. All through the letter Paul has said you plural, to churches. Here, at the point of the conclusion, he narrows to the singular: you, one person, are no longer a slave, but a son. He wants each believer to hear it personally.

And if a son, then an heir through God. Three words in that verse are worth carrying about all week. No longer: a door has shut behind you, and slavery is now your history rather than your condition. Son: the status, given. Heir: sons inherit, and believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). And Paul adds, through God, lest anyone suppose an inheritance of this size could be got any other way. It comes by his grace, not by the law.

What exactly do I inherit? First and greatest, God himself: the LORD is my portion (Lamentations 3:24), and eternal life is to know him (John 17:3). Then everything that is Christ’s, because you are a fellow heir with him: the new heavens and new earth, the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5), an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4). You have a share of it now, in the Spirit, who is the guarantee or down payment of the rest (Ephesians 1:14). And it cannot be lost, because it is not kept by you. It is kept for you, and you are kept for it.

What if I do not feel any of this? Then you are in the company of many of God’s dearest children. The Spirit’s witness is not always a feeling of warmth. Often it is quieter: you cannot stop coming back to Christ; you hate your sin and want to be holy; when you are in trouble, the word that rises to your lips is still Father. Those are the Spirit’s work. Feelings come and go with sleep, health and circumstance; your adoption does not. Rest on the promise, keep praying the word Father even when it feels dry, and let the feeling follow when God gives it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is our Father in the same way he is Christ’s. Christ is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption and grace. Jesus kept the distinction carefully: I am ascending to my Father and your Father (John 20:17), not our Father as though the two were the same. But in Christ, we share his place, and the Father loves us with the love with which he has loved him (John 17:23).

In a sentence. Because you are his sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who calls out, “Abba, Father.” So you are no longer a slave, but God’s child; and since you are his child, God has made you also an heir.

On a Tuesday. Pray today with the confidence of a child: Abba, Father. Begin your praying with that word, and stay on it for a moment before you ask for anything. When you are anxious at work, or lying awake, say it under your breath. And when you are tempted to slink back to God like a hired servant, rehearsing why he should let you in, remember the prodigal: he had his speech ready, and his father never let him finish it (Luke 15:18–24).

For worship. Here is the whole of God in one verse: a Father who wanted sons, a Son who came to make them, a Spirit who comes to live in them and teaches them to say the family word. The Son who could say Abba by right, from all eternity, shares that word with people who had no right to it at all, and the Spirit puts it in their mouths so that their poorest prayers arrive at the throne in the accent of the Son. We were slaves; we are sons; we shall be heirs of everything, and the inheritance is God.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before they knew God, the Galatians were enslaved to beings that are not really gods. Now that they know God, or rather are known by him, how can they turn back to those weak and worthless principles and want to be enslaved again, observing special days and seasons? Paul fears his labour among them was wasted. He pleads with them to become like him, as he became like them. He recalls how they welcomed him when he first preached to them because of a bodily illness, treating him like an angel of God, even like Christ, and would have torn out their eyes for him. Has he become their enemy by telling the truth? The rivals court them for selfish ends. Paul, like a mother in labour again until Christ is formed in them, wishes he could be with them, because he is at a loss about them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Symmetry of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

Paul’s equation in vv. 8–10 of Judaizing observance with the pagan calendar the Galatians had left is about function, not moral equivalence: any God-given thing made the ground of acceptance will behave like an idol. Reformed theology has always held that moralism is not a minor error but a rival gospel that produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 also contains one of Paul’s clearest incidental statements of election, dropped in as a pastoral correction rather than a seminar topic. To be known by God is not for God to learn facts but for God to set his love on a person and claim him (Jer. 1:5). And v. 19 supplies the only metric for ministry the New Testament finally accepts: not attendance, giving or doctrinal precision, but Christ formed — morphōthē, taking shape from within, the word used of a child forming in the womb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly in vv. 14–15 and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain the mechanism. The Judaizers courted them, flattered them, and held the door a few inches short of open. Verse 20 shows what Paul wanted instead: not their allegiance to him but Christ formed in them, which is why he would rather have been in the room than winning on paper.

Now:Verse 10 raises the question every honest reader asks about Christmas, Easter and Sunday, and Paul answers it himself in Romans 14:5–6: what he attacks here is not the observance but the ground. Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy, and v. 13 belongs to the reader whose life has been rerouted by his body.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?

Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. Paul now turns the argument on the Galatians’ own past, and it is a hard turn to watch. Be clear what it describes. These were not philosophical atheists. Galatia was crowded with religion: the mother goddess with her ecstatic priests, the imperial cult with its temples in every colony town, the household shrines, the local shrines at the springs. The Galatians had been intensely religious and enslaved at the same time, which is a combination most people assume is impossible. By nature are not gods: there was nothing behind the statues (1 Corinthians 8:4–5). The whole apparatus of fear and appeasement had been built around beings who did not exist as gods, and it had still owned them.

Are idols nothing, or demons? Both, in different senses. The gods the idols represent do not exist as gods; they are by nature not gods. But Paul says elsewhere that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). Behind the empty idol stand real spiritual powers who use the worship of nothing to enslave people (compare v. 3). So an idol is a lie with a liar behind it.

But now that you have come to know God. Through the gospel, they have come to know the living God. And then Paul begins a sentence and corrects himself in the middle of it, and the correction is one of the great small moments in his letters. He stops.

Or rather to be known by God. Why the change? Because the first way of saying it puts the Galatians in the active seat and God in the passive one, as though the decisive event were their discovery. Paul cannot let that stand even for the length of a clause. Yes, they know God now; that is real, and it is the sweetest thing about them. But if you ask what actually happened, the verb belongs to God. They were known: sought, chosen and drawn, before they had turned a single thought toward him. Salvation begins with God’s initiative.

Known means loved. And known here does not mean God learned some facts about them. In Scripture, for God to know a person is for God to set his love on him and claim him: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5); you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2); the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19); if anyone loves God, he is known by God (1 Corinthians 8:3). Some read known by God as meaning only that God recognised or foresaw their faith. But that turns Paul’s correction upside down. He corrects himself on purpose: the Galatians came to know God because God first knew them. This is election, and Paul introduces it not as a seminar topic but as a pastoral correction on the way past.

Where the doctrine earns its keep. If your Christian life began with you, it can be ended by you, and every wobble is a threat to it. If it began with God knowing you, then the thing underneath your faith is not your grip. Ask the assurance question the right way round: not, do I know God well enough? Nobody does. Ask, does God know me? And the evidence that he does is that you are asking at all. Nobody who has not been sought goes looking.

How can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world. Then the wound in the sentence. Weak (asthenēs): they cannot deliver what they demand. Worthless (ptōchos): literally beggarly, poor, with nothing in the account. Going back to the law as a system of righteousness is as much slavery as going back to idols. Both are religion without Christ, and both leave a man begging from a pauper.

Whose slaves you want to be once more? Why would freed slaves want to go back? Paul will not let them describe this as being pressured. Somewhere in them, they wanted it. That is worth sitting with, because it is the strangest fact about religious bondage: a system that tells you exactly what to do and exactly where you stand is restful in a way that grace, at first, is not. Grace gives you nothing to hold. Slavery hands you a list. Israel in the wilderness, a month out of Egypt, was already remembering the cucumbers and the melons and forgetting the whips (Numbers 11:5).

Why would anyone want to go back? Because slavery feels safe and freedom feels exposed. Under a list, you always know where you stand, and you can measure yourself against other people. Under grace, you stand where Christ has put you, and you have nothing to bring and nothing to boast about. For proud hearts that is hard. It is also the only place where rest is real. If you notice in yourself a longing for a system that would tell you precisely how good you are, treat that longing as Paul treats it: not as a sign of seriousness, but as the old slave in you reaching for his chains.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law of Moses is the same as idolatry. But relying on it instead of Christ is a similar slavery.

In a sentence. Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods. But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and miserable forces? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?

On a Tuesday. When you doubt whether you are really a Christian, change the question. Stop examining the strength of your grip on God and look at his grip on you: the fact that you were found, called, brought to hear the gospel, and kept until today. Then ask what in your life is acting as a beggarly master, the thing you serve because it tells you where you stand, and bring it to Christ.

For worship. He knew us first. Before the Galatians had heard the name of Jesus, while they were still carrying offerings to statues that could not see them, the living God had set his love on them and was sending a sick missionary up the road to find them. We did not discover God; he came looking, and found us among the idols, and called us by name. The God who knows every star by name knows ours, and has written it where no beggarly power can erase it.

parallels.desc: no gods, but the work of men’s hands

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.

You observe days and months and seasons and years! There is no verb of judgement in the sentence. Paul simply reports what they are doing, and the exclamation mark carries the whole weight. He is a Jew, raised on that calendar, and he is looking at Gentile converts keeping it and he can hardly speak. The verb, paratēreō, means to watch scrupulously, to observe with anxious care.

The whole year. Four terms, and they map onto the Jewish year as a whole: the Sabbaths, the new moons, the festivals, Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, and the sabbatical years (Colossians 2:16). Not a stray superstition. The God-given calendar of the Old Testament, in the book Paul believed to be the word of God, being kept by people who wanted to please him. The Galatians were adopting the Jewish calendar as a requirement for righteousness, on the advice of men who told them their faith was insufficient without it.

The ground, not the observance. So what is Paul attacking? Not the observance in itself. The ground. The Galatians were not marking Passover in gratitude; they were taking on the calendar as the thing that would complete their standing with God. The same act can be worship or slavery depending entirely on what it is being asked to do. Writing to Rome about holy days, Paul says that one person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike, and each one should be fully convinced in his own mind, and neither is to despise the other, because both are doing it to the Lord (Romans 14:5–6). That is not the language of a man abolishing calendars. He allows both practices in the same congregation, provided neither is made a ladder to God.

Where Christians differ: holy days. Some say this verse forbids Christians from keeping any special days, including Sunday, Christmas or Easter. Others insist on strict keeping of the Jewish seventh-day Sabbath. And many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds as the Christian Sabbath, now kept on the Lord’s Day, so that Paul here condemns only the Jewish ceremonial days (Westminster 21.7–8); they are serious, godly brothers, and their reading deserves respect. Verdict: Paul condemns observing days as a requirement for being right with God, as part of the old covenant law. The Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), who is himself our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Gathering on the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is not a return to the law, but a privilege of the new covenant (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). Christians may also remember events like Christ’s birth and resurrection, as long as these are not made a means of righteousness or bound on others’ consciences.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regular worship is legalism. It means no observance can add to Christ. The early church met on the first day of the week from the beginning, and the writer to the Hebrews warns against neglecting to meet together (Hebrews 10:25).

So should I keep Sunday differently from other days? Yes, gladly, but as a gift, not a test. The Lord’s Day is the day Christ rose, and his people have gathered on it since the first Easter. Make it the day you meet with the church, hear the word, share the Lord’s Supper, and rest from ordinary work as far as your calling allows. Many find a quieter Sunday a great blessing to the soul. But do not make your way of keeping it the measure of other Christians, and do not imagine that a well-kept Sunday puts God in your debt. It is a feast with your Father, not a payment to him.

Everybody has a calendar. Which makes this verse far more searching than an argument about holy days. Sunday attendance, the daily reading before work, the annual conference, the fast in Lent, the family devotions after supper. All good. All potentially either. The test is simple enough to run this week: when you keep it, is it gratitude, and when you miss it, is the loss the fellowship you missed or the credit? A Christian who has missed church through flu and feels sorrow is worshipping. A Christian who has missed church through flu and feels exposed is observing days.

I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain. Then verse 11, and the mood drops. No thunder now. The man who has been issuing anathemas admits to being frightened. He does not say they are lost: he never does in this letter, and the restraint is deliberate. He says he is afraid, and he says it to their faces, which is a different and far more disarming thing than a warning. He has years in these towns: the stoning at Lystra, the nights teaching, the walking. He is telling them he can see all of it going.

Does Paul fear that the Galatians are lost? He fears for them; he does not pronounce on them. Some of those in the churches may never have been truly converted, and Paul knows that a church can contain both. But he writes to them as his little children (v. 19), and his fear is the anguish of a father. Warnings like this are one of the means God uses to keep his people from falling away (compare 5:4): the true child hears the warning and runs back, and in running back proves that God’s hold on him was real. Those whom God has truly known he will keep (John 10:28–29), and he keeps them partly by letters like this one.

In a sentence. You are observing special days and months and seasons and years! Paul fears for you, that somehow he has wasted his efforts on you.

On a Tuesday. Do you rely on religious routines to feel right with God? Rely on Christ alone. Pick the habit you are proudest of and, before you do it this week, thank God that you are accepted without it. Then do it as a son, for the joy of his company.

For worship. All the days and months and seasons and years of the old calendar were sketches of one Person. The Sabbath pointed to the rest he gives; the Passover to the Lamb he is; the Day of Atonement to the blood he shed once for all; the feast of Tabernacles to the day he will dwell with us for ever. When the substance has come, the shadows bow to him. Every Lord’s Day his people gather on the morning of his rising, not to earn his favour but to celebrate that the work is finished, and that the One who rested in the tomb on the Sabbath rose on the first day to make all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.

Brothers, I entreat you. The tone changes completely, and the first word is the tell: brothers, family. Then entreat, deomai, the verb for begging, the word a man uses when he has run out of arguments and is simply asking. The tone shifts from argument to pleading.

Become as I am, for I also have become as you are. The sentence is compressed to the point of obscurity, and it is often misread as a general appeal to imitate Paul’s character. It is much more specific than that, and once you see it, it is very moving. I have become as you are: Paul was a Jew of impeccable pedigree, circumcised the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). He had every marker the Judaizers were selling, and he had them by birth. And he had laid them down. He lived among Gentiles as a Gentile lived, ate at their tables, sat loose to the calendar, and refused to make his heritage the ground of anything (1 Corinthians 9:21). He had walked away from the whole apparatus of privilege and become, in the eyes of his own people, a man with no standing at all. So the appeal is: become as I am, free from the law as a way of righteousness. I gave up my law-keeping to stand where you stand, on Christ alone. Do not now take up the law-keeping I put down. Do not walk into the room I walked out of.

What it cost him. It is worth weighing that, because the appeal is only as strong as the price behind it. Writing to Philippi he made a list of everything he had laid down, the pedigree, the tribe, the blamelessness under the law, and said he counted it all as loss, as rubbish, because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). The word he used is not delicate; it is what you throw out. This was not a man with nothing to lose recommending detachment to people who had everything. He had held the whole hand the Judaizers were dealing, and he had thrown it in the fire, and he was asking the Galatians not to go scrabbling for it.

What are you holding on to? Which puts a question to anyone reading who has never had to give anything up for Christ. Not a guilty question: some believers are simply spared it. But most of us are carrying something we have never once considered laying down: a family standing, a competence we are known for, a record of respectability, a theological rigour that has become an identity. None of those is wrong to have. Every one of them is fatal to hold on to as the thing that makes you acceptable, and the way to find out which you are doing is to ask what it would take from you if it were gone.

You did me no wrong. Then a short sentence that would be easy to skip. When he was with them, they treated him well. He is answering something. Nobody says that unless the other party might think he is nursing a grievance. And the Galatians could be forgiven for wondering: he is furious in this letter, and people who are furious usually have a personal injury somewhere in it. Paul forecloses it. This is not a personal quarrel. They have not slighted him, offended him or failed him personally, and he wants that off the table so it cannot be used to explain away what he is saying.

The weapon he laid down. That is worth a moment for anyone who has to say a hard thing to someone they love. The temptation, always, is to let the personal hurt do the work, to let it be understood that you are wounded, because a wound wins arguments. Paul refuses the advantage. He wants them to have nothing to react to except the truth of the case, so he clears his own grievance out of the way first. It is one of the most self-disciplined sentences in the letter, and it costs him the easiest weapon he had.

How do I raise a hard truth without making it about me? Separate the issue from your feelings before you speak. Ask yourself honestly whether you are hurt, and if you are, deal with that before God first, so that it does not leak into the conversation. Then speak about the thing itself, the teaching, the behaviour, the danger, in plain words. Say, as Paul does, that you are not nursing a grievance, and mean it. Make clear that you love the person and want their good. And if they are hurt by what you say, do not reach for your own hurt to win the exchange. Let the truth carry its own weight.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they should copy everything about Paul, his celibacy, his trade, his travels. It means they should share his freedom in Christ.

In a sentence. Paul pleads with you, brothers and sisters: become like him, for he became like you. You did him no wrong.

On a Tuesday. Name one thing you lean on, besides Christ, for your sense of being acceptable: your reputation at church, your knowledge, your family’s standing, your track record. Do not throw away the good gift. Simply tell God that you are not standing on it, and that if he took it away you would still be his.

For worship. Paul became as the Galatians were, but he was only following his Lord a long way behind. The Son of God did not merely set aside a pedigree; he set aside the glory of heaven and became as we are, flesh and blood, under the law, numbered with the transgressors, so that we might become as he is: sons, free, beloved, heirs. He did us no wrong, and we did him every wrong, and he still came down to stand where we stood.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first. Now Paul does something that changes the temperature of the whole chapter: he takes them back to the day he arrived. Read it again, because it is easy to slide past. The gospel came to Galatia because Paul was ill. He had not planned to preach there. Something happened to his body that stopped him or diverted him, and while he was in that condition he preached, and churches were born that are still being written to. God used illness to bring Paul to them.

What was the ailment? We do not know, and the honest answer is better than a confident one. Some have suggested malaria caught in the coastal lowlands, which would drive a man up onto the Anatolian plateau where these towns are. Some suggest a disease of the eyes, on the strength of the gouged-out eyes in verse 15 and the large letters of 6:11. Others have thought of the thorn in the flesh of 2 Corinthians 12. Paul does not say, and every generation of sick Christians has been the richer for his silence, because it means no one can be told that their particular affliction is not the kind God uses.

Not the obstacle but the mechanism. What he does say is that the illness was the occasion. Not the obstacle to the mission: the mechanism of it. That is a hard providence to receive while it is happening. Nobody lying in a fever in a foreign town counting his losses is thinking about the churches that will come of it. Paul only saw it afterwards, which is how this almost always works. The pattern is everywhere in Scripture, and it is worth naming plainly for the reader whose life has been rerouted by his body: Joseph in the pit, Jeremiah in the cistern, John on Patmos, Paul in chains writing the prison letters. God’s habit of building his church out of interrupted plans is not an occasional exception. It is nearly the rule.

And though my condition was a trial to you. Then verse 14, and a detail that most translations soften. Whatever it was, it was hard to look at, and it made him hard to receive. In that culture, some saw illness as a sign of demonic attack or divine displeasure. A visibly sick preacher announcing the favour of God was an awkward package.

You did not scorn or despise me. The second verb is exeptysate, from ekptyō, and it means literally you did not spit out. In that world, when you met a person visibly diseased, you might spit, to ward off the contagion and the evil eye that was assumed to be behind it. They did not. Hold that beside 3:1, where Paul asked who had bewitched them, a word that carried the idea of the evil eye. The Galatians had once refused to treat a sick preacher as a man under a curse. Now someone has looked at them and they are enchanted. They would not spit at Paul when it would have been the normal thing to do; they will not look at his gospel now that it has become the popular thing not to. Paul is not making a debating point. He is reminding them what they used to be like.

But received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. That is the height of it. They took a sick, unimpressive, possibly repellent stranger and treated him as God’s messenger, even as though the Lord himself had come to town; and in the only sense that matters, he had. Whoever receives you receives me, Jesus said, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me (Matthew 10:40). They recognised Christ speaking through a weak man.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they worshipped Paul. At Lystra, in this very region, the crowds tried to, calling him Hermes and bringing oxen and garlands, and he tore his clothes and refused (Acts 14:11–15). It means they received his message as from Christ.

Does God really use sickness for good, or is that just something people say? He really does, though not always in ways we can see at the time, and never by making the sickness itself good. Illness is part of the curse, and Christ came to undo it. But God, who rules all things, bends even the curse to serve his children (Romans 8:28). Here the evidence is a whole province of churches. In your case it may be a doctor who hears the gospel, a nurse who watches you trust God, a friendship that would never have happened, or simply a deepening of your own faith that nothing else could have worked. You are allowed to pray for healing, and you should. You are also allowed to believe that the months you thought were wasted are not.

How should I treat a sick or weak Christian, or a weak preacher? As the Galatians first treated Paul. Do not measure a messenger by his health, polish or charm. Visit the sick, sit with the disabled, listen to the preacher who stammers, and receive Christ’s word through them. Many churches quietly honour the strong and forget the weak, and in doing so they miss the very people through whom God most often works (1 Corinthians 1:27; 12:22).

In a sentence. As you know, it was because of an illness that Paul first preached the gospel to you, and even though his illness was a trial to you, you did not treat him with contempt or scorn. Instead, you welcomed him as if he were an angel of God, as if he were Christ Jesus himself.

On a Tuesday. God can use your weakness and illness to bring the gospel to others. If your plans have been interrupted by your body, ask not only when it will end but who God has put in front of you while it lasts. And do not despise those who are sick: the next time you see someone hard to look at, remember that the Galatians once looked at Paul.

For worship. The gospel arrived in Galatia carried by a sick man, and it arrived in the world carried by a crucified one. He had no form or majesty that we should look at him, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, one from whom men hide their faces (Isaiah 53:2–3). The world spat on him, literally, and he bore it. And through his wounds the Father healed the nations. Our God has always loved to put his treasure in jars of clay, so that the surpassing power belongs to him and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?

What then has become of your blessedness? The word is makarismos, from the same root as the Beatitudes’ blessed: the state of being congratulated, the joy and happiness of people who know they have been given everything. Paul is not asking where their doctrine went. He is asking where their joy went, and he asks it as a man who remembers what they were like.

Legalism changes the atmosphere first. That is diagnostic, and it is worth pausing on. Legalism does not usually announce itself by error first. It announces itself by a change of atmosphere. The doctrine is still broadly right, the meetings still happen, the language is still Christian, and the gladness has gone out of the room, replaced by an earnest, watchful, slightly anxious carefulness that everyone mistakes for seriousness. If you want to know whether a church has drifted, do not start with its confession. Start with whether anyone in it looks relieved.

For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. They loved him so much they would have given anything. It may be a proverb for giving away what you value most, and it may be pointing at what was actually wrong with him, a hint that his ailment affected his eyes. Either way the shape is the same: there was nothing they would not have given him.

Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth? And then verse 16, one of the loneliest sentences in the New Testament. The word for telling the truth is alētheuōn: truthing, dealing truthfully. It is the same word Paul uses in Ephesians when he tells the church to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). And notice the position he is now in. He has not changed. He has said the same thing he always said. What has changed is what they are willing to hear, and the effect is that the man who loves them most is now filed as the opposition. Truth-tellers are often treated as enemies.

Reclassified by people you helped. Every pastor eventually arrives at this verse, and so does every Christian who has told a friend something true. There is a particular grief in it that is different from being disliked by strangers: it is being reclassified by people you helped. Yesterday you were the one who brought them the best news they ever had; today the same voice saying the same thing is a threat, and you can watch it happening in their faces.

Two things held together. First, the possibility that you have become the enemy is not proof that you were wrong: the whole letter assumes Paul is right and unwelcome at the same time. Second, it is not proof that you were right either. Some men are treated as enemies because they told the truth, and some because they enjoyed telling it. The test is what Paul does next: he does not withdraw, and he does not harden. He goes on writing, and within three verses he is calling them my little children and speaking of labour pains. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6), and Paul wrote his hardest letters out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears (2 Corinthians 2:4). Truth-telling that has stopped hurting the one who does it has usually stopped being love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean feelings of joy prove faith, or that a believer passing through a dark season has lost his salvation. It means joy in the gospel is lost when we drift from it, and that a settled, spreading joylessness in a church is a symptom worth investigating.

I have lost my joy. Does that mean I have drifted into legalism? Not necessarily. Joy can be dimmed by grief, illness, depression, exhaustion or long trials, and those are not sins. But it is worth asking one honest question: has my confidence before God become tied to my performance? If you find that you feel accepted only on good weeks, that is very often where the joy has leaked away. Go back to the gospel itself. Read Galatians 2:20 and Romans 8:1 slowly and believe them about yourself. Joy grows where grace is believed, not where it is merely agreed with.

What if someone treats me as an enemy for telling them the truth? Check yourself first: were you right, and were you loving? If you were harsh, apologise for the harshness without withdrawing the truth. Then keep loving them. Do not cut them off, do not gossip about them, do not harden. Keep praying for them, and keep the door open. Paul did not stop writing to the Galatians; he wrote them this letter.

In a sentence. Where, then, is your blessing of me now? Paul can testify that, if you could have done so, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to him. Has he now become your enemy by telling you the truth?

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself, or ask someone who knows you well: do I look like someone who has been forgiven everything? If the honest answer is no, do not try to manufacture cheerfulness. Go back to the cross and look at what was done for you until you are glad again. And if there is a hard truth you owe someone, say it this week, gently, and be prepared to be misunderstood.

For worship. The truest Friend who ever lived told the truth and was made an enemy for it. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him; the crowd that spread their cloaks for him on Sunday shouted for his death on Friday. And he did not withdraw, and he did not harden. He prayed for them from the cross. That is the love that restores the joy of salvation (Psalm 51:12): not a mood, but a Saviour who loved us while we counted him our enemy, and made us his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,

They make much of you, but for no good purpose. Paul now names the technique, and it is worth naming plainly, because it has never gone out of use. The verb is zēloō: to be zealous for, to court, to pay ardent attention to. It is the word for a suitor. The Judaizers were not bullying the Galatians; they were paying court to them. Flattering them. Singling them out. Making them feel that they, particularly, were worth the trouble of a long journey and a personal interest. But their motives were selfish.

They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. And then the second move, which is the whole point of the first. They wanted to exclude the Galatians from Paul and from the true fellowship, so that the Galatians would depend on them and court them in return. The courting is bait; the shutting out is the hook. Draw a person close enough to feel the warmth of belonging, then hold the door a few inches short of open, so that the belonging is always nearly his and never quite. A man treated that way will work harder and harder for the approval that is always about to be granted, and he will end up defining himself by the people withholding it.

The anatomy of manipulation. That is the pattern of spiritual manipulation, the same mechanism that runs a cult, and it does not require a heretic. It happens wherever a leader’s significance depends on being needed, and it can be entirely sincere. The signs are consistent: unusual attention early; a suggestion that you have been seen more clearly here than anywhere else; a group with an inside; a standard you are always approaching; a gentle discouragement from friendships or teaching outside the group; and a quiet impression that leaving would be a betrayal rather than a departure. If a reader recognises the pattern in a room he is currently sitting in, this verse is written for him.

It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you. Paul then does something careful in verse 18. He does not conclude that all such attention is wrong. He is not sour about affection; he has just spent four verses saying how much he enjoyed theirs. Zeal is good when it is for the right purpose. There is a zeal that is entirely healthy, and he names its two marks.

Two marks of healthy zeal. The first is purpose: for a good purpose. So the question is never whether someone is courting you. It is what they want you for. A teacher who wants Christ formed in you will be delighted when you grow past needing him, because that was the object. A teacher who wants you to make much of him will find your independence threatening, and will say so in spiritual language. The second mark is durability: not only when I am present. Attention that is switched on in the room and off outside it was never about you. The love that is worth having is the kind that keeps working when the person is far away and cannot see whether it lands, which is precisely what Paul is doing as he writes this. He is absent, unpopular, and still labouring over them. The letter in the reader’s hand is the demonstration of the standard it is setting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean warm attention from others is always manipulative, or that a church that welcomes newcomers eagerly is suspect. It means watch the motive, and watch where the attention is leading: toward Christ and the wider body of his people, or toward one leader and one group.

I think I may be in a group like this. What should I do? Start by testing it against Scripture and against wise believers outside the group. Ask: am I free to read and hear other faithful teachers? Am I encouraged to have Christian friends elsewhere? Is my standing with God tied, openly or quietly, to my loyalty here? Would leaving be treated as sin? If the answers worry you, talk to a trusted pastor or mature Christian from another church. You do not owe a group your conscience; you owe that to Christ. And if there is abuse, spiritual or otherwise, it must never be tolerated or covered: seek help, and if a crime has been committed, report it.

How do I make sure I am not the one doing this? Ask what you want from the people you help. Are you glad when they grow, find other friends and teachers, and need you less? Do you speak well of other faithful churches and leaders? Do you keep loving people who disagree with you or move on? If you are a leader, invite others to examine your influence. The aim of all ministry is that people make much of Christ, not of us (John 3:30).

In a sentence. Those people are zealous to win you over, but for no good. What they want is to alienate you from us, so that you may have zeal for them. It is fine to be zealous, provided the purpose is good, and to be so always, not just when Paul is with you.

On a Tuesday. Beware of teachers who flatter you and try to cut you off from other believers. That is a warning sign. And look at your own zeal: is there someone you have been warm to only while they were useful to you, or only in their presence? Send them a message this week that asks nothing back.

For worship. There is one who has courted us for a good purpose, and only one whose zeal for us never switches off when we are out of the room. Christ sought us when we had nothing to give him, drew us in not to keep us at the door but to bring us all the way into his Father’s house, and he does not want us to need him less as we grow. He wants us to need him more, because he is the only one whose love grows by being leaned on. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do it (Isaiah 9:7), and his zeal is for our joy in him.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.

My little children. The anger drops out of the letter completely, and what is left is a parent. The word is teknia, little children, the only time Paul uses this tender address in his letters, and it comes at the point where he has the least reason to be tender. It is a father’s, or a mother’s, love.

For whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth. Then the image, and it is startling from a man. Elsewhere he calls himself the churches’ father (1 Corinthians 4:15). Here he is their mother, and specifically a mother in labour: ōdinō, the word for birth pangs. He had gone through this once already, to bring them to birth when they were converted. Now he is going through it a second time, and anyone who has watched a birth knows that this is not a picturesque way of saying he is concerned. It is a way of saying he is being torn.

Until Christ is formed in you! Notice what he is in labour for. Not until they come back to him. Not until they see he was right, or repudiate his opponents, or apologise. Until Christ is formed in you. The verb is morphoō, to take shape, from the root that gives us transformed in Romans 12:2 and conformed to the image of his Son in Romans 8:29. It is not a word for imitation or improvement. It is the word for something taking its proper shape from the inside, and the image sits inside the birth metaphor exactly, since it suits the picture of a child taking form in the womb. Paul is saying: I am in labour, and the child in the womb is Christ taking shape in you. Not that they look like Paul, or keep the law, but that they look like Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18).

The metric of ministry. That is the goal of all Christian ministry, and it is worth measuring things by it, because almost everything else that gets measured is easier. Attendance can be measured, giving can be measured, doctrinal precision can be examined, and a congregation can be strong in every one of them while Christ is no more formed in them than he was a decade ago. Paul’s metric is brutal in its simplicity: do these people look more like Jesus than they did? A ministry that produces admirers, or partisans, or well-informed critics of other churches, has produced something, but not this.

What does Christ formed in me actually look like? It looks like the fruit Paul names in the next chapter: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (5:22–23). It looks like a growing humility that does not need to be noticed, a readiness to forgive, a love for the unlovely, courage in suffering, and a deepening delight in the Father. It does not happen by willpower. The Spirit forms Christ in us through the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church and the daily trials God sends.
